Choice guide: use this section when White avoids the main systems: each branch below gives a safe and a sharp…
notes.original: Choice guide: use this section when White avoids the main systems: each branch below gives a safe and a sharp option. Against 2.Bc4 (Hillbilly Attack) and 2.Nc3 d5 3.Qf3 the sharp refutations are important; the other sidelines are harmless if you develop and fight for the centre. Risk level: low unless you misplay the early moves. The rare second moves all give Black an easy game if the usual principle is applied: challenge the centre with ...d5 and develop.

notes.text: Part one: the main systems, with pointers only.
notes.original: Part one: the main systems, with pointers only. 2.d4 is White's main try and the backbone of this entire course. Depending on White's third move this transposes into: 3.exd5 cxd5 (Exchange Variation, 🔵 01, 02 and 🟢 01), 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 dxe4 (Classical Variation, 🔵 07 to 10, 🟢 03 and 04), 3.e5 (Advance Variation, 🔵 11 to 14 and 🟢 05 to 07), or 3.f3 (Fantasy Variation, 🔵 18 and 🟢 11). See the Course Map and Scaffolding Guide chapters for the full breakdown of which third move leads where.

notes.text: The Panov Attack is an aggressive opening choice against the Caro Kann.
notes.original: The Panov Attack is an aggressive opening choice against the Caro Kann. First of all white voluntarily creates an isolated pawn which would be a clear target for Black to take on. Second of all White is willing to create weaknesses in exchange for initiative and attack. Even a pawn sacrifice would not matter if White has enough counterplay. Black's goal is to further fortify the position. Develop the pieces with ease and is looking forward to a great game.

notes.text: 2.c4 is the Accelerated Panov Attack.
notes.original: 2.c4 is the Accelerated Panov Attack. See 🔵 06 and 🟢 02 for the full treatment. (The main, non-accelerated Panov-Botvinnik Attack, 🔵 03 to 05, arises instead after 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5, with White then playing 4.c4.)

notes.text: White is slightly better.
2.Nf3 is the Two Knights Attack.
notes.original: 2.Nf3 is the Two Knights Attack. See 🔵 15 to 17 and 🟢 08 to 10 for the full treatment (Tartakower, Karpov, Classical, Dano-Russian and ...a6 Variations, and rare third-move tries). No new content here.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Part two: sidelines covered elsewhere, in short form, each with its home chapter.
notes.original: Part two: sidelines covered elsewhere, in short form, each with its home chapter. 2.Nc3 d5 mostly just transposes (3.d4 = main systems above, 3.Nf3 = Two Knights Attack above), but White also has two odd early queen sorties here, both already fully annotated in 🔵 19, recovered condensed below.

notes.text: Plan: ...d5 and ...e5
2.d3 is a quiet, positional way to meet the Caro-Kann.
notes.original: 2.d3 is a quiet, positional way to meet the Caro-Kann. White is not after a quick attack. It is probably not his strongest try, but it keeps the game calm.

notes.text: White delays d4 entirely and aims for a King's Indian Attack style setup with Nd2, g3, Bg2 and O-O, keeping…
notes.original: White delays d4 entirely and aims for a King's Indian Attack style setup with Nd2, g3, Bg2 and O-O, keeping the center flexible rather than committing to a specific pawn structure right away. Black's plan: this system lives or dies on Black's central response. Grabbing full central space immediately with ...e5 (rather than waiting) is the single most important practical lesson here - it denies White any chance of a favorable King's Indian Attack-style kingside buildup and leaves Black with at least equal, often slightly better, chances with completely natural development.

notes.text: 2.d3 Systems.
notes.original: 2.d3 Systems. See 🔵 19 and 20 for the full treatment (Breyer Variation and the King's Indian Attack & Leela Setup). That same 🔵 19 also contains White's odd 3.Qf3/3.Qe2 queen sorties after 2.Nc3 and the Hillbilly Attack/Gambit after 2.Bc4, both recovered in condensed form below.

notes.text: Another variation in this particular opening is the move Bc4 the Hillbilly Attack.
notes.original: Another variation in this particular opening is the move Bc4 the Hillbilly Attack. This move is complete nonsense against the Caro Kann but it is indeed playable. Its nonsense because after the move d4 the bishop on c4 fails to stop the d5 breakthrough and at the same time once the d5 pawn has been played. The bishop has to reroute back to either e2 or b3.

notes.text: 2.Bc4, the "Hillbilly Attack".
notes.original: 2.Bc4, the "Hillbilly Attack". Active-looking but the bishop just gets kicked by ...d5 with tempo. Full treatment (including the "Hillbilly Gambit" 3.Bb3!?) in 🔵 19.

notes.text: 2.b3, a quiet Nimzowitsch-style fianchetto try.
notes.original: 2.b3, a quiet Nimzowitsch-style fianchetto try. Harmless: just develop normally. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.f4, the "La Bourdonnais Attack".
notes.original: 2.f4, the "La Bourdonnais Attack". An old, aggressive-looking try that overextends more than it threatens. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.g3, a fianchetto try that develops quietly rather than fighting for the center with d4.
notes.original: 2.g3, a fianchetto try that develops quietly rather than fighting for the center with d4. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.Ne2, keeps options open (the knight can go to g3 or later support a d4 push).
notes.original: 2.Ne2, keeps options open (the knight can go to g3 or later support a d4 push). Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.c3, a kind of reversed Alapin idea, preparing d4 with extra support.
notes.original: 2.c3, a kind of reversed Alapin idea, preparing d4 with extra support. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.e5?!, premature; the pawn gets no real support and Black challenges it at once.
notes.original: 2.e5?!, premature; the pawn gets no real support and Black challenges it at once. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.Qf3?!, an eccentric try, developing the queen far too early for no real gain.
notes.original: 2.Qf3?!, an eccentric try, developing the queen far too early for no real gain. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: 2.Be2, a quiet developing move that keeps options open.
notes.original: 2.Be2, a quiet developing move that keeps options open. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: Part three: other second moves.
notes.original: Part three: other second moves. These ten moves (2.g4, 2.h4, 2.b4, 2.f3, 2.a3, 2.h3, 2.Na3, 2.Nh3, 2.Qh5, 2.Qg4) do not appear anywhere else in this 64-chapter course - this is the first time they have been checked and written up. 2.g4!?, a flank lunge that weakens the kingside for no real gain. Black just takes the center.

notes.text: 2.h4, a flank expansion with no real point yet, since there's nothing on the kingside to attack.
2.b4!?, a wing-gambit-style try, grabbing queenside space instead of fighting for the center.
2.f3, supports a later e4/d4 setup but blocks White's own king's knight from its natural square and loses time.
2.a3, a pure waiting move with no point at all against the Caro-Kann.
notes.original: 2.a3, a pure waiting move with no point at all against the Caro-Kann. Just develop normally.

notes.text: 2.h3, another pure waiting move, slightly more useful than 2.a3 since it at least prevents a future ...Bg4 pin, but…
notes.original: 2.h3, another pure waiting move, slightly more useful than 2.a3 since it at least prevents a future ...Bg4 pin, but still no real try.

notes.text: 2.Na3, an odd rim development with no clear follow-up, the knight will likely need to re-route via c4 or c2…
notes.original: 2.Na3, an odd rim development with no clear follow-up, the knight will likely need to re-route via c4 or c2 later.

notes.text: 2.Nh3, develops to the rim instead of the natural f3/e2 squares, blocking the kingside pawns and achieving little.
2.Qh5?!, a very premature queen sortie with no target, Black's center play comes with tempo on the misplaced queen.
2.Qg4?!, another premature queen sortie, this time eyeing the kingside with nothing to actually attack yet.
This is the Exchange Variation (the ECK, or Exchanged Caro-Kann).
The core of the Caro-Kann argument lies here.
notes.original: The core of the Caro-Kann argument lies here. In this semi-open game, minor piece play tends to dominate certain lines. White may handle the resulting tension.

notes.text: The main Exchange Variation position.
notes.original: The main Exchange Variation position. See 🔵 01. Everything in this chapter has been a detour around this single, reliable backbone move: whatever White tries on move two, ...d5 (or the matching central break for that specific try) gets Black to a comfortable, well-understood structure.

notes.text: The Exchange Variation removes most of the theory and gives White a simple, safe structure, close to an improvised London…
notes.original: The Exchange Variation removes most of the theory and gives White a simple, safe structure, close to an improvised London System with Black's c-pawn traded off. Black's practical task is to avoid a passive position. This chapter uses the Grunfeld-style setup, which aims at the kingside and the centre at the same time and keeps queenside play optional. The quieter ...e6 route is about as good objectively, so the choice is about structure and playability, not objective strength.

notes.text: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White: development comes easily, and the same formation turns up against the…
notes.original: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White: development comes easily, and the same formation turns up against the Sicilian, the Philidor and the French as well. Black usually answers with the solid 3...dxe4, among the most heavily analysed Caro-Kann lines. Sidesteps exist, but 3...e6 blocks the c8-bishop and amounts to a French a tempo down, which makes it a dubious choice.

notes.text: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White: development comes easily, and the same formation turns up against the…
notes.original: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White: development comes easily, and the same formation turns up against the Sicilian, the Philidor and the French as well.

notes.text: Black usually answers with the solid 3...dxe4, among the most heavily analysed Caro-Kann lines.
notes.original: Black usually answers with the solid 3...dxe4, among the most heavily analysed Caro-Kann lines. Sidesteps exist, but 3...e6 blocks the c8-bishop and amounts to a French a tempo down, which makes it a dubious choice.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Part three (continued): gambits inside the Classical Variation.
notes.original: Part three (continued): gambits inside the Classical Variation. The normal replies here, 3.exd5 (Exchange, 🔵 01) and 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 dxe4 (Classical Variation, 🔵 07 to 10, 🟢 03 and 04), are both covered in full elsewhere. Nested a little deeper inside that same Classical tree, though, are three named gambits/sidelines that do not appear anywhere in those chapters or in the rest of this 64-chapter course. Recovered here for completeness.

notes.text: The Advance Variation is one of the most challenging tries against the Caro-Kann.
notes.original: The Advance Variation is one of the most challenging tries against the Caro-Kann. White gains space and has kingside attacking chances, much as in the French Defence. The principled, classical way to meet it is recommended here: Black makes full use of the bishop on f5 and gets strong queenside counterplay. In the French that same bishop is often the problem piece, and Black may even have to double the b-pawns just to trade it for a White bishop or knight; in the Caro-Kann Black avoids that fate because the bishop is developed before ...e6.

notes.text: This is the Fantasy Variation of the Caro Kann.
notes.original: This is the Fantasy Variation of the Caro Kann. The Fantasy Variation of the Caro Kann is an aggressive opening choice against the Caro Kann. White actually wants a fantasy land where he has an open f file for his rook to take advantage of. Second to that white wants to get a fortified center following a principled development on the center. So far white just wants an easy play against black but at the same time get the initiative and advantage.

notes.text: The Modern Variation is played for exactly this one reason: to avoid the Gurgenidze system.
notes.original: The Modern Variation is played for exactly this one reason: to avoid the Gurgenidze system. Now White has still the option to play c3, and then a bishop on g7 wouldn't be very effective. With the Nd2 move order. Black is free to take the pawn and play something like Bf5 or Nf6, Nd7 or even h6! Which brings us back to the Classical Caro Kann.

notes.text: The quieter move order; the Alien Gambit below is normally reached this way rather than via 3.Nc3.
Avoid.
notes.original: Avoid. Recapture with the pawn. The queen comes out early and White gains time with 4.Nc3.

notes.text: Avoid.
notes.original: Avoid. Without recapturing, Black falls a pawn behind after 4.dxc6, and the development it gets back does not fully make up for it.

notes.text: White's most flexible development.
notes.original: White's most flexible development. From here Black fights for the f4 and f5 squares and looks to neutralise White's bishop pair.

notes.text: Many experienced Exchange Variation players choose Bd3 to take a key square away from Black.
notes.original: Many experienced Exchange Variation players choose Bd3 to take a key square away from Black. Contesting the f4 square at once and neutralising White's bishop pair is the right response.

notes.text: 4.Bf4 - develops actively onto the long diagonal, delaying the usual Nc3/Bd3 setups.
4.c3 - a quiet supporting move, preparing Bd3 and keeping d4 well defended before developing the pieces.
The Panov-Botvinnik Attack.
notes.original: The Panov-Botvinnik Attack. After the pawn exchanges White is left with an isolated d-pawn and accepts that weakness in return for open lines, piece activity and attacking chances. Black's task is to blockade, trade pieces and keep the structure healthy.

notes.text: An odd move against the London structure, but White is still going for the e4-e5 idea.
Thus, many players would play something like Nf3 sticking to their e4 e5 principle.
Choice guide: choose this if you want to meet 4.Bd3 with 4...Nf6 and keep your structure flexible with an early…
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want to meet 4.Bd3 with 4...Nf6 and keep your structure flexible with an early ...e5 break (more active and more varied than the quiet Rubinstein-style play elsewhere in these chapters). Risk level: medium. For a calm, structure-based game stay with 🔵 01 and 02. After 4.Bd3 Nf6 White has 5.h3, 5.Bf4 and 5.c3 as the main tries.

notes.text: Plan: ...g6 and ...Bg7
Watch out: ...Nxd4? drops a piece on moves 5 to 9.
White supports d4.
notes.original: White supports d4. Black has two sound moves here: 5...Nf6 (main line) and 5...Qc7.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Fully playable.
notes.original: Fully playable. The queen covers f4, so White's dark-squared bishop has fewer good squares. Black answers the most accurate 6.h3 with ...e6, ...Bd6 and ...Nge7.

notes.text: Never take on d4 with the knight.
notes.original: Never take on d4 with the knight. White recaptures and wins a piece for a pawn. The same capture fails on moves 6 to 9, whichever White piece recaptures.

notes.text: The main move.
notes.original: The main move. White develops the bishop before playing e3 or Nf3 and keeps control of e5 and the f4 square.

notes.text: A move-order point worth knowing: rather than develop the bishop right away, White rules out ...Bg4 for good first.
notes.original: A move-order point worth knowing: rather than develop the bishop right away, White rules out ...Bg4 for good first. Playing Bf4 a tempo later is not weaker in itself. See the note after 7.h3 below for why this move order is the one Black players find hardest to meet.

notes.text: A third move order: develop the knight first and meet ...Bg4 with h3 only once Black actually plays it, rather…
notes.original: A third move order: develop the knight first and meet ...Bg4 with h3 only once Black actually plays it, rather than inserting the prophylactic pawn move unprompted.

notes.text: Idea: Against White's quiet 4.Bd3 and 5.c3, fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, then offer to trade the light-squared bishops with…
notes.original:
Idea: Against White's quiet 4.Bd3 and 5.c3, fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, then offer to trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bf5. The structure is symmetrical, so the game turns on the pieces: aim for a knight on e4 and play on the queenside.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 g6
Watch out: ...Nxd4? drops a piece on moves 5 to 9, and ...Nxc3? or ...Nxf2? do the same later. Recapture on d5 with the pawn, and at move 10 take back with ...gxf5.
Next: 🔵 02 continues the Exchange Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11. Model game: 🟡 Game 15.

notes.text: Black aims for a Grunfeld-style structure.
notes.original: Black aims for a Grunfeld-style structure. The bishop on g7 pressures d4, and Black can play on the kingside and in the centre, not only on the queenside. This is about as good as the quieter 6...e6, and 6...Bg4 is slightly better still, so 6...g6 is chosen for its structure and playability.

notes.text: A surprising choice against a White player who has settled for the London-style setup.
notes.original: A surprising choice against a White player who has settled for the London-style setup. The knight heads to e4 to use that square, centralise itself and block the d3 bishop's diagonal. From there Nd6 and ...Bf5 become possible, so Black can offer to trade off White's strong light-squared bishop.

notes.text: This is the move order that actually gives Black the hardest practical choice in the whole Bf4 plan - and…
notes.original: This is the move order that actually gives Black the hardest practical choice in the whole Bf4 plan - and it is the reason some players find Bf4 so awkward to meet, rather than Bf4 itself being a poor idea. With ...Bg4 ruled out for good, White is a free tempo ahead of the main line below for the same eventual kingside expansion, and the question becomes which of Black's two main replies absorbs that extra tempo best.

notes.text: Black provokes the trade on f5.
notes.original: Black provokes the trade on f5. It costs a little compared with the best moves 9...Bg4, 9...Qb6 and 9...Nh5, but it leads to clear, well-understood positions.

notes.text: One of the best moves here.
notes.original: One of the best moves here. It attacks the bishop on f4.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's best and the critical test.
notes.original: White's best and the critical test. Black recaptures with the g-pawn.

notes.text: White keeps the bishop pair but loses time.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop pair but loses time. Black gets easy development.

notes.text: This pin merely loses a tempo, since White must either trade off the bishop pair or pull the bishop back.
notes.original: This pin merely loses a tempo, since White must either trade off the bishop pair or pull the bishop back. It is the line recommended by WGM Sopiko Guramishvili.

notes.text: White's knight jump.
notes.original: White's knight jump. Black takes it.

notes.text: It avoids the trade on f5, but Black gets an easy game.
The queen gets in the way of the rook.
Black gives up the light-squared bishop and doubles the f-pawns, but the pawns control e4 and g4 and the open…
notes.original: Black gives up the light-squared bishop and doubles the f-pawns, but the pawns control e4 and g4 and the open g-file gives Black kingside play. Mueller-Kieninger, Beverwijk 1965, was drawn: Black kept the position solid and White could not make progress.

notes.text: White's best.
notes.original: White's best. The knight takes the e5 square and prepares to trade on c6.

notes.text: The main line.
notes.original: The main line. It is a little more accurate than 11...Nxe5 and clearly better than 11...Qb6 and 11...Kh8 below. Black keeps the knight on c6 for the moment and meets 12.Nxc6 with ...bxc6, taking doubled c-pawns in return for the open b-file and the bishop pair. White has a wide menu of tries here: 12.Nxc6, 12.Ndf3, 12.Re1, 12.Nd3, 12.Bg5 and 12.Qe2 are all close together, plus the weaker 12.Qf3!? and 12.f3?!, but none of them change the picture much. White keeps a small edge here, which is normal for this chapter.

notes.text: Playable and close to 11...e6, so treat 11...e6 above as the main recommendation and this as a sound backup.
Slightly inaccurate.
notes.original: Slightly inaccurate. White keeps a slightly bigger edge than after 11...Nxe5 or 11...e6.

notes.text: A natural waiting move, but it does not deal with the knight on e5, so it is a little worse…
notes.original: A natural waiting move, but it does not deal with the knight on e5, so it is a little worse than 11...e6 or 11...Nxe5.

notes.text: White's most testing try here, slightly stronger than 12.Nxc6.
notes.original: White's most testing try here, slightly stronger than 12.Nxc6. Black meets it comfortably with either knight move or the queenside break.

notes.text: Pins the knight instead of trading it off on c6.
A flexible developing move that keeps every recapture option open.
Playable, but not White's most testing try.
A real inaccuracy: it loosens e3 and g3 for no gain, and Black's reply hits the bishop at once.
Black starts a kingside build-up instead of a passive defence.
The most-played reply in practice, but looser: it trades off Black's strong e4 knight for White's less active one and…
notes.original: The most-played reply in practice, but looser: it trades off Black's strong e4 knight for White's less active one and costs a little compared with retreating.

notes.text: Black slowly reinforces the kingside pieces to provoke weaknesses.
The position is equal.
0-1 (35) Doyle-Rosenlund, Haifa 1976.
White's rook trade leaves your pawn on g4.
notes.original: White's rook trade leaves your pawn on g4. You now play on the h-file with the queen and your rook, and White's king remains uncomfortable.

notes.text: White could have grabbed the a7 pawn first and returned to defend.
notes.original: White could have grabbed the a7 pawn first and returned to defend. Black has no way in.

notes.text: The pawn hits the rook on g2 and forces White to retreat.
You switch the rook to the queenside and push c5-c4, but White shuffles and finds no way in for either…
notes.original: You switch the rook to the queenside and push c5-c4, but White shuffles and finds no way in for either side, so expect equality.

notes.text: White has used the open queenside lines to fix your structure.
notes.original: White has used the open queenside lines to fix your structure. After the exchange, the Bd6 jump is annoying, but ...Rfb8 targets b4 and you have a sound game.

notes.text: White offers the queen trade to head for a rook ending where the b-pawn is a nuisance.
notes.original: White offers the queen trade to head for a rook ending where the b-pawn is a nuisance. Your c4 and d5 pawns are strong and you have enough counterplay.

notes.text: Your knight on e4 attacks the bishop on g5, so it has to retreat.
notes.original: Your knight on e4 attacks the bishop on g5, so it has to retreat. White's plan is Ng3 to challenge the e4 knight and then Nh5 to trade off your g7 bishop and leave the dark squares thin.

notes.text: Kh8 and Rg8 cover g7, so Nh5 only wins a trade of minor pieces.
notes.original: Kh8 and Rg8 cover g7, so Nh5 only wins a trade of minor pieces. When the bishop comes to h6 you just step the rook aside; White keeps a small edge but has no real target.

notes.text: White goes for g7 at once, but ...Nf6 and ...Bxh6 trade off the attackers.
The pawn on a4 fixes b2 and cuts down the knight.
notes.original: The pawn on a4 fixes b2 and cuts down the knight. You regroup with Ne7-g6 and Ne4. White's knight on e5 is annoying but not decisive.

notes.text: Step off the g-file so that ...Rg8 and ...Ng6 can follow and challenge the e5 knight.
notes.original: Step off the g-file so that ...Rg8 and ...Ng6 can follow and challenge the e5 knight. White's bishop on g5 and both knights are aimed at your kingside, so you want to trade pieces.

notes.text: Once you have traded a knight White keeps only a small edge.
A calmer set-up that offers the bishop trade on f6.
Your knight challenges the Ne5, so White retreats it.
notes.original: Your knight challenges the Ne5, so White retreats it. Then Ng4 trades off the dark-squared bishop and Bf8 covers the dark squares. White has a small edge, but your pieces are placed sensibly.

notes.text: You trade White's best minor piece, then support the e5 square with ...f6.
notes.original: You trade White's best minor piece, then support the e5 square with ...f6. The Bd6 looks strong but Rf7 and Qb6 deal with it. White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: The point: the bishop on f4 has to move, and Black seizes the initiative.
Take at once: White's f3 pawn has taken the best square from its own knight, so trading the bishop leaves…
notes.original: Take at once: White's f3 pawn has taken the best square from its own knight, so trading the bishop leaves White's pieces badly coordinated.

notes.text: ...e5 hits d4 and opens the diagonal for your g7 bishop.
Your pieces swarm around d4, e5 and b2 while White's king is stuck behind its own pawns.
The quiet ...Re8 lets White keep the bishop, and the loose knight on h5 becomes a target.
Also strong, about as good as 12.Bxe5, but it trades the solid d4 point for a pawn on e5 that…
notes.original: Also strong, about as good as 12.Bxe5, but it trades the solid d4 point for a pawn on e5 that needs long-term support, instead of keeping the bishop actively posted there. 12.Bxe5 stays the simpler recommendation.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
Black's structure is solid.
notes.original: Black's structure is solid. Typical Black plans: ...Kh8 and ...Rg8 to use the g-file, ...Ne4 and ...f6 to challenge the bishop on e5, and ...a5 to gain queenside space. Typical White plans: keep the bishop on e5 or f4, bring the knight to f3 and expand with a4-a5.

notes.text: A useful waiting move that prepares ...Rg8 and a direct kingside plan.
notes.original: A useful waiting move that prepares ...Rg8 and a direct kingside plan. It is as good as 12...e6.

notes.text: White's best.
notes.original: White's best. 13.Nb3, 13.Bf4 and 13.Qe2 are about as good. Black is solid and White's edge is the better structure, not an attack.

notes.text: Natural, but not White's most accurate move.
Black offers the trade of White's strong bishop.
White keeps the bishop.
Black gains queenside space and prepares ...f6.
Do not grab material on c3 or f2.
notes.original: Do not grab material on c3 or f2. White recaptures and Black has lost a piece for a pawn. The knight on e4 is a strength, not a target.

notes.text: A typical setup.
notes.original: A typical setup. Black has no weaknesses, and White keeps a small edge. The bishop on f4 has to guard e5, and the doubled f-pawns cover e4 and g4.

notes.text: White steers the knight to d3 so that e5 and f4 are covered.
Do not wait: ...e5 hits the Bf4 and the d4 pawn and activates your bishop.
White opens lines against your king with Qh5 and f4, but ...exd4 and then ...Rb8 give you counterplay on the…
notes.original: White opens lines against your king with Qh5 and f4, but ...exd4 and then ...Rb8 give you counterplay on the b-file. White keeps a small initiative.

notes.text: White is winning.
You are a piece down for a pawn, since the knight on c3 was lost.
notes.original: You are a piece down for a pawn, since the knight on c3 was lost. White consolidates with Re1 and g3 and keeps trading, because your doubled f-pawns and king are not worth the piece.

notes.text: You can pile up on the g-file, but White covers everything.
This trades White's good bishop for a knight and gives up part of the edge.
Loses most of the remaining edge.
White now has only two good moves, 18.g3 and 18.Qh3.

notes.original: The key practical improvement for this exact move order: rather than the immediate 9...Bf5 trade (see the note just below), Black first prepares a central break with ...e5. Once White has already spent a tempo on h3, trading light-squared bishops hands White an extra supporting move for a later g4 push (compare the 9...Bf5 note), so meeting it with the central break instead is the cleaner practical answer - the actual reason 6.Bf4 can feel notoriously awkward to handle well against this exact move order if Black insists on the normal trading plan regardless.

notes.original: Black is doing fine here too with precise play, but it is a sharper, more demanding version of the normal structure than the central-break plan below, exactly because the h3 insertion gives White's pawn storm extra teeth.

notes.text: Put the rook against the c5 outpost.
White's trumps are the c5 knight, the rook on g1 and the knight on h4 pointed at f5; you must…
notes.original: White's trumps are the c5 knight, the rook on g1 and the knight on h4 pointed at f5; you must trade pieces and challenge with ...Ng6.

notes.text: This is worse: White gets his bishop to e5 and attacks.
White plays g4 to break your doubled f-pawns; you trade the dark-squared bishops and bring the knight to e7 and…
notes.original: White plays g4 to break your doubled f-pawns; you trade the dark-squared bishops and bring the knight to e7 and g6.

notes.text: Strikes back at the overextended pawn at once, the standard response to a flank pawn storm, and already starts to…
notes.original: Strikes back at the overextended pawn at once, the standard response to a flank pawn storm, and already starts to turn the position in Black's favour.

notes.text: Keeps the kingside closed, but hands Black a completely free hand in the centre instead.
Black's pieces are far more active than White's, and the king has nowhere comfortable to go - a direct demonstration…
notes.original: Black's pieces are far more active than White's, and the king has nowhere comfortable to go - a direct demonstration of why 7.g4 is more risk than reward even with h3 already supporting it.

notes.text: Nb5 attacks your queen and c7, but gets nothing.
White cannot castle, the bishop on e2 is pinned by your rook, and your pieces swarm in.
notes.original: White cannot castle, the bishop on e2 is pinned by your rook, and your pieces swarm in. You are winning.

notes.text: Trying to hit first with Ne5 loses material.
Black has an easy, comfortable game and in fact a clear edge; the g5-pawn is more of a long-term weakness…
notes.original: Black has an easy, comfortable game and in fact a clear edge; the g5-pawn is more of a long-term weakness than a real space gain here.

notes.text: This central break is stronger than comfort: the pawn hits c3 and e3, and opens lines for the bishop on…
notes.original: This central break is stronger than comfort: the pawn hits c3 and e3, and opens lines for the bishop on e5 and the knights.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen with tempo and the centre pawns are gone, so you keep a lasting edge.
This gets activity but is less accurate than ...d4.
You exchange or harass White's strongest bishop and keep the long diagonal b1-h7 under control.
notes.original: You exchange or harass White's strongest bishop and keep the long diagonal b1-h7 under control. The point of the move is to meet Bb5 with ...Bg7 and keep the bishop pair safe. Plan: ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...Qc7 to pressure c3 and ...a6 to gain space on the queenside. Avoid passive moves like ...Qc7 first, because White can then play Ne5 with tempo.

notes.text: The c6 knight is pinned slightly but you finish development.
Time to ask the bishop on b5 a question; it retreats and you have gained space.
The structure is equal, and White has a small initiative that you can neutralise by exchanging pieces on the light…
notes.original: The structure is equal, and White has a small initiative that you can neutralise by exchanging pieces on the light squares and playing ...e6. This is a symmetrical pawn structure with White having played h3 and Bd3, so the centre is fairly closed and neither side has a big space advantage. Both kings will go short. Your plan: finish development with ...Bg7, castle, then challenge the c6 pin with ...a6, followed by ...Bf5 or ...Rd8 and ...e6 to trade light-squared pieces. White wants to play Ne5 or Bf1, and tries to build a small initiative using the e-file. You meet it by trading pieces. The risk is allowing Ne5 with tempo, and dropping a pawn on d5. If White deviates with Qb3 or Ne5, keep your pieces coordinated and trade when you can.

notes.text: The pin on the knight keeps d4 under pressure.
The idea behind ...Ne4 is to bring the knight to d6; ...Bg4 and further development can follow.
White finishes development and puts the king away before the pin on f3 starts to matter.
notes.original: White finishes development and puts the king away before the pin on f3 starts to matter. It is a very common move in practice (played in about 1.2 million games), so you will meet it often. It carries no direct threat; White wants a calm position with the bishop on d3 aimed at your kingside and the possibility of Re1 and Bf4 later.

notes.text: Retreating to h5 keeps the pin on Nf3 and avoids an early trade.
Transposes back toward the normal Exchange Variation structures covered throughout this chapter; nothing about this particular move order changes Black's…
notes.original: Transposes back toward the normal Exchange Variation structures covered throughout this chapter; nothing about this particular move order changes Black's basic plan of trading down the dark-squared pieces and racing for the standard breaks.

notes.text: The knight is excellent here: it is supported by d5 and forces White to decide the fate of the bishop…
notes.original: The knight is excellent here: it is supported by d5 and forces White to decide the fate of the bishop on f4. If White plays 10.Qb3 you reply ...Bd6, offering a trade of the dark-squared bishops. After 11.Bxd6 you recapture with the queen and your d5 pawn is well defended. The game is level with a very solid position for Black.

notes.text: You swap the dark bishops and then offer the light-bishop trade to avoid a cramped game.
notes.original: You swap the dark bishops and then offer the light-bishop trade to avoid a cramped game. White's Qb1 is lined up behind the d3 bishop, but your bishop on g6 trades it off.

notes.text: The queen steps to c7 so that it looks at h2 once the f3 knight moves, and it frees d8…
notes.original: The queen steps to c7 so that it looks at h2 once the f3 knight moves, and it frees d8 for a rook. It also keeps your d5 pawn well supported without committing the e-pawn yet. Your plan is to answer h3 with ...Bh5, bring the rook to d8 or c8, play ...e6 and then ...Bd6 to swap off White's good bishop, and castle short. Avoid ...e5 too early: after dxe5 your pieces lose their coordination and White's bishops come alive.

notes.text: White gives the bishop on h5 nothing to attack but weakens the dark squares around h3 and f3, so do…
notes.original: White gives the bishop on h5 nothing to attack but weakens the dark squares around h3 and f3, so do not hurry to take on f3. Keep the pin and look for activity.

notes.text: The knight uses the e4 outpost, eyes g3 and c3, and prepares to challenge the bishop on d3.
The queen leaves the diagonal of the bishop on f4 and keeps an eye on the kingside, while the knight…
notes.original: The queen leaves the diagonal of the bishop on f4 and keeps an eye on the kingside, while the knight stays strong on e4.

notes.text: After White breaks in the centre, you retreat and keep everything protected.
notes.original: After White breaks in the centre, you retreat and keep everything protected. You are fine and equal here, and your simple plan of ...e6, ...Bd6 and short castling gives a solid, comfortable game.

notes.text: This is a symmetrical Exchange structure with a closed-ish centre: White's pawn on d4 faces your pawn on d5, and…
notes.original: This is a symmetrical Exchange structure with a closed-ish centre: White's pawn on d4 faces your pawn on d5, and neither side has a clear space edge. Both kings will most likely castle short. Your plan: first play ...e6 to give the queen's bishop a home and free the f8 bishop, then ...Bd6 to trade off the active white bishop on f4, then castle and put a rook on e8. White wants to break with c4 or push the e-pawn for a kingside attack, and you meet c4 by recapturing calmly with the knight on f6. The risk is a hasty ...Bxf3 or ...Nxd4 that loses time. If White deviates, keep developing.

notes.text: White's most accurate move.
Less accurate but common.
notes.original: Less accurate but common. Black develops the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6.

notes.text: A solid, weakness-free position.
notes.original: A solid, weakness-free position. White keeps a slight, easily managed edge.

notes.text: Your rook supports the d5 pawn and the e5 break before White can aim at it.
A useful prophylactic move: White's knight wants Nb5 hitting the queen, and ...a6 takes that square away.
White is rerouting the knight via c2 and e3 to pile up on d5 and aim for c4.
notes.original: White is rerouting the knight via c2 and e3 to pile up on d5 and aim for c4. Your pieces cover d5 and the f6/f7 setup keeps everything protected.

notes.text: 7...Bh5 is the most accurate.
notes.original: 7...Bh5 is the most accurate. 7...Bxe2 sets a trap, but only if White recaptures the wrong way.

notes.text: White's most testing move: the queen heads for h4 or g3.
notes.original: White's most testing move: the queen heads for h4 or g3. Black continues with ...Nf6, ...h6 and ...Bd6 and equalises.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White has at most a tiny edge, within normal opening imprecision.
notes.original: White has at most a tiny edge, within normal opening imprecision. Black is comfortable.

notes.text: White trades off your good bishop so that f3 can kick the Bg4 and the knight can reroute to c2…
notes.original: White trades off your good bishop so that f3 can kick the Bg4 and the knight can reroute to c2 and e3. Do not worry: the edge is tiny.

notes.text: If White ever plays g4 here, ...Bg6 trades the light bishops and the pawn advance has only loosened White's king.
Your central break ...e5 is the equaliser: it opens the e-file in front of the white queen and leaves White…
notes.original: Your central break ...e5 is the equaliser: it opens the e-file in front of the white queen and leaves White with no real target.

notes.text: Black takes the initiative.
The light-squared bishop has escaped the pawn chain, so White has no pressure.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop has escaped the pawn chain, so White has no pressure. Black is slightly better.

notes.text: White wants to harass your bishop with g3 and Nh4 and so free the bishop on d3.
Your answer is to attack the knight and keep the bishop alive.
You get the bishop pair for a knight and slightly better chances.
White swaps off the bishop, but you keep the better structure
The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
White unpins the Ne2 and gets ready for Bf4 hitting your queen, so the bishop on h5 must decide.
Your queen hits b2 and d4 and forces White to find a clean way to develop.
You have all your pieces out and a healthy structure.
Qb3 stares at b7 and d5, but both are guarded and ...e6 settles the matter.
Loses material.
Aims at the white king, but White keeps a slight edge.
White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Declining Be3 leaves White's king on f1 with no castling rights, so White needs a few slow moves to get…
notes.original: Declining Be3 leaves White's king on f1 with no castling rights, so White needs a few slow moves to get it to safety. Develop with tempo and do not touch the d5 pawn.

notes.text: Your rooks belong on the open e-file.
notes.original: Your rooks belong on the open e-file. White wants Nf3 and Bf4 to hit the queen and cash in the bishop pair, so a quick ...Qc7 is natural.

notes.text: Your queen is hit by the bishop but it steps away with a useful move, and the d5 pawn remains…
notes.original: Your queen is hit by the bishop but it steps away with a useful move, and the d5 pawn remains a solid centre.

notes.text: Trap: 11...Qh5+? 12.g4 Qe5 13.Kf1 Be7 14.Qf3 Qf6 and Black is clearly worse.
Black is better here: White's structure is damaged and the king is exposed.
Your queen steps off the e-file so that White's king no longer has anything to hit.
White's idea is to pressure Nc6 and the a-pawn while the king tucks away on f2, but b7 holds everything…
notes.original: White's idea is to pressure Nc6 and the a-pawn while the king tucks away on f2, but b7 holds everything together.

notes.text: The e3 pawn is a permanent weakness and the white king cannot castle, so you double on the e-file and…
notes.original: The e3 pawn is a permanent weakness and the white king cannot castle, so you double on the e-file and keep playing against it.

notes.text: The knight takes with tempo.
Nb1 blocks the a1-rook, so White cannot recapture on c1.
notes.original:
Nb1 blocks the a1-rook, so White cannot recapture on c1. Black is clearly better.
Trap: 9...Qa5+? 10.Nc3 e6 11.a3 Bd6 12.O-O Qd8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White offers a queen trade at once, since it cannot recapture on c1 and has to cut its losses.
Do not hurry anything.
notes.original: Do not hurry anything. White's king has lost castling and you hold a clean extra pawn, so just finish development.

notes.text: White's only plan is to use the c-file with Rc1 and bring the king to e2.
notes.original: White's only plan is to use the c-file with Rc1 and bring the king to e2. You contest the file with ...Rc8 and keep the pawn.

notes.text: ...h5 gains space and gives the h8 rook a role while White's pieces are still tangled.
White is winning.
White just develops, and the isolated d4 pawn is safe.
There is no compensation: you are a knight down for one pawn.
4...Nc6 develops naturally; the bishop on f4 is a reasonable square for White but creates no extra problems for Black…
notes.original: 4...Nc6 develops naturally; the bishop on f4 is a reasonable square for White but creates no extra problems for Black to solve.

notes.text: 5.c3 supports the center solidly before developing the knight, keeping options for both Nf3 and Nd2.
...and the position stays level.
You are solid, and White's plan is Rb1 to defend b2 against your queen.
Compact development.
A compact structure.
notes.original: A compact structure. You are not worried about the bishops: the light-squared ones are already traded.

notes.text: Hitting b2 forces White to waste time.
Your queen hits b2 and forces White to defend.
Level, and you can follow with ...Rac8 and ...Na5 to pressure.
Your queen hits b2 and forces White's rook to b1.
notes.original: Your queen hits b2 and forces White's rook to b1. Your pieces are comfortable and the structure is symmetrical, so it is level.

notes.text: Level.
notes.original: Level. You can follow up with ...Rac8 and ...Rfd8 and meet White's moves with ...Ne4 or ...Nb4 ideas.

notes.text: Loses a piece for a pawn, since d4 is guarded twice
4...Nf6 is simplest; the tempo White spends on c3 is close to a non-factor once development finishes.
The simplest development: Nf3, then Bd3 and Bf4.
White adds pressure on the c6 knight, the defender of your d5 pawn and of e5, hoping to double your…
notes.original: White adds pressure on the c6 knight, the defender of your d5 pawn and of e5, hoping to double your pawns or gain time with Ne5. It is a common but slightly speculative move: it develops, yet the bishop may become a target. For you, this is an invitation to hit it with tempo and to use the loose b5 square.

notes.text: You trade the dark bishops soon and are fine, though White is slightly better.
Now you challenge White's good bishop, making the position simple and solid.
Pin the f3 knight and then trade White's active dark bishop with ...Bd6; the extra c3 tempo is not a…
notes.original: Pin the f3 knight and then trade White's active dark bishop with ...Bd6; the extra c3 tempo is not a real factor.

notes.text: You trade off White's good dark bishop and reach a solid, level game.
Your queen attacks the bishop and the d4 pawn at the same time, so White must act.
notes.original: Your queen attacks the bishop and the d4 pawn at the same time, so White must act. This is both a useful developing move and a way to deny White easy play. Your plan afterwards is ...e6, ...Be7, castling short, and ...a6 to push the bishop away when needed. Avoid ...Bg4 without careful thought, since White gets h3 with tempo.

notes.text: White offers the c4 pawn for quick development.
notes.original: White offers the c4 pawn for quick development. You accept and complete your own development; do not cling to the extra pawn at all costs, but return it at the right moment if needed.

notes.text: With ...a6 you ask the bishop what it wants.
notes.original: With ...a6 you ask the bishop what it wants. White's idea is d5 to hit your knight, so be ready to answer it with ...exd5. Hit the bishop with ...Qb6, take the offered pawn calmly, finish development, and keep your position flexible; the line is equal. This is a position with an open centre after the c4 pawn was taken: you have pawns on e6 and a6, White has queen on b3 and bishop on e3, and your queen guards the position. Your plan: finish development with ...Nf6 and ...Bd7, castle short, then return the pawn at the right moment with ...b5. White wants d5 to hit your knight and open lines, so be ready to recapture with ...exd5. The risk is hanging on to the extra pawn when White has a lead in development, and a bishop check can be awkward; if White plays Rd1, keep your king safe.

notes.text: Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together, but ...Qc8 covers b7 and the Nf6 guards d5.
Qb3 hits b7 and d5 but Qc8 covers.
White hits b7 with the queen and the f5 bishop with Nh4, but ...Qc8 and ...Bd7 meet both threats.
White is slightly better.
Get the bishop out beyond the pawns ahead of ...e6, which makes White burn a tempo on f3.
White's plan is to castle long and attack; you trade pieces with ...Nd5 and use the h5 bishop to harass…
notes.original: White's plan is to castle long and attack; you trade pieces with ...Nd5 and use the h5 bishop to harass the king.

notes.text: An equally good alternative.
White is slightly better.
White is a pawn up, so you must open the centre; ...e5 hits d4 and opens lines for your pieces.
You get open lines and quick development, but White keeps the extra pawn.
Too slow: White consolidates the pawn.
7.Bxe4 dxe4 gives Black a strong pawn on e4 and a free hand in the centre.
notes.original: 7.Bxe4 dxe4 gives Black a strong pawn on e4 and a free hand in the centre. Taking on e4 does White no good.

notes.text: Idea: Here you meet 6.Bf4 with 6...Ne4 straight away.
notes.original:
Idea: Here you meet 6.Bf4 with 6...Ne4 straight away. The knight drops back to d6 so that ...Bf5 can trade off White's good bishop. Then finish with ...e6, ...Be7 and ...O-O.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 Ne4 7.Nd2 Nd6 8.Ngf3 Bf5
Watch out: ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 5 to 8. ...Nfxd4? loses material on moves 10 to 14.
See also: 🟢 01 covers more of the Exchange Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White makes luft and uses a4 for queenside space; you counter with ...b6 and ...Na5-c4, planting a knight on the…
notes.original: White makes luft and uses a4 for queenside space; you counter with ...b6 and ...Na5-c4, planting a knight on the outpost. The position is equal.

notes.text: Trying to break through White's one and only central pawn gives Black enough counterplay in the centre.
The position is equal.
The knight on e6 forks your queen and rook, so you take it.
White's queen takes with check and the bishop pair is gone, leaving an equal position.
If White delays, ...Kb8 sidesteps the fork and you are a bit better.
A fresh way to face the Exchange Variation with Nf3 is the plan ...Nf6 followed by ...Ne4.
White castles and wants to finish development before deciding on a plan: Re1, c3 or Bg5, and possibly h3 followed…
notes.original: White castles and wants to finish development before deciding on a plan: Re1, c3 or Bg5, and possibly h3 followed by Bf4 and Qb3 against d5. The move is extremely common in practice (played in about 1.4 million games). So White keeps tension in the centre and you must choose where your bishop goes.

notes.text: 7.Bxe4 dxe4 gives up the bishop pair, and the new pawn on e4 kicks the knight off f3.
notes.original: 7.Bxe4 dxe4 gives up the bishop pair, and the new pawn on e4 kicks the knight off f3. It takes White a few moves to sort that out. 7.O-O was the better move.

notes.text: Against Nd2, ...Nd6 is the answer.
notes.original: Against Nd2, ...Nd6 is the answer. Black should not trade knights for White's modest Nd2 and should keep the position dynamic.

notes.text: Bf4 comes before Nd2 because otherwise the dark-squared bishop would be shut in.
notes.original: Bf4 comes before Nd2 because otherwise the dark-squared bishop would be shut in. The drawback is ...Bf5, which stabilises the knight on e4.

notes.text: White supports the e4-pawn.
notes.original: White supports the e4-pawn. Black plans ...Bf5 followed by ...e5, a strong central break.

notes.text: White is left with an ugly isolated pawn, which is a poor outlook.
The position is equal.
You attack the e5 pawn, the one thing keeping White a pawn up.
The bishop hits the rook and gains a tempo.
The pawn is back.
Another tempo: the bishop forks Rd1 and Nb1.
You have the bishop pair and White's extra pawn has gone.
notes.original: You have the bishop pair and White's extra pawn has gone. If White repeats, so can you.

notes.text: Grabbing f7 looks greedy, but the Bd3 fork forces White's hand and you regain e5 with active pieces.
Exchanging bishops helps Black here: White's light squares on the b1-h7 diagonal slowly weaken.
The position is equal.
Castling keeps things simple.
...a5 gains queenside space and takes b4 away.
Centralise ...Ne4 and trade dark bishops with ...Bd6; your c6 pawns are doubled but your pieces are active and the…
notes.original: Centralise ...Ne4 and trade dark bishops with ...Bd6; your c6 pawns are doubled but your pieces are active and the position is equal.

notes.text: A Nc5 jump is met by ...Nf5 and ...Bd6.
The position is equal.
White cannot answer with a similar ...Ne4 idea: Nxd5 dxe5 a6 and so on would make the position simpler, with…
notes.original: White cannot answer with a similar ...Ne4 idea: Nxd5 dxe5 a6 and so on would make the position simpler, with Black's knight on e4 still intact.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Your Nc5 forks the queen and the bishop on d3, so White must take the knight.
You recapture the bishop and get the bishop pair and the e5 break.
The bishop trade does not stop the fork; you win the queen for a knight (over a rook's worth).
This stops the idea of Bb5 pinning the queen; otherwise Black would be in serious trouble.
The position is equal.
The position is level, so you only need a sensible plan.
notes.original: The position is level, so you only need a sensible plan. White's pawn on e5 cramps you, but it is also a target: your Bg7 and the open c-file hit it and c3 at once.

notes.text: White's h4 grabs space and hints at h5, and ...h6 stops that cheaply.
You are castled, the queen is active and the game is balanced.
You pin the knight and take the c8 bishop out before it is shut in by ...e6.
notes.original: You pin the knight and take the c8 bishop out before it is shut in by ...e6. Your plan is ...e6, ...Bd6, ...O-O, with ...Qd7 and a quiet game. The pin on f3 matters because it stops White from playing e5-style jumps and makes h3 a necessity. After 7.c3 e6 8.h3 Bh5 9.Bf4 you can keep the bishop alive with ...Ne4.

notes.text: This is a fairly open, symmetrical centre: the d5 pawn is solid, White has traded his dark-squared bishop and you…
notes.original: This is a fairly open, symmetrical centre: the d5 pawn is solid, White has traded his dark-squared bishop and you have a safe king still to castle. Your plan: castle short at once, play ...Qxd6-style recapture structure with the queen on d6 or d7, then bring the rooks to c8 and e8 and use the knight on e4 as your best piece. White wants the open c-file and the queen on b3 against b7, so keep b7 guarded and watch d5. The risk is hurrying ...O-O into Qxb7 tactics without checking; if White avoids the trade on d6, retreat calmly.

notes.text: A natural fianchetto, but it is a little passive: White gets Re1 and Bg5 with a comfortable edge and your…
notes.original: A natural fianchetto, but it is a little passive: White gets Re1 and Bg5 with a comfortable edge and your light squares are loose. Avoid this if you want a dynamic game.

notes.text: 5.h3 stops ...Bg4 for good and prepares a quiet development.
notes.original: 5.h3 stops ...Bg4 for good and prepares a quiet development. Black replies ...Nc6 and ...e5.

notes.text: 5.Bf4 develops actively and keeps h3 in reserve.
notes.original: 5.Bf4 develops actively and keeps h3 in reserve. ...Nc6 answers it naturally.

notes.text: White brings out the knight, keeps the bishop on d3 and prepares c3 and Bf4 or O-O.
notes.original: White brings out the knight, keeps the bishop on d3 and prepares c3 and Bf4 or O-O. It is very common (played in about 743,000 games). White hopes for a slight pull from the pin ideas and a calm, solid structure.

notes.text: White develops the knight so that he can keep his structure flexible, and the f1 bishop is on d3 so…
notes.original: White develops the knight so that he can keep his structure flexible, and the f1 bishop is on d3 so the knight cannot go to f3 without blocking. The knight on e2 also prepares to go to f4 and keeps the f-pawn free. It is very common in practice (played in about 250,000 games), so you will meet it often. So White is aiming for a quiet game without early pawn tension.

White's check forces simplification but gives Black the easier game.

The most testing line: Black's bishop pins the knight and White's queen hits b7, which forces Black to react.
notes.original: The most testing line: Black's bishop pins the knight and White's queen hits b7, which forces Black to react. ...Qc7 solves the problem.

notes.text: 6.f3 tries to chase the bishop but weakens the e3-square.
notes.original: 6.f3 tries to chase the bishop but weakens the e3-square. Black retreats with ...Bh5 and ...Bg6 and equalises.

notes.text: 7.Ne2 offers a trade on e2; after ...Bxe2 Bxe2 e6 Black reaches a solid, equal position.
Black unpins and heads for ...e5.
notes.original: Black unpins and heads for ...e5. The position is balanced and Black's pieces are well placed.

The position is equal.
Pin the knight at once, before h3.
notes.original: Pin the knight at once, before h3. The bishop would like to trade itself for the knight, which relieves your cramped position. After h3 retreat to h5, then ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...Bd6 to challenge the strongest white bishop. Your plan is to exchange pieces, keep the d5 pawn solid and castle short. Avoid ...g6 here, which lets White play Bf4 and c3 comfortably with extra space. The position is about level, with a very small plus for White.

notes.text: Less ideal.
notes.original: Less ideal. After c3 Bg7 h3 Bf5 White can swap bishops and then Bf4 gives a lasting initiative, so you stay a little passive.

notes.text: The knight guards d4 and pressures the centre.
notes.original: The knight guards d4 and pressures the centre. Your next moves are ...e6 and ...Bd6.

notes.text: After the exchange you have a healthy position with no weaknesses and only a tiny deficit, which is a good…
notes.original: After the exchange you have a healthy position with no weaknesses and only a tiny deficit, which is a good outcome in this line. This is a balanced position with symmetrical pawns and a pin from your bishop on h5, where White has recaptured on d6 with the bishop. Your plan: recapture with ...Qxd6, then play ...Bg6 to trade White's bishop on d3, castle short, and bring a rook to e8. White wants g4 to trap or bother the bishop on h5, then Qe2 and O-O-O. If g4 comes, retreat with ...Bg6 and recapture on g6 with the h-pawn. The mistake is ignoring the pin on f3, which you can exploit with ...Bxf3 at the right moment. If White deviates with Qe2, continue ...Bg6.

notes.text: You support d5 and prepare ...Bd6 and castling.
notes.original: You support d5 and prepare ...Bd6 and castling. Your plan is simple: develop ...Nc6, ...Bd7 and ...Bd6 and then castle short, putting pressure on the white queenside with ...Rc8. If White plays Bf4 you must challenge it with ...Bd6 when possible, since trading the dark squared bishops helps you. Avoid ...Bg4 too early unless you check White's reply.

notes.text: The bishop goes to d7 to prepare ...Nh5 which hits the bishop on f4.
You gain the bishop pair or force the bishop to retreat.
You have solid development and equal chances.
This is a closed centre with the symmetrical Exchange Variation structure: d4 against d5, with White's pieces more active but…
notes.original: This is a closed centre with the symmetrical Exchange Variation structure: d4 against d5, with White's pieces more active but your bishops trading in your favour. Both kings castle short. Your plan: castle short, play ...Rc8 and ...Qe7, retreat the knight from h5 to f6 when needed, and keep the bishop on d6 well placed against the dark squares. White wants Nf4 to hit your knight and the d5 pawn, and a later Bd3 plan against h7. Meet Nf4 with ...Nxf4 and Bxf4, then ...Bxf4. The risk is leaving the knight stranded on h5 without a retreat, where a pinned or trapped piece loses time.

notes.text: This is another fine reply.
Another route to the same position.
This resembles a Marshall-style set-up and is quite playable, since White's e-pawn is gone.
notes.original: This resembles a Marshall-style set-up and is quite playable, since White's e-pawn is gone. Black has two sensible plans: the Grunfeld-style set-up or a Queen's Gambit Declined structure.

notes.text: This is the Horwitz-style answer to the Panov-Botvinnik Attack, an improvised Queen's Gambit.
notes.original: This is the Horwitz-style answer to the Panov-Botvinnik Attack, an improvised Queen's Gambit. It blocks the light-squared bishop but lets Black steer towards a Queen's Gambit Declined.

notes.text: Another Panov Botvinnik line, this move could transpose to the main line or go off the sidelines.
The Grunfeld-style approach is sometimes called dubious or inaccurate, yet it is the preferred way here to meet the Panov-Botvinnik…
notes.original: The Grunfeld-style approach is sometimes called dubious or inaccurate, yet it is the preferred way here to meet the Panov-Botvinnik Attack. Black's position stays solid, if somewhat passive, and has no major weaknesses.

notes.text: Choice guide: choose 5...Nc6 if you want a flexible, active reply The ...a6 idea covers the d5 square cheaply.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose 5...Nc6 if you want a flexible, active reply The ...a6 idea covers the d5 square cheaply. For a quieter, structural game see 🔵 03 and 04. After 5...Nc6 White's main moves are 6.Nf3, 6.Bg5 and 6.Bf4. Black replies ...a6 or ...g6 depending on the system.

notes.text: ...e6 is another good alternative, although it is difficult to play against the Panov this way and is discouraged; players…
notes.original: ...e6 is another good alternative, although it is difficult to play against the Panov this way and is discouraged; players who want a simpler, safer game may find it acceptable.

notes.text: 6.Qb3 hits d5 and b7 at once.
notes.original: 6.Qb3 hits d5 and b7 at once. White wants to win a pawn while developing, so Black has to react quickly and finish development.

notes.text: Nf3 prepares White's principled Queen's Gambit plan.
This variation tends to help Black because the pressure on the centre has disappeared.
Black need not rush to protect the d-pawn.
notes.original: Black need not rush to protect the d-pawn. Even if White wins it, that pawn is weak, with no other pawns to support it, and will probably fall soon. Development matters more than safety here.

notes.text: Idea: Against the Panov you can fianchetto with 5...g6.
notes.original:
Idea: Against the Panov you can fianchetto with 5...g6. White grabs the d5 pawn with Qb3 and cxd5. Don't rush to win it back: castle, bring the knight to b6 and put pressure on d5.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 g6 6.Qb3 Bg7 7.cxd5 O-O
Watch out: ...Nxd5? loses material on moves 7 to 9. ...Nfxd5? loses material on move 10.
Next: 🔵 04 continues the Panov-Botvinnik Attack. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.text: White tries once more to hold on to the pawn.
White can also let the d-pawn go and develop freely.
notes.original: White can also let the d-pawn go and develop freely. White keeps full flexibility while Black also develops easily, so both sides get what they want and the outcome is more drawish.

notes.text: 8.Bg5 hits the knight on f6, one of the pieces aiming at the isolated d4 pawn, and tries to slow…
notes.original: 8.Bg5 hits the knight on f6, one of the pieces aiming at the isolated d4 pawn, and tries to slow Black down.

notes.text: Black removes the main support of the d5-pawn.
It matters for two reasons: Black has to retake with the e-pawn, producing an isolated pawn, and since the dark-squared…
notes.original: It matters for two reasons: Black has to retake with the e-pawn, producing an isolated pawn, and since the dark-squared bishop protects d5, ...e6 is not a sensible alternative.

notes.text: Recapturing with the e-pawn leaves an isolated pawn.
notes.original: Recapturing with the e-pawn leaves an isolated pawn. White seems to have gained something, but both sides now have an isolated d-pawn and each can be targeted. An isolated pawn can serve as an attacking asset too.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White kicks the b6 knight so the queenside pawn majority starts to move.
You secure b5 and keep the queenside shut.

The bishop returns and defends d5.

White has taken a pawn but Black has activity, so the game is balanced.
A simple line that gives Black a full game.
Black is happy to get the e file open for his rook to take advantage of.
A queen exchange would favour Black: White has doubled, isolated pawns that are likely to fall, and Black has enough…
notes.original: A queen exchange would favour Black: White has doubled, isolated pawns that are likely to fall, and Black has enough pieces to attack them. The initiative and the advantage lie with Black.

notes.text: White declines the queen trade and hopes for rapid development, unwilling to give up the initiative and wanting Black to…
notes.original: White declines the queen trade and hopes for rapid development, unwilling to give up the initiative and wanting Black to defend.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White places the knight on d6 to hit b7 and the e8 and f7 squares.
notes.original: White places the knight on d6 to hit b7 and the e8 and f7 squares. Black has the bishop pair but a ragged structure.

notes.text: You cement the knight outpost, but White hopes for Ra6.
Equal, and the doubled f6 and b4 pawns are not a real worry.
A pawn push that hits b6, but Black is fine and a touch better.
The a4 pawn is a target for Black.
notes.original: The a4 pawn is a target for Black. White's position is slowly crumbling: it is defensible, yet White is under constant pressure and may not enjoy defending it.

notes.text: White regroups the f1 knight to cover c4 and d5, because the a4 pawn is under pressure.
You kick the knight and gain space.
Black keeps pressing on the kingside with ...h4 ideas.
notes.original: Black keeps pressing on the kingside with ...h4 ideas. Black stays slightly better.

notes.text: If White lets a4 fall, the passed c2 pawn is a monster.

notes.original: Bg5 is imprecise: White intends to take on f6 and then win the unprotected pawn on d5, but this can be defended.

notes.text: White cannot capture the knight, because this would open lines for three black pieces to attack the d-pawn.
Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
Black is winning.

notes.original: Black is a pawn up with a monster on d4. White tries to keep the b2 pawn and the queen.

Black has the extra pawn and a solid central majority.
Black just rolls the kingside pawns, winning.
White cannot regain the pawn and Black is winning.
...Be6 may look poor but it is fine.
notes.original: ...Be6 may look poor but it is fine. The d-pawn is under attack and must be defended; ...e6 would shut in the light-squared bishop behind the pawn chain, so ...Be6 is better as the bishop is no longer barricaded.

notes.text: White wants to expand on the queenside!
notes.original: White wants to expand on the queenside! b4 would soon be played but White first has to take care of his knight since h4 would only hang his knight.

notes.original: White prepares to fight for the open c-file and to attack with Qd2. The bishop pair compensates for the weakness on d4.

notes.original: A pawn grab, but check for tricks. Black is a bit better.

notes.original: The queen eyes the e-file and White's idea is to use the bishop pair to attack the king. The f3 pawn weakens the white king.

White's pawns are shattered and the bishop on c1 is passive, so Black keeps a slight edge.
The rook raid fails and Black is better.
Black has tripled e-pawns yet is still a pawn up and can give back material for the initiative.
notes.original: Black has tripled e-pawns yet is still a pawn up and can give back material for the initiative. Pushing ...e3 is even possible: if White captures, the e-file is shut so the rook cannot go after the doubled pawns, and White's own pawn structure stays damaged. (Gusev-Muratov, Novgorod 1961, 0-1.)

notes.text: White pins down your king with the bishop on g4 which eyes e6.
The queen attacks b2 and the bishop on g4.
The bishop blocks the check and White's attack runs out of steam, so Black keeps a slight edge.
Another tough defence, Black has the initiative.

A queen on an exposed central square can be harassed, so it is risky to leave it there.
The queen on d5 is exposed, so White develops with tempo, attacking it and hoping to follow with Nb5 or…
notes.original: The queen on d5 is exposed, so White develops with tempo, attacking it and hoping to follow with Nb5 or Be3.

notes.original: Offer the trade. Black's pieces are more active than White's.

notes.original: The d4 pawn is isolated and the bishop is safe on c6. You keep a small edge.

notes.original: White sets a trap. The knight eyes e6 and f7, and the bishop on c4 supports both. If you ignore it, Nxe6 wins a pawn.

White tries a combination to break through.
White has given two minor pieces for a rook and two pawns, so material is about level and the position…
notes.original: White has given two minor pieces for a rook and two pawns, so material is about level and the position is balanced. It is critical to keep the bishop b7 on the long diagonal.

notes.text: A quieter alternative, equal.
The position is equal.
White pins the f6 knight so that you cannot easily play ...dxc4 or ...Ne4, and prepares Nf3 with Rc1 and…
notes.original: White pins the f6 knight so that you cannot easily play ...dxc4 or ...Ne4, and prepares Nf3 with Rc1 and a pull on d5. It also eyes the possibility of c5, gaining space on the queenside. This is a very common move and is not especially dangerous, but you must be careful about the d5 pawn.

notes.text: White gives up the tension in the centre to open the c-file and put the pressure on your d5 pawn.
notes.original: White gives up the tension in the centre to open the c-file and put the pressure on your d5 pawn. It is very common in practice and leads to a symmetrical pawn structure with a slight pull for White. As Black you need to recapture sensibly and to keep your king safe.

notes.text: Playable, but Bb4 is more accurate.
Pinning the knight right away, as usually seen in the Bogo Indian Defence.
notes.original: Pinning the knight right away, as usually seen in the Bogo Indian Defence. Black doesn't necessarily have to exchange bishop for knight. Black just need to ease up white's forces on his central fortification.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White develops the bishop to d3, where it eyes your kingside and prepares castling.
notes.original: White develops the bishop to d3, where it eyes your kingside and prepares castling. He is ready to answer ...dxc4 with Bxc4 and ...O-O with cxd5. This is the most natural developing move (played in about 134,000 games). It keeps the structure flexible.

notes.text: White has two acceptable options here, Bb5+ and Bd3, and both are covered in this study.
Bd3 prepares kingside castling; little needs to be added.
The position is equal.
White pins the f6 knight against the queen and threatens to wreck your pawns with Bxf6.
You answer the pin with a pin of your own on the f3 knight.
The pawn thrust gains time because the bishop has to retreat.
Black heads for Nf5 or Ne4, using the weakened c3 pawn as the target.
White gives up the bishop to open lines but Black keeps a healthy centre.
White is slightly better.

notes.original: White keeps the bishop pair and avoids ...Nxc4, which would give it up. The bishop also x-rays f7.

notes.text: You threaten ...a4 to trap or harass the bishop on b3.
The knight attacks Bd2 and hits f2.
White keeps the bishop pair and a slight space edge, but the kingside is loosened by g4.
A more modest retreat, Black is fine here.
Capture now, before White can play cxd5 and Nb5 type ideas.
notes.original: Capture now, before White can play cxd5 and Nb5 type ideas. After Bxc4 White has used time and you get a good development. Follow with ...O-O, ...b6 and ...Bb7. Do not wait too long with ...O-O: it is the safest square for your king.

notes.text: Also playable.
You aim to put the bishop on b7 and fight for the e4 square.
notes.original: You aim to put the bishop on b7 and fight for the e4 square. Avoid ...Nc6 here: it blocks the b7 bishop idea.

notes.text: You trade your dark bishop for the knight to remove the piece that guards d5 and e4.
White has a pawn structure with c3 and d4 weaknesses, but good bishops.
notes.original:
White has a pawn structure with c3 and d4 weaknesses, but good bishops. Equal, with an easy plan of ...Nbd7 and ...c5 or ...Qc8 and ...Ne4.
This is a Panov-type position with an isolated-looking centre: White has pawns on c4 and d4 against your d5, and after the trade on c3 he has doubled c-pawns. The centre is semi-open and kings will castle short. Your plan: play ...b6 and ...Bb7 to fight for the e4 square, trade the dark bishop on c3 to remove the defender of d5, then play ...Nbd7 and ...c5 or ...Qc8 and ...Ne4. White wants to use his bishops and the c4 and d4 pawns to attack. You meet it by pressing on c3. The risk is playing ...Nc6, which blocks the b7 bishop. If White deviates, keep control of e4.

notes.text: You get a normal isolated pawn position with the bishop on d6 well placed.
The same position as in 🔵 03 (Fianchetto Defence).
notes.original: The same position as in 🔵 03 (Fianchetto Defence). Castling is the best move here, ahead of two decent alternatives.

notes.text: Also possible: b6.
Also possible: Ne4.
The position is equal.
Black develops the bishop and covers b5, and the White knight on a4 is offside, so there is no hurry.
Black hits d4 and prepares ...Ng4.
The queen steps off the c-file before White's rook arrives on c1.
Equal.
notes.original: Equal. Black has easy play against d4.

notes.text: A more direct break, also fine for Black.
The position is equal.
You trade White's active bishop.
notes.original: You trade White's active bishop. The pin on d7 loses its sting once the bishop on b5 is exchanged, and Black reaches a comfortable equal position.

notes.text: The queen eyes b2 and the a4 knight.
White gains queenside space but Black has no weaknesses.
notes.original: White gains queenside space but Black has no weaknesses. Equal.

notes.text: The knight lands with tempo on the a8 rook and White gets the upper hand.
notes.original: The knight lands with tempo on the a8 rook and White gets the upper hand. Do not weaken b6 like this.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The right square.
notes.original: The right square. White's Ne5 hits the queen and the c6 and f7 squares, but from c7 the queen keeps an eye on e5 and prepares castling.

notes.text: The bishop attacks the d4 pawn and you keep the powerful knight on e4.
Black grabs space on the kingside.
notes.original: Black grabs space on the kingside. White has a small edge, thanks to the pawn centre.

notes.text: Now the king has lost castling and White is clearly better.
The position is equal.
Exchanging bishops is acceptable, as the light-squared bishop is somewhat restricted here.
The main line's Nb5 idea (aiming for Nd6+) is well known, but simple development with Nf3 first is actually the…
notes.original: The main line's Nb5 idea (aiming for Nd6+) is well known, but simple development with Nf3 first is actually the most accurate move order, keeping options flexible rather than committing the knight early.

notes.text: Black's follow-up would have been to undermine the white centre gradually; the isolated d4-pawn would then be a target.
You open the a-file against Ra1.
Your pieces keep pressing d4 and c3.
notes.original: Your pieces keep pressing d4 and c3. A modest edge for Black.

notes.text: The pawn runs forward but falls.
Very close to equal either way; the main line's chosen try is perfectly reasonable in practice, but Nf3 is slightly…
notes.original: Very close to equal either way; the main line's chosen try is perfectly reasonable in practice, but Nf3 is slightly more accurate and worth knowing about.

notes.text: White gains queenside space with b4 and b5.
notes.original: White gains queenside space with b4 and b5. You counter with ...f5, supporting your Ne4.

notes.text: The c6 wedge cramps you but is also a target.
notes.original: The c6 wedge cramps you but is also a target. Near equal.

notes.text: ...b6 aims to undermine the white centre.
notes.original: ...b6 aims to undermine the white centre. White can either maintain the broad pawn centre or release it.

Trap: 13.Nxc5? Rxa1 14.O-O Ra7 15.Ne5 Nxe5 16.dxe5 and White is losing.
The position is equal.
Bg5 hits Rd8, so the rook goes to d5.
Everything simplifies.
notes.original: Everything simplifies. Level.

notes.text: The passed pawn looks dangerous but ...Bd4 and ...Re8 pick it off.
White has only one good move, Kf1: after Bd2 and a bishop exchange Black's king would be stuck in the…
notes.original: White has only one good move, Kf1: after Bd2 and a bishop exchange Black's king would be stuck in the centre, or the knight on a4 would be lost if the queen interposes.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White has lost the right to castle, so the first job is to tuck the king away.
notes.original: White has lost the right to castle, so the first job is to tuck the king away. The knight on e5 is the only active White piece and the knight on a4 is offside, so Black attacks e5 and develops.

notes.text: White hopes h4 and Bg5 will pester the f6 knight and open the h-file.
The knight on e4 is a perfect outpost and the queen eyes a4 and g2.
notes.original: The knight on e4 is a perfect outpost and the queen eyes a4 and g2. Black keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Unpin by developing the bishop, preparing ...O-O.
notes.original: Unpin by developing the bishop, preparing ...O-O. Do not rush ...dxc4 before castling: White gets e4 or Bxc4 with the initiative.

notes.text: You ask the bishop a question.
notes.original: You ask the bishop a question. If it retreats to h4, your knight on f6 is still pinned, so you do not mind; otherwise you may trade bishops.

notes.text: Your bishops are developed on active squares, your knight pressures d4, and your pawn on d5 is a strength.
notes.original: Your bishops are developed on active squares, your knight pressures d4, and your pawn on d5 is a strength. Your plan is ...dxc4 at the right moment, or ...Qe7 with ...Rd8. Avoid ...Ne4 until your pieces are connected.

notes.text: Unpin with ...Be7, castle, then challenge the centre with ...Nc6 and ...Bd6; the position is equal and balanced.
notes.original: Unpin with ...Be7, castle, then challenge the centre with ...Nc6 and ...Bd6; the position is equal and balanced. This is a closed, balanced position with pawns on d5 and e6, where White has c4 and d4 and you have just developed your pieces on active squares. Your plan: castle short, complete development with ...Nc6 and ...Bd6, then challenge the centre with ...dxc4 or ...Rd8. White wants to push d5 or capture on c4 and play Bxc4 with an initiative, so keep your knight and pawn on d5 well supported. The risk is hurrying ...Ne4 or ...dxc4 before you have castled, since White gets Bxc4 with a lead. If White avoids Bd3, keep calm, develop and castle.

notes.text: The natural move: you get a healthy centre and an easy plan.
notes.original: The natural move: you get a healthy centre and an easy plan. After Bb5+ you answer ...Nc6 and then ...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Bg4 to pin the knight on f3. Your aim is to trade pieces and play ...a6 against the bishop on b5 only when it helps you. Avoid ...Bd7 and ...Nbd7, which are passive.

notes.text: You have a balanced position and can play for equality with simple moves.
notes.original: You have a balanced position and can play for equality with simple moves. This is a symmetrical, open-centre position with your pawn on d5 against White's d4, both kings castled short, and a roughly balanced game. Your plan: play ...h6 to ask the bishop on g5 a question, consider ...Bxf3 to remove a defender of d4, then bring the rooks to e8 and c8 with ...Re8, ...Qd7 and ...Rac8. White wants to pile up on d5 with Qb3, Rc1 and Bxf6 followed by Nxd5 ideas, so keep d5 guarded before moving the f6 knight. The risk is passive play with ...Bd7 or a careless move that lets Bxf6 win a pawn; if White drops the bishop back, trade pieces calmly.

notes.text: This is the other common recapture.
notes.original: This is the other common recapture. It leads to a similar position with active pieces, but the pawn on d4 can become weak and you must avoid trading your well-placed knight too early.

notes.text: This ignores the pawn on d5, and White wins a pawn.
notes.original: This ignores the pawn on d5, and White wins a pawn. Do not do this.

notes.text: Nc3 will eventually transpose into the main line.
Watch out: ...Nxd5? loses material on moves 7 to 9.

Black stands well here.

notes.original: You unpin the queen from d8 and eye d4. Black is already comfortable.

notes.original: The knight on b5 eyes c7 and d6 but Black has everything covered. Equal.

This knight manoeuvre is worth remembering; it echoes set-ups from the Colle-Zukertort and the Yusupov-Rubinstein systems.

White keeps the more active pieces and the passed pawn on e5.
