notes.original: Instead of the calm developing move Be2 shown in the main line, White has the more ambitious c5, gaining space and kicking the bishop on d6 before Black can react.

notes.text: c5 is more accurate.
Idea: 4...e6 gives you a solid, Queen's Gambit Declined type of position.
notes.original:
Idea: 4...e6 gives you a solid, Queen's Gambit Declined type of position. If White locks the queenside with c5, keep the bishop on c7, castle, and get ready to break with ...e5.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 Nf6 6.Nf3 Bd6 7.c5 Bc7
Watch out: ...Bxh2+? loses material on moves 9 to 11. ...Bxc5? loses material on move 7.

notes.text: This gives White a if modest, space-based edge that the passive Be2 does not.
notes.original: This gives White a if modest, space-based edge that the passive Be2 does not. Black is still solid after retreating the bishop, but should be aware c5 is the sharper and more testing option for White here.

notes.original: 9.c5 gains space and chases the bishop, so White has the extra room. Black counterattacks from the flank and by undermining the c5 pawn with ...b6.

notes.original: White pins the knight: if the black queen moves, White can take the knight, wreck Black's kingside pawns and expose the king.

notes.text: Known as the Capablanca Variation, this is a deviation from the standard classical move order.
notes.original: Known as the Capablanca Variation, this is a deviation from the standard classical move order. Black wants to play e6, but in order to avoid his bishop from being stranded on the chain of light square pawns, he must instead play f5. White may, and almost always does, keep to the standard line, which consists of Ng3 and forces the bishop to retire; nevertheless, the risky Nc5 and aggressive Burris Gambit have given white with surprising victory.

notes.original: With move 4...h6 Black creates escape square for light squared bishop's later use. It is usually considered as an inaccuracy and it is therefore rarely seen in higher levels. White's most usual respond is 5. Nf3. Natural development move 5. Bc4 is also played often and usually with an aim to sacrifice bishop in f7.

notes.original: Rarely seen, but the knight's poor positioning on c5 must be punished. White wants to win a pawn since Black's b pawn is hanging. However after e5! White is pretty much force to take the b pawn or retreat the knight and lose material.

notes.text: The reason to hurry: h4-h5 forces your bishop to e4.

8.Nh3 reroutes the knight toward f4 instead of the more natural Nf3, aiming to hit the bishop on g6 directly.
White attacks your bishop at once with a pawn push and tries to win time or even trap it.
notes.original: White attacks your bishop at once with a pawn push and tries to win time or even trap it. It is common in practice (played in about 850,000 games). So the bishop must go to a safe square immediately, and only one square really works.

notes.text: 10.Bd3 offers the trade of light-squared bishops immediately, a move earlier than most main lines which delay it with h5…
notes.original: 10.Bd3 offers the trade of light-squared bishops immediately, a move earlier than most main lines which delay it with h5 first.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
This is the major route.
notes.original: This is the major route. White prepares to castle queenside, so a kingside pawn storm with h2-h4-h5 is natural. After 11...Ngf6 or 11...Be7 Black keeps improving, and then castling kingside is the only option. If both sides race pawns toward the enemy king, a sharp fight follows. To counter it, Black can try queenside castling: 11...Qc7 takes control of the b8-h2 diagonal and 12...O-O-O lets Black fight for the initiative.

notes.text: This move asks White to play c3, which removes any queenside castling and ends the kingside attack.
notes.original: This move asks White to play c3, which removes any queenside castling and ends the kingside attack. Even so, White tends to keep the upper hand because the kingside attack usually continues undisturbed.

notes.text: Whats the point of launching a pawn storm on the kingside only for White to castle?
notes.original: Whats the point of launching a pawn storm on the kingside only for White to castle? This would effectively weaken white's assault on the kingside and it's pretty much postponed for now.

notes.text: The a-pawn advances to break open White's queenside, with an all-out attack.
The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
White lifts the rook to join the attack along the third rank and the g-file.
Attacks the pawn on a3, but your Be7 guards it.
Small White edge.
notes.original: Small White edge. You have the better pawn structure but White has more active rooks; keep ...Nf6 and ...Rc8 handy.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Develops the rook to the c-file while keeping your a3 pawn in place.
Level.
notes.original: Level. Your a3 and b4 pawns cramp White and keep him from attacking freely.

notes.text: White's rooks aim at g7 and your king comes under pressure.
White is slightly better.
White puts a rook on the d-file and prepares Be5.
You offer a pawn to open the queenside and free your pieces.
Your knight hits the bishop on f4.
White has grabbed a pawn, but your pieces are very active and the position is close to level.
notes.original: White has grabbed a pawn, but your pieces are very active and the position is close to level. Look for ...Bd6 and ...Rac8 to regain activity.

notes.text: 12.c3 blocks the check with a pawn rather than interposing a piece, keeping the knight on b1 flexible for d2…
notes.original: 12.c3 blocks the check with a pawn rather than interposing a piece, keeping the knight on b1 flexible for d2 or a3.

notes.text: After c3 White's king becomes less safe if it castles queenside, so White is discouraged from castling long, or else…
notes.original: After c3 White's king becomes less safe if it castles queenside, so White is discouraged from castling long, or else risks being hit by something like h5 and ...g5.

notes.text: 13.Ne4 centralizes the knight immediately after the bishop interposes the check, offering a trade of light pieces.
White holds more space.
15.O-O-O castles into the center rather than the more modest Kb1 some sources prefer, accepting a sharper middlegame.
The position is equal.
White puts the rook on the open e-file to harass the queen and bishop.
Centralises and offers to trade.
The trades leave an equal endgame.
notes.original: The trades leave an equal endgame. White's king on f1 is slightly awkward, so you can play for ...Rd8.

notes.text: ...reaching a double-edged but balanced position.
Puts the rook behind the d-file and prepares ...c5.
Strikes in the centre before White's pawn storm starts.
The pawn hits the queen.
Level and sharp.
notes.original: Level and sharp. Open the h-file with ...hxg5 and bring pieces back to defend.

notes.text: An alternative break, level.
...and Black holds comfortably.
Forces the issue with check, since Nb7 attacks the queen on a5.
Hits both the knight and d4.
The knight escapes with a hit on the f7 pawn, and the position is level.
You end up a pawn down.
...and Black's piece activity gives a real edge once the position opens up.
The simple answer: you win the bishop.
Hits the knight on f4 and b7 at once.
You are a pawn up.
notes.original: You are a pawn up. The price is a slightly exposed king, so tuck it away with ...Ke8 and ...Rd8 and trade pieces.

notes.text: The natural recapture lets the bishop escape and White gets ahead in development.
White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
Retreats back the knight on the 1st rank to fuel white's attack on the kingside.
Before starting the kingside pawn storm with g4, White's most precise move is actually the prophylactic Kb1 first, tucking the…
notes.original: Before starting the kingside pawn storm with g4, White's most precise move is actually the prophylactic Kb1 first, tucking the king away from any future ...Na4 or queenside counterplay.

notes.text: Trying to keep the position equal by exchanging queens.
This is how White keeps equality: he trades queens, which ends any attack on the g-file and your threats on…
notes.original: This is how White keeps equality: he trades queens, which ends any attack on the g-file and your threats on the queenside.

notes.text: Attacks the bishop on d2 and eyes the g-pawn.
Pawns have been swapped on both wings and the position is level.
notes.original: Pawns have been swapped on both wings and the position is level. Your knight on h5 guards g7 so Bxg7 is not a worry.

notes.text: White has given up a pawn for nothing.
A small improvement in move order rather than a real change - Black's position stays sound, but White's attack flows…
notes.original: A small improvement in move order rather than a real change - Black's position stays sound, but White's attack flows slightly more safely after Kb1 first.

notes.text: White prepares c4 and Ne5, and keeps the a-pawn from being rolled up.
Challenges the strong knight on e5.
The check forces matters.
notes.original: The check forces matters. White's g-pawn storm is dangerous but your pieces dominate the centre; White is only a shade better.

notes.text: Gives up a pawn for a wedge on h7 and the d5 break; it is roughly level but be careful…
notes.original: Gives up a pawn for a wedge on h7 and the d5 break; it is roughly level but be careful with your king.

notes.text: Trying to get rid of black's major defences on the kingside to get a upper hand on white's assault on…
notes.original: Trying to get rid of black's major defences on the kingside to get a upper hand on white's assault on the kingside.

notes.text: Offering a queen trade.
notes.original: Offering a queen trade. The doubled b-pawns are actually a strength, since they claim d5 for the knight and open the c-file.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White points the bishop at the h6 pawn, which your h-pawn push left weak, and keeps h5 as a cramping…
notes.original: White points the bishop at the h6 pawn, which your h-pawn push left weak, and keeps h5 as a cramping wedge.

notes.text: Hits the bishop and f2 at once.
Returns the knight to guard h7 and d5.
White keeps a small edge: the pawn on h5 cramps your kingside.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge: the pawn on h5 cramps your kingside. But your position is sound, so aim for ...Rfd8 and ...c5 to free it.

notes.text: White plays Qd5 to avoid any tactical sequences with d5 thrust for white and also threatening to take white's a2…
notes.original: White plays Qd5 to avoid any tactical sequences with d5 thrust for white and also threatening to take white's a2 pawn.

notes.text: 16.c4 looks active, but it weakens the white king on c1 and invites Black to attack on the queenside.
An even keel has been reached here.
notes.original: An even keel has been reached here. This is favorable for black Since Bxf4 Nxf2 forks the two rooks, f4 is the primary danger at the moment.

notes.text: White prepares to take over the e-file and avoids ...f4 tricks.
A quiet position with a small White edge.
notes.original: A quiet position with a small White edge. White's plan is to pressure b7 and expand with a5; you hold the c-file and play ...Rc8 to meet it.

notes.text: The king walk looks crazy but is roughly level.
One of the most analysed positions in the Classical Variation: the queen drops back to c7 after the usual bishop…
notes.original: One of the most analysed positions in the Classical Variation: the queen drops back to c7 after the usual bishop trade, before White decides where to put the king. This exact move order runs a little differently from our main Classical repertoire choices elsewhere in the book, so treat this as supplementary deep-theory reference for one of the position's most famous branch points rather than a required addition to your main lines. All three of White's top tries here keep only a small, well-known and long-since-fully-explored edge - nothing that should concern a well-prepared Black player.

notes.text: Also possible: Bd2.
Also possible: Be3.
White is slightly better.
White has to recapture with the queen.
Hits the queen again and gains a tempo.
Takes the pawn.
Supports the knight on g4, so Rg1 attacks nothing.
notes.original: Supports the knight on g4, so Rg1 attacks nothing. White's attack is slow and he keeps a small edge.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Retreats the bishop and keeps the structure compact, with a small edge for White.
Your freeing break, striking the d4 pawn.
Hits the queen.
An equal-looking endgame with a small White edge.
notes.original: An equal-looking endgame with a small White edge. Your king is in the centre but it is safe in this endgame: aim for ...Ke7 and ...Rc8.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The queen has to leave e4.
notes.original: The queen has to leave e4. Qh4 adds pressure on f6 and h6 while keeping the queen safe.

notes.text: Offers a knight for the bishop.
Hits the queen.
The pawns are damaged and White has a small edge.
notes.original: The pawns are damaged and White has a small edge. Play for ...Rhg8 and keep the knight routes open.

notes.text: Counterattacks the queen on c7, but you win it first and the knight forks the rooks.
...reaching a very level position with simplified piece count.
Develops and keeps ...c5 in reserve.
The counter in the centre.
White has a pawn storm against your king, so the position is sharp but balanced.
notes.original: White has a pawn storm against your king, so the position is sharp but balanced. Open lines with ...hxg5 and bring pieces back to defend.

notes.text: Also fine for you.
...and the position remains level with chances for both sides.
The thematic freeing move: it challenges d4 and opens the way for your pieces.
The position is level.
notes.original: The position is level. White's knight on d4 is strong, but you have easy development and a healthy structure.

notes.text: ...reaching a position that's actually a touch pleasant for White without being dangerous.
Solid: it blocks the diagonal of the bishop on c4 and opens the f8-a3 diagonal for your bishop.
White jumps in to hit f6 and g7.
Defends g7 so that Nxf6+ and Nxg7+ do not win a pawn.
You trade the dark-squared bishops and the position is level.
The bishop retreats to h7, where it still watches the long diagonal b1-h7 and cannot be harassed again.
notes.original: The bishop retreats to h7, where it still watches the long diagonal b1-h7 and cannot be harassed again. This is the only sensible reply, and your plan afterwards is simple: develop with ...Nf6, trade the bishop pair by ...Bxd3 when White commits the bishop to d3, play ...e6 and ...Be7, then castle short and use ...c5 to open lines. Avoid any retreat to f5 or any capture on c2.

notes.text: Trading White's strong bishop removes the danger of Bxh7 ideas and costs you nothing.
notes.original: Trading White's strong bishop removes the danger of Bxh7 ideas and costs you nothing. The e6 pawn fixes the dark squares and opens the way for the kingside bishop.

notes.text: You have a fully developed, flexible position, only slightly behind in space, and ...c5 or ...Nbd7 with ...c5 is your…
notes.original: You have a fully developed, flexible position, only slightly behind in space, and ...c5 or ...Nbd7 with ...c5 is your plan. This is a semi-open position with White's pawn on h5 next to an advanced h-pawn structure; the centre is open and White has a small space edge on the kingside. Both sides may castle on opposite wings, White long and you probably short or even queenside. Your plan: trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bxd3, develop with ...e6 and ...Be7, then strike in the centre with ...c5 or ...Nbd7 followed by ...c5. White wants a quick attack with Bd2, O-O-O and the h-file, using the pawn on h5. You meet it by keeping your pieces flexible and your king safe. The risk is leaving the bishop on g6 loose, because White can hit it, and an early ...h5 weakens you. If White deviates, avoid weakening moves and trade the strong bishop.

notes.text: ...and Black completes development without difficulty.
Guards e5 and prepares ...Qc7 and ...Nbd7.
notes.original: Guards e5 and prepares ...Qc7 and ...Nbd7. White's plan is f5 to hit both the bishop on g6 and the e6 pawn.

notes.text: The h-file opens for your rook.
White's pieces watch e6 and f7 but your structure holds, so the position is level.
notes.original: White's pieces watch e6 and f7 but your structure holds, so the position is level. Aim for ...c5 or ...b5.

notes.text: White gets f4 and f5 in quickly.
...and the position stays balanced once Black meets the pawn storm with normal development.
Guards e5 and prepares ...Qc7 and ...Ne7.
notes.original: Guards e5 and prepares ...Qc7 and ...Ne7. White's idea is f5, which attacks both the bishop and e6.

notes.text: You have traded both bishops for knights.
notes.original: You have traded both bishops for knights. White has the bishop pair but you get d5 and f5 for the knights and the structure is stable, so the position is level.

notes.text: Trap: 6.dxe5? Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Bxc5 8.f4 Na6 9.Bxa6 and White is losing.
Trap: 6...exd4? 7.Nxd8 Kxd8 8.Nf3 Ke8 9.Qe2+ Be7 and Black is losing.
Black eventually wins the pawn back, but White is behind in development and a little cramped.
notes.original: Black eventually wins the pawn back, but White is behind in development and a little cramped. Black dominates.

notes.text: White uses the bishop to take control of e4 and hopes for Bxh7.
Kicks the bishop and gains space.
Grabbing b2 is possible, but your queen is far from home and White's lead in development gives him chances, so…
notes.original: Grabbing b2 is possible, but your queen is far from home and White's lead in development gives him chances, so the position is level.

notes.text: The solid alternative, level.
Trap: 6...Bxe4? 7.Nxd4 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 e5 9.Nf5 g6 and Black is losing.
Safe or risk-free?
notes.original: Safe or risk-free? Not quite: White gets big attacking chances for the pawn, similar to the Smith-Morra Gambit in the Sicilian. White leads in development, but if Black defends accurately Black ends up a pawn ahead after a short attack.

notes.text: Trying to solidify the position.
The light-squared bishop is off the board, which removes a burdensome piece and can change the outcome of the game.
Black need not fear the bishop eyeing the queen; there is no hidden tactic behind it.
The position is equal.
White trades off the strong knight and goes for a sharp sequence against h7.
A wild sequence that ends level: White regains his pawn and takes on b7 with the rook, but ...Rd2 gives…
notes.original: A wild sequence that ends level: White regains his pawn and takes on b7 with the rook, but ...Rd2 gives you counterplay against the queen and the second rank.

notes.text: White just loses time and you are better.
Solid and good.
notes.original: Solid and good. It opens the way for the f8 bishop and takes away the threat on e6 by the knight. Your plan is to develop with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bxd3, and challenge the centre with ...c5. Castle short. Avoid ...Nf6 too early without taking care of Qf3, since the queen can bother f5 and f7 together. The position is balanced with a tiny edge for you.

notes.text: Also fine.
notes.original: Also fine. After Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 h6 you drive the knight back, then play ...e6 and ...Be7 with a clear plan.

notes.text: You trade the pair of bishops and develop with a solid structure.
notes.original: You trade the pair of bishops and develop with a solid structure. Next is castling.

notes.text: You strike in the centre at the right moment and your position is solid, with a small advantage in the…
notes.original: You strike in the centre at the right moment and your position is solid, with a small advantage in the numbers and easy development. This is an open position where White is a pawn up but his pieces are undeveloped, with the knight still on g1 and the king on e1, and the queens are facing each other on the d-file. Your plan: trade queens with ...Qxd3 Nxd3, then play ...Nbd7 and ...Nxc5 or ...Bxc5 to win the pawn back, and castle short. White wants to hold c5 with b4 and develop with Nc3 and Bd2. The mistake is ...Qxd3 Nxd3 Bxc5? because Nxc5 wins a piece, so always bring the knight first. If White plays b4, remain patient and target c5 with ...a5.

notes.text: White wants to retreat the knight from g5 only after bringing the other knight out, and hopes to gain time…
notes.original: White wants to retreat the knight from g5 only after bringing the other knight out, and hopes to gain time with Nh4 against your bishop on f5. It is very common in practice, but the knight on g5 is stuck with no good square, which makes the move a little dubious.

notes.text: White has lost two knight moves for nothing and the game is level.
The position is equal.
Develop the knight to d7 so that ...Ngf6 trades off the strong e4 knight.
notes.original: Develop the knight to d7 so that ...Ngf6 trades off the strong e4 knight. Your plan is ...e5, which challenges d4 and opens lines for your bishops; the c8 bishop is already outside, so ...e5 is your natural break. Avoid ...e6 too early, which shuts in your f5 bishop.

notes.text: Strike at once.
notes.original: Strike at once. The f5 bishop is shielded by the knight on e4, so you can afford the break.

notes.text: Recapture with the queen so f5 stays protected after the discovered attack from d3.
You retake the pawn with a knight that jumps to the centre; the queen on f6 keeps defending f5.
notes.original: You retake the pawn with a knight that jumps to the centre; the queen on f6 keeps defending f5. Do not recapture with the queen on e5, which would allow Bxf5.

notes.text: After the trades you have a comfortable, active position with the queen on f5 and a good knight on e5.
notes.original: After the trades you have a comfortable, active position with the queen on f5 and a good knight on e5. This is an open, active position where your queen on f5 and knight on e5 are well placed, and the position is level. It is White's move, so he may play f4 or Nd4 to hit your queen. Your plan is, first, to develop ...Bd6 and castle long, bringing the rooks to the d-file. Second, keep the knight on e5 strong. Third, use ...Rhe8 and ...Nc4 for pressure. If White plays f4, retreat ...Ng6 or ...Nc6, and if he plays Nd4, move the queen to g6. The risk is losing a tempo to attacks on the queen or on the knight.

notes.text: The normal move, and the reason 5.Ng5 is only a sideline.
notes.original: The normal move, and the reason 5.Ng5 is only a sideline. White trades the knight that has just recaptured on e4 and Black accepts a slightly doubled f-pawn, getting the bishop pair and a very comfortable game in return. White loses nothing here. The Alien move does the opposite: it spends a tempo on an attack that Black can switch off with one pawn move.

notes.text: Ng3!? White wants to preserve his knight hoping to find some more sophisticated game and to keep things imbalanced.
notes.original: Ng3!? White wants to preserve his knight hoping to find some more sophisticated game and to keep things imbalanced. However after the move h5! Black gets a strong initiative on the kingside.

notes.text: 5.Ng5 tries to provoke ...h6 and unsettle Black's kingside.
notes.original: 5.Ng5 tries to provoke ...h6 and unsettle Black's kingside. After 5...h6 Black's kingside is a little weaker and White gets some initiative, but 6.Nxf6+ was the stronger follow-up.

notes.text: The "Alien Gambit": an eccentric, mostly-for-fun knight sacrifice on f7, occasionally seen in blitz and rapid play.
5.Qd3 brings the queen out early, offering a trade of knights on e4 to simplify toward an endgame-leaning structure.
5.Bd3 develops immediately, offering Black the chance to grab the d4 pawn with ...Qxd4 for a quick, sharp fight.
Idea: 4...Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 gives you a very solid kingside and easy development.
notes.original:
Idea: 4...Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 gives you a very solid kingside and easy development. Bishop to d6, castle, rook to e8, and reroute the knight via d7 to f8. White's queenside majority is the long-term issue, so keep your pieces active.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Bxh2? loses material on moves 7 to 8.
Next: 🔵 09 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 02. Model game: 🟡 Game 13.

notes.text: B15 Caro-Kann Defense: Tartakower Variation Viktor Korchnoi has played 5...exf6 many times (including in a world championship match).
notes.original: B15 Caro-Kann Defense: Tartakower Variation Viktor Korchnoi has played 5...exf6 many times (including in a world championship match). 5...exf6 is sounder than 5...gxf6!? of the Bronstein-Larsen Variation and offers Black rapid development.

notes.text: Idea: 5...gxf6 is the fighting choice.
notes.original:
Idea: 5...gxf6 is the fighting choice. You use the open g-file, castle long after ...Qd5, ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O, and play for an attack. Your structure is worse, so you have to stay active.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ gxf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Qxf3? loses material on move 7.
Next: 🔵 10 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plans: 🟠 Plan 02, 🟠 Plan 10.

notes.text: The Bronstein-Larsen Variation is the most aggressive way to play against the Classical Caro Kann.
notes.original: The Bronstein-Larsen Variation is the most aggressive way to play against the Classical Caro Kann. First and foremost black weakens his kingside and voluntarily makes a double pawn but in exchange of a dangerous attack on the kingside. The g file is open and further play would be met on the kingside or on the center. Playable, but exf6 is more accurate.

notes.text: This dislodges the bishop; ...Be6 is not possible because it would weaken the kingside badly.
notes.original: This dislodges the bishop; ...Be6 is not possible because it would weaken the kingside badly. ...Be7 and ...0-0 are the right follow-up.

notes.text: Bd3 is another idea, offering a pawn for early development and aggression.
notes.original: Bd3 is another idea, offering a pawn for early development and aggression. There is no need to suffer through the defence: just play ...Bd6 and follow the standard procedure of the Korchnoi Variation.

notes.text: Be3 - develops to a quiet square instead of the main c3/Bc4/Bd3 tries, preparing Qd2 or long castling without committing…
notes.original: Be3 - develops to a quiet square instead of the main c3/Bc4/Bd3 tries, preparing Qd2 or long castling without committing the bishop to an exposed diagonal.

notes.text: 6.Nf3 develops instead of the sharper c3/Bd3 setups, heading for a quick O-O.
White develops the bishop to its best square before playing Nf3 or Ne2, and so asks you how you want…
notes.original: White develops the bishop to its best square before playing Nf3 or Ne2, and so asks you how you want to deal with it. With your pawn on f6 the e5 and d6 squares are the key points.

notes.text: There is little to add about the Tartakower: follow the usual ...Bd6 and ...0-0 set-up and you will most likely…
notes.original: There is little to add about the Tartakower: follow the usual ...Bd6 and ...0-0 set-up and you will most likely be fine. Other interesting lines in the Tartakower are included as well.

notes.text: Black plans ...Re8, ...Be6, ...Nd7, ...Nf8 and ...h6 if necessary - the set-up Black should always aim for here.
8.Qc2 is the most common try here, eyeing h7 and preparing to meet ...Re8+ by developing rather than castling queenside…
notes.original: 8.Qc2 is the most common try here, eyeing h7 and preparing to meet ...Re8+ by developing rather than castling queenside immediately. This is arguably the main line here, not just a sideline alongside 8.Ne2.

notes.text: Contrasting case: compare this to the 8.Qc2 move-order, where the same ...Re8 IS check.
notes.original: Contrasting case: compare this to the 8.Qc2 move-order, where the same ...Re8 IS check. Here White played 8.Ne2 first, and that knight now physically sits on the e-file between the rook and the king, so ...Re8 is just a normal developing/centralizing move, not a check. The lesson: whether a rook lift on the open e-file comes with tempo depends entirely on whether White's knight has already occupied e2, not on the rook move itself.

notes.text: 9.O-O completes development immediately instead of delaying with Qc2 first.
...h6 is the logical and safer choice; the more ambitious ...f5!? is also possible.
9...h6 stops any future Ng5 ideas and gives the king some luft before continuing with ...Nd7/...Bf5/...c5 depending on White's setup.
...h5 aims at White's kingside.
notes.original: ...h5 aims at White's kingside. With the help of the bishop pair, White's king will be in real danger once the attack gets going.

notes.text: 10.O-O connects the rooks and gets the king fully safe before deciding how to use the extra space; Black meets…
notes.original: 10.O-O connects the rooks and gets the king fully safe before deciding how to use the extra space; Black meets it with the natural developing ...Nd7, and now White has a real choice of four plans at move 11.

notes.text: 10...Nd7 heads for b6 or f8 depending on which bishop move White chooses next.
11.Be3 is the most natural square for the bishop, eyeing c5 and supporting a future d4-d5 break.
11.Ng3 eyes f5/h5 and keeps options open about which bishop develops where.
11.Bf4 offers the trade of dark-squared bishops immediately rather than keeping it on the board.
11.Bd2 keeps the bishop flexible (can still swing to e3, c1, or stay put) while preparing Rae1.
11...Nf8 keeps flexibility, just as against Bf4/Bd2.
12.Rfe1 contests the open file Black opened back on move 8.
12...Bg4 develops actively, hitting f3/e2 and preparing ...Qd7 or ...Rad8.
White's strongest try here, stronger than Rad1.
Trap: 13...Bxa2? 14.b3 Qc7 15.Qxa2 Bxh2+ 16.Kh1 Rxe3 and Black is in serious trouble.
The opening phase is over and Black is fine.
Trap: 14...Bxa2? 15.b3 f5 16.Nxf5 Bxh2+ 17.Kh1 g6 and Black is clearly worse.
The knight retreats to reroute via e3 and free the e2 square for the rooks.
White gains queenside space; the plan is b4 and c5 to give the bishops room.
Fix g3 and take the kingside squares from the knight.
Black stands solid.
notes.original: Black stands solid. Your knight lands on e6 and the doubled pawn on f6 controls e5 and g5.

notes.text: 9.Be3 develops the bishop before committing the king, an alternative to the immediate O-O or h3 tries at the same…
notes.original: 9.Be3 develops the bishop before committing the king, an alternative to the immediate O-O or h3 tries at the same node.

notes.text: 9.Bd2 develops the bishop flexibly, keeping the option of O-O-O alongside the more common O-O.
10.Bd2 prepares O-O-O.
notes.original: 10.Bd2 prepares O-O-O. ...c5 hits the centre and Black gets counterplay.

notes.text: 11.Bf4 offers the trade of dark-squared bishops right after castling, instead of developing the queenside pieces first.
The opening phase is over and Black is fine.
notes.original: The opening phase is over and Black is fine. Pieces should be exchanged to avoid complications on the kingside.

notes.text: This is the idea: trade every piece that could attack your kingside.

notes.original: 8...Re8+ is the natural, forced response, using the open e-file with tempo before White's king finds safety. Contrasting case: compare this to the 8.Ne2 move-order elsewhere in this chapter, where the identical-looking move ...Re8 is not check. The difference has nothing to do with the rook move itself: here White has not yet moved the e1-knight, so the e8-e1 file is completely open and ...Re8+ is a real check; in the 8.Ne2 line, that same knight already sits on e2, blocking the file, so ...Re8 there is just a normal developing move with no check. Whether a rook lift on an open file comes with tempo depends entirely on what already occupies the file, not on the rook move itself. Choice guide: choose this if you want a very solid pawn structure with easy plans (doubled f-pawns that guard e5 and g5) and the bishop pair in some lines (low risk, medium theory). The queen check on e8 forces White to decide how to block it: 9.Ne2 and 9.Be3 are the main choices.

White grabs space but leaves d4 a bit loose. An equal position where you have solid pieces and no weaknesses, and you should aim for ...Ne6 and ...Qf6.
This is a closed centre where White has traded the f-pawn structure and you have pawns on c6, d6 and f6, so the position is solid with no space advantage for either side. Both kings will castle short, you may wait. Your plan: bring the knight round with ...Nf8 and then ...Ne6 or ...Ng6, play ...Qd7 and ...Bf5, then castle short. White wants to push c4 and make space but this leaves d4 a little loose. You meet it by targeting d4 with ...Ne6 and ...Qf6. The risk is playing ...Nb6, which lets White gain time with Bd3 or Bb3. This is a semi-open position in which White has just traded the dark-squared bishop on d6 and your queen side expansion ...b5 is in the air. Your plan: recapture ...Qxd6 or ...cxd6, castle short, and push ...b4 and ...a5 to gain space on the queen side. White wants to castle long and attack with g4 and h4, so keep your king safe and do not castle too early. Choice guide: after 5.Ng5 the safe and most popular reply is 5...Ngf6 (about two games in three), which is safe and positional and leads to a small White edge. 5...e6 and 5...Ndf6 are balanced alternatives that score about the same. 5...h6 is the one to avoid: it scores worst for Black because of 6.Ne6!. The key is to trade knights at once and not allow the white knights to jump to g5.

Your knight lands on a strong central post and eyes c4.
You hit the queen and the f2 and h2 squares again; White's edge is tiny and you are well coordinated.
White gains space, which is not necessarily bad but has drawbacks: the d-pawn may become isolated, which is a liability,…
notes.original: White gains space, which is not necessarily bad but has drawbacks: the d-pawn may become isolated, which is a liability, and Black is encouraged to attack the space advantage. Black's aim is to fight against it and create complications for both sides.

notes.text: Beware of castling queenside, sometimes it is alright to castle queenside if White does not have any major attack on…
notes.original: Beware of castling queenside, sometimes it is alright to castle queenside if White does not have any major attack on the queenside.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White puts a rook on the e-file to prepare c4 and Ne4.
Offer a queen trade so you can untangle.
White's c4 kicks the knight but you gain a solid setup.
You expand on the kingside, and the position stays balanced.
Keep this trap in mind: after 8...Bxf3, recapturing 9.Bxf3? loses a pawn to 9...Nxc4.
White has no other choice other than to take back with the g pawn since other options would not be…
notes.original: White has no other choice other than to take back with the g pawn since other options would not be necessary since the pawn will hang.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White hits the c4 knight to regain the pawn, but your knight has a safe retreat.
Fianchetto the bishop to guard the long diagonal.
You are a clean pawn up and White has little to show for it.
White's king is dragged out and White falls further behind.
White is slightly better.
White has the bishop pair and the g-file; Be3 and Qd2 prepare Qa5 against your queenside.
Strike at the centre before White consolidates.
You reach an endgame with sound pawns and White keeps only a tiny edge.
The calm reply: after Bd3 Bd6 and Qe2 h6 the game transposes to the main line of the chapter.
The ambitious reply - kick the knight at once.
notes.original: The ambitious reply - kick the knight at once. White has no good retreat: 7.Bd3? hxg5 wins a piece and 7.Nxf7 Kxf7 just gives the knight away. The best White can do is 7.Nh3, after which Black takes space on the kingside. This is a sharp but balanced choice that scores better for Black in practice than the main-line ...e6.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White supports the Ne5 jump and the e-file.
Freeing break that opens the bishop.
You offer the bishop trade to kill the pressure on the e5 knight.
You then develop the Bb7; White's edge is tiny with no concrete threats.
Take the knight, and after Bxe4 return with ...Nf6, kicking the bishop.
notes.original: Take the knight, and after Bxe4 return with ...Nf6, kicking the bishop. This removes the dangerous white knight and keeps your position sound.

notes.text: This looks natural but runs into 7.Neg5, with threats on h7 and on e6, and White keeps a clear initiative.
What White plays next: 6.Bd3 is the main move and the line given above.
notes.original: What White plays next: 6.Bd3 is the main move and the line given above. 6.Bc4 and 6.N1f3 are the two other common moves, and 6.Nxf7!? is the speculative knight sacrifice that is seen a lot in online play. Each is covered below, with the one reply Black should remember.

notes.text: This move seems logical, as Nxf7 doesn't work.
notes.original: This move seems logical, as Nxf7 doesn't work. However, White can get a slight edge with Ne6! and can win quickly if Black makes a blunder. A grandmaster lost to this trap. The e8-h5 diagonal is slightly weakened, and so is f7. The main line is Ne6! Qb6 (Wisely avoiding fxe6?? Qh5+ g6 Qxg6#) Nxf8 Nxf8 with two Bishops and a slight edge.

notes.text: The knight sacrifice.
notes.original: The knight sacrifice. White gives up a whole piece to drag the king into the open. In online games it scores a little over half, because Black has to find a few accurate moves, but it is unsound. Choice guide: this is White's gamble, not yours - just take the knight and then follow the rules in the notes below.

notes.text: The bishop eyes f7 at once.
notes.original: The bishop eyes f7 at once. It is the second most common move after 6.Bd3. The structure is normal and White keeps a small plus, but there is one big trap: ...h6? loses on the spot to Bxf7#. Choice guide: the safe and standard reply is 6...e6; 6...Nd5 is a good, slightly sharper alternative.

notes.text: A flexible developing move: the other knight comes out so that the g5-knight is supported.
notes.original: A flexible developing move: the other knight comes out so that the g5-knight is supported. White usually follows with Bd3 and Qe2. Choice guide: 6...e6 is the safe and positional reply and transposes to the main line; 6...h6 is the more ambitious reply that actually scores slightly better for Black and is the most accurate move.

notes.text: Watch out: this is the move that scores worst for Black here (White wins two-thirds of the games).
notes.original: Watch out: this is the move that scores worst for Black here (White wins two-thirds of the games). The point is 7.Ne6! and the knight cannot be taken profitably.

notes.text: A second main move: White develops the queen first and keeps the choice of knight development for later.
notes.original: A second main move: White develops the queen first and keeps the choice of knight development for later. After ...Bd6 N1f3 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Qc7 the position transposes to the main line. White plays 7.Qe2 about once in five games here.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The sacrificial try: the knight takes on e6, offering a piece.
notes.original: The sacrificial try: the knight takes on e6, offering a piece. Black recaptures - a piece for two pawns is not enough. Played in about one game in five here and it scores a little over half for White in practice, but it is not sound. Choice guide: the safe and correct answer is 9...fxe6.

notes.text: Another sacrifice that does not work.
notes.original: Another sacrifice that does not work. Black takes the knight and then develops.

notes.text: The knight retreats to the rim and White loses the edge.
notes.original: The knight retreats to the rim and White loses the edge. Black castles or plays ...Qc7 and is slightly better.

notes.text: The problem with the Ng5 knight manoeuvre, black if black knows what he is doing black tendencies might even get…
notes.original: The problem with the Ng5 knight manoeuvre, black if black knows what he is doing black tendencies might even get an edge since this would allow black to play for this e5! Breakthrough. Effectively dislodging white's grasp on the center.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The bishop hits the rook on f1.
Level.
notes.original: Level. Take care with White's other moves: your Be5 and queen aim at h2.

notes.text: The point: Bxh2+ drags the king out and the pin on the e-file gives you the advantage.
Watch out: checking first is a mistake.
notes.original: Watch out: checking first is a mistake. After c3 fxe6 Bg6+ Black loses the bishop on b4 and the king is exposed.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White is winning.
Black is clearly better.
The queen is attacked and White keeps a clear edge.
The only move - Black takes the knight with the king.
notes.original: The only move - Black takes the knight with the king. Any other reply (for example ...e6 or ...h6) allows Nxd8 and White wins the queen. After the king capture White has two serious tries: 7.Nf3 (developing first) and 7.Bc4+ (check at once).

notes.text: Watch out: not recapturing is a blunder because the knight on f7 takes the queen.
The most common move: bring the knight out and keep the Bc4+ idea in reserve.
notes.original: The most common move: bring the knight out and keep the Bc4+ idea in reserve. Black's king is exposed, but every White piece is still on its starting square, so Black has time to consolidate.

notes.text: The immediate check.
notes.original: The immediate check. Black has three sensible answers: ...e6 (safest), ...Nd5 (most active) and ...Ke8 (playable but scores worse in practice).

notes.text: The simplest setup: the e6 pawn shuts the c4-g8 diagonal for good, so Bc4 is no longer check, and the…
notes.original: The simplest setup: the e6 pawn shuts the c4-g8 diagonal for good, so Bc4 is no longer check, and the bishop can later come out to d6.

notes.text: White attacks the e6 pawn and aims at the king.
notes.original: White attacks the e6 pawn and aims at the king. Black has three equally good replies: ...Nd5, ...h6 and ...Nb6, all clearly better for Black. The one move to avoid is 8...Qa5+?!, which lets White trade queens and lose the least.

notes.text: Black centralises the knight and takes the sting out of Bb3.
notes.original: Black centralises the knight and takes the sting out of Bb3. After ...Bd6 and ...h6 the king is safe on f7 and Black keeps the extra piece.

notes.text: Kick the bishop right away.
notes.original: Kick the bishop right away. After Bb3 Bd6 Black should watch the Ng5+ check but remains clearly better.

notes.text: A useful waiting move that stops Ng5+ forever and gives the king the h7 square.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
The solid reply, and the one most players choose.
notes.original: The solid reply, and the one most players choose. The pawn blocks the check and Black plans ...Nb6, ...Be7 and ...Kg8.

notes.text: The most active reply, blocking with the knight and keeping the pawn structure intact.
notes.original: The most active reply, blocking with the knight and keeping the pawn structure intact. It is not the best move but it scores best for Black in practice.

notes.text: Also good objectively, but in practice White scores better here because the king is back in the centre and Black…
notes.original: Also good objectively, but in practice White scores better here because the king is back in the centre and Black has to find ...Nb6 and ...c5 to free the position. Choose this only if you know the line.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
White is winning.
The reply played in nearly every game - the pawn guards f7 and prepares ...Nb6 to kick the bishop.
This blocks the bishop's diagonal and prepares ...Be7.
A good alternative to 6...e6: the knight blocks the bishop's path to f7 and Black keeps the e-pawn flexible.
notes.original: A good alternative to 6...e6: the knight blocks the bishop's path to f7 and Black keeps the e-pawn flexible. White keeps a modest edge.

notes.text: Watch out: the natural-looking ...h6?? loses at once to Bxf7# - the knight on g5 guards the bishop and the…
notes.original: Watch out: the natural-looking ...h6?? loses at once to Bxf7# - the knight on g5 guards the bishop and the king has no square.

notes.text: Watch out: this one loses a pawn and more - Bxf7+ wins material because the knight on g5 supports the…
notes.original: Watch out: this one loses a pawn and more - Bxf7+ wins material because the knight on g5 supports the capture.

notes.text: White adds pressure to e6 and prepares to develop.
notes.original: White adds pressure to e6 and prepares to develop. Black answers with ...Nb6 and ...h6, getting a normal Caro-Kann position.

notes.text: Now your knight hits the bishop with tempo and heads towards d5 or c4, so White has to spend time…
notes.original: Now your knight hits the bishop with tempo and heads towards d5 or c4, so White has to spend time retreating.

notes.text: Black has gained queenside space and the game is balanced.
White is slightly better.
White is winning.
White is winning.
The knight steps back to the edge, the awkward but best move.
Black has expanded on both wings and White has spent a lot of moves with the knight.
The only good move which actually holds the position onwards.
notes.original:
The only good move which actually holds the position onwards.
Trap: 6...fxe6? 7.Qh5+ g6 8.Qxg6# and Black gets mated.

notes.text: Trap: 7...Qb4+? 8.c3 Qd6 9.Nxd7 Bxd7 10.Nf3 O-O-O and Black is losing.
notes.original:
Trap: 7...Qb4+? 8.c3 Qd6 9.Nxd7 Bxd7 10.Nf3 O-O-O and Black is losing.
Trap: 7...Qa5+? 8.Bd2 Qa4 9.Nxd7 Qxd4 10.Bc3 Qe4+ and Black is losing.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Break open the centre.
White's bishop pair gives a small edge, but your knights are active and you can chip at d4 with ...c5.
An early a4 push loses time and you equalise.
You challenge the e4 knight and develop at the same time.
notes.original: You challenge the e4 knight and develop at the same time. The other knight stays on d7 in reserve, because ...Nb6 can later hit the bishop with tempo. Your plan is ...e6, ...Be7, castle short and then free your game with ...c5. If White trades on f6, recapture with the knight and keep your healthy structure. White keeps only a small edge here.

notes.text: This looks natural but is less accurate: after Ng3 White keeps his strong knight and your ...h5 and ...h4 pawn…
notes.original: This looks natural but is less accurate: after Ng3 White keeps his strong knight and your ...h5 and ...h4 pawn advances cost time while the kingside gets loose.

notes.text: White doubles up on f7 and eyes h7.
notes.original: White doubles up on f7 and eyes h7. Stay calm and keep the pieces covered.

notes.text: Kick the knight away so that your kingside stays safe.
This is the freeing break.
notes.original: This is the freeing break. You complete development with ...Be7 and ...O-O next.

notes.text: White gets an advanced knight, but you can challenge it with ...Nbd7 or ...Bd6 ideas.
notes.original: White gets an advanced knight, but you can challenge it with ...Nbd7 or ...Bd6 ideas. Your pieces are safe and ...c5 gives you real counterplay. This is an open-centre game with a pawn on d4 for White and your c5 pawn already challenging it, and both bishops still to develop. White's knight on e5 is advanced but needs support from d4. Your plan: challenge it with ...Nbd7, finish development with ...Be7 and ...Bd7 or ...O-O, and take on d4 when it wins time. White wants to keep the knight on e5, add Be3 and pressure f7 and the h-file. The risk is f7, where Nxf7 and Qh5 tricks appear if you neglect it, and opening the d-file with ...cxd4 before you castle. If White deviates by playing Bxe6, recapture with the f-pawn or bishop calmly.

notes.text: This is the safe reply: the d7 knight steps to f6 and the g8 knight stays home, so you are…
notes.original: This is the safe reply: the d7 knight steps to f6 and the g8 knight stays home, so you are ready to trade on e4. The point is that you never leave the e7 pawn pinned in front of your king. Your plan is ...Nxe4, ...Nf6, then ...g6 and ...Bg7 or ...Bf5 ideas, with ...Qa5+ as a useful resource against the d2 square. Keep the structure flexible and trade pieces. White keeps only a small edge here.

notes.text: This is the trap.
notes.original: This is the trap. The queen pins the e7 pawn against your king, so the knight jumps in with mate:

notes.text: Trade off the strong knight.
With tempo you hit the queen.
Your bishop will go to g7 and the queen can use a5.
This check forces White to put a piece on d2, which hampers his own development.
A calm, solid position where you complete development with ...Bg7 and ...O-O and aim for ...c5.
notes.original: A calm, solid position where you complete development with ...Bg7 and ...O-O and aim for ...c5. This is a quiet, semi-open structure with White's pawn on d4 and your solid c6, e7 and g6 pawns. You will castle short with your bishop on g7. After the check, your queen on a5 is attacked, so retreat it with ...Qd5 or ...Qb6, then play ...Bg7, ...O-O and ...Bf5 to hit the queen on d3. Aim for the freeing break ...c5 once you are castled. White wants to castle long or short, play c4 and use his space and the d4 pawn. The big risk is at the fifth move, where ...Ngf6?? loses to Nd6 mate, so always play ...Ndf6. Never grab the a2 pawn with the queen.

notes.text: 3...Bf5 is the standard reply to the Advance Variation.
notes.original: 3...Bf5 is the standard reply to the Advance Variation. The bishop gets outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in.

notes.text: The standard Short Variation setup covered in the main Advance Variation chapters.
notes.original: The standard Short Variation setup covered in the main Advance Variation chapters. This chapter covers two respectable independent tries White has instead of the main 4.Nf3: 4.Nd2 and the immediate 4.c4. Black's plan against both: these sidelines avoid committing the king's knight to f3 immediately, but they don't change Black's fundamentals - develop the e7-knight (toward f5 or g6), challenge the center with ...c5 (or accept a favorable structure if White trades on d5/c4 first), and use the extra tempo White spends on these knight/pawn maneuvers to finish development slightly ahead of schedule.

notes.text: An interesting move that gives the position a French flavour.
notes.original: An interesting move that gives the position a French flavour. Black strikes at the centre at once and starts undermining White's Advance set-up. White must either keep the centre together or release it by taking the pawn, in which case Black spends several moves chasing the c- or e-pawn.

notes.text: Nf3 is the most natural reply: White will castle kingside and develop the bishop pair.
notes.original: Nf3 is the most natural reply: White will castle kingside and develop the bishop pair. Sidelines such as c4?! are treated in this chapter as well.

notes.text: 4.Bd3 offers the immediate trade of light-squared bishops before developing anything else, a distinct system from the Nf3-first approach the…
notes.original: 4.Bd3 offers the immediate trade of light-squared bishops before developing anything else, a distinct system from the Nf3-first approach the chapter otherwise builds around.

notes.text: 4.Ne2 develops flexibly, keeping the option of either Ng3 or Nf4 depending on Black's setup.
4.c3 supports the center quietly before committing the king's knight anywhere, keeping options for both Nf3 and f4 later.
4.Be3 develops toward c5/d4 immediately, preparing a later Nd2-Nf3 setup without blocking the c-pawn.
A strong Advance Variation sideline: Nc3!? first, with c3 not strictly needed since White can hold the centre anyway.
notes.original: A strong Advance Variation sideline: Nc3!? first, with c3 not strictly needed since White can hold the centre anyway. Delaying c3 keeps the square free for the knight, which can cover e4 in lines where Black tries to place a bishop there (typical of the Bayonet Attack with g4, here delayed until Nc3 has been played). After ...e6 g4! White gets dangerous play. Despite the age of the idea, it remains effective.

notes.text: The Shirov Variation - a flexible try that develops a piece and keeps the option of a later g4 pawn…
notes.original: The Shirov Variation - a flexible try that develops a piece and keeps the option of a later g4 pawn storm in reserve. Black's plan: whichever way White times the g4 advance (immediately, as in the 4.g4!? branch below, or after Nc3 first), the bishop steps back to g6 and then h7 - it is never actually trapped, just relocated to a long, safe diagonal. Once that is settled, Black's normal freeing break ...c5 followed by ...Nc6/...Ne7 and, if White grabs the h5-pawn, a well-timed ...cxd4 tactical point (explained below) give Black completely comfortable, often better, positions in practice.

notes.text: The early c4 move is rather a bit inaccurate since Black's fortified center is unbreakable.
notes.original: The early c4 move is rather a bit inaccurate since Black's fortified center is unbreakable. The early c4 move would be met with e6.

notes.text: A pure, immediate challenge to the center, associated at the top level with Magnus Carlsen.
notes.original: A pure, immediate challenge to the center, associated at the top level with Magnus Carlsen. White doesn't bother developing the king's knight first at all.

notes.text: This move order of the Bayonet Attack is not good, since it exposes White's kingside at once, but it contains…
notes.original: This move order of the Bayonet Attack is not good, since it exposes White's kingside at once, but it contains a few traps, so be prepared.

notes.text: The Bayonet Attack - a completely different try from the Tal Variation above.
notes.original: The Bayonet Attack - a completely different try from the Tal Variation above. Instead of preparing the pawn storm with h4 first, White goes straight for the point: a pawn on g4 attacks the Bf5 bishop directly (gxf5 is a real threat next move), forcing an immediate decision. Black has three reasonable retreats - 4...Be4, 4...Bg6, and 4...Bd7 - each covered below. Black's general plan across this whole branch: none of the three retreats loses material or the game by force; the practical difference between them is how much central/kingside space Black concedes versus how active the bishop stays, and whether Black is willing to meet White's typical e5-e6!? pawn sacrifice by capturing (...fxe6, opening the f-file for a rook) or declining it (...Qd6, keeping the structure intact at the cost of a tempo).

notes.text: The immediate, more committal try - grab the bishop's retreat square before Black can complete development at all.
4.h4 gains space and prepares g4.
notes.original: 4.h4 gains space and prepares g4. Black has to be careful with ...e6 here: after 5.g4 Bg6 6.h5 the bishop is driven back to h7 and White gains a lot of space.

notes.text: The Tal Variation, named for Mikhail Tal.
notes.original: The Tal Variation, named for Mikhail Tal. It is a different system from the Bayonet Attack covered later in this chapter: here White pushes the h-pawn first while the bishop can still sit on f5, instead of hitting it at once with g4. It is a serious, popular try, not a minor sideline.

notes.text: Plan: ...e6, ...Qb6 and ...Ne7
An idea popularized at the top level by Wesley So.
notes.original: An idea popularized at the top level by Wesley So. Rather than the natural-looking 4.Nf3, White routes the knight to b3 instead, eyeing c5 and d4 while keeping f3 open for the other knight or a future f4 push.

notes.text: Black has locked in the position with a very solid pawn chain, is comfortable defensively and positionally, and can look…
notes.original: Black has locked in the position with a very solid pawn chain, is comfortable defensively and positionally, and can look for activity in the middlegame.

notes.text: 5.Bd3 swaps the light-squared bishops at once and simplifies.
notes.original: 5.Bd3 swaps the light-squared bishops at once and simplifies. Black fights back in the centre with ...c5 and then castles kingside.

notes.text: This was the move Magnus Carlsen played against Alireza Firouzja at the 2021 World Rapid and Blitz Championship; Firouzja went…
notes.original: This was the move Magnus Carlsen played against Alireza Firouzja at the 2021 World Rapid and Blitz Championship; Firouzja went on to lose after errors in the middlegame. It hits Black's centre immediately, but the position is defensible and less worrying than other move orders. Caro-Kann players should be ready for such surprises.

notes.text: Perhaps this move is a bit unorthodox but white probably wants to play c4.
White does have to option to play Be2 to keep the tension on the center and make the position less…
notes.original: White does have to option to play Be2 to keep the tension on the center and make the position less complicated since an exchange would help simplify the position.

notes.text: Other players of this line may play c3 to avoid theory, and White may well succeed in that.
White develops the knight to pressure d5 and prepares Bd3 or Be2 without losing control of e5.
notes.original: White develops the knight to pressure d5 and prepares Bd3 or Be2 without losing control of e5. White does not mind trading bishops on d3 if the pawn recapture is useful. For you the question is where to put your knights while your light-squared bishop is already outside the chain.

notes.text: Idea: Against 4.Nf3, play ...e6, take the bishop if White offers it with Bd3, and bring your knights to d7…
notes.original:
Idea: Against 4.Nf3, play ...e6, take the bishop if White offers it with Bd3, and bring your knights to d7 and f5. Your breaks are ...c5 and ...f6 against White's centre.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nf3 e6 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.Qxd3 Nd7
Watch out: ...Nxe5? loses material on moves 7 to 12. ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 9 to 10.
Next: 🔵 12 continues the Advance Variation. Plans: 🟠 Plan 06, 🟠 Plan 08. Model games: 🟡 Game 01, 🟡 Game 02.

notes.text: ...Nd7 is useful in case White attacks on the kingside: from d7 the knight can go to f8 and add…
notes.original: ...Nd7 is useful in case White attacks on the kingside: from d7 the knight can go to f8 and add another defender of h7, forming a fortress.

notes.text: With the light-squared bishops traded, you strike at d4 at once: the e5 pawn depends on it, and your pawn…
notes.original: With the light-squared bishops traded, you strike at d4 at once: the e5 pawn depends on it, and your pawn chain on d5 and e6 stays solid.

notes.text: You have already traded your light bishop, so ...c5 hits d4 at once.
notes.original: You have already traded your light bishop, so ...c5 hits d4 at once. White wants to support e5 with Be3 and f4 and keep a space edge. You trade on d4 and develop with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7.

notes.text: The break at d4 is the standard way to free your game and fits the simplified structure after the bishop…
notes.original: The break at d4 is the standard way to free your game and fits the simplified structure after the bishop trade.

notes.text: Challenge d4 now, before White completes development with c3 and Nbd2.
notes.original: Challenge d4 now, before White completes development with c3 and Nbd2. The pawn break is the thematic way to free your position.

notes.text: An in-between check that makes White decide how to block it.
notes.original: An in-between check that makes White decide how to block it. The knight on d2 ends up pinned along the diagonal, which is why Qa6 is playable next.

notes.text: White's strongest try here, stronger than Nc3.
Playable, but c5 is more accurate.
Another plan is to focus on the queenside rather than the kingside and find counterplay there.
notes.original: Another plan is to focus on the queenside rather than the kingside and find counterplay there. Note that ...c5 is not possible because of the Nb5 threat, after which a knight outpost on d6 would cause great problems for Black.

notes.text: White is playing with fire: the kingside is at risk, but White can play Kh1 and stack rooks on the…
notes.original: White is playing with fire: the kingside is at risk, but White can play Kh1 and stack rooks on the g-file to launch an attack.

notes.text: If White does not play g4, Black can castle, play ...c5 and then storm the queenside with ...a7-a5.
Other quiet moves are possible, such as ...g5, when Black attacks the white kingside with a pawn storm.
If White retreats the knight, ...h5 lets Black attack the king at once.
The f-file will be open for Black's rook whether or not White takes the f-pawn.
notes.original: The f-file will be open for Black's rook whether or not White takes the f-pawn. Black is better because White's kingside is weak with little counterplay, and White lacks pieces to switch to the queenside. With the open f-file and a bishop on h4, Black gets a very dynamic attack on the king.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White wants to use the queen on the e-file and the bishop on f4 to pile up on e5 and…
notes.original: White wants to use the queen on the e-file and the bishop on f4 to pile up on e5 and the d-file, since your knight on d7 is the key defender. You reply with ...Qf8, which defends the f-file and keeps an eye on f2, then bring the rook to e8 and f7. The position is level, so keep your pieces coordinated around the loose bishop on h4.

notes.text: Be5 aims to trade your good knight, and f4 gains space.
notes.original: Be5 aims to trade your good knight, and f4 gains space. Both ideas are met by ...h6 and the central break ...Nxe5.

notes.text: A sharper try: after 18.gxh5 Qxh5 you get active play against the king.
Black is slightly better.
White wants to bring the bishop to g3 and double on the f-file, while the queen eyes the loose a7…
notes.original: White wants to bring the bishop to g3 and double on the f-file, while the queen eyes the loose a7 pawn. You answer with ...Rf7 to guard the seventh rank and prepare ...Raf8. When the dark bishops come off on g3, a lone knight on d7 is enough to keep e5 under pressure.

notes.text: You take the pawn only because the knight on d4 gives White very little in return.
If White spends a tempo on the king, the e5 pawn falls once the queens leave the board.
11...h5 starts the kingside pawn storm, with the knight on h4 helping.
White cannot take due to the Bc5 pin.
Black is clearly better.
White offers a queen trade and covers b2, hoping to take the sting out of your extra pawn.
notes.original: White offers a queen trade and covers b2, hoping to take the sting out of your extra pawn. Do not worry: the d4 pawn cramps White and the knight on h4 is annoying, so you retreat ...Bd8, which still guards h4 along the diagonal, and bring a rook to c8. Then ...Rc4 hits the weak g4 pawn while keeping d4 alive.

notes.original: This is the same idea as in the 7.dxc5 move order: White hits c6 so that ...O-O Nxc6 bxc6 wrecks your structure. Bxc5 and Nc4 then pick on the c-pawns, while ...Qd5 and ...Bd3 are your counterplay against the bishop on e2.

One of the most debated modern lines of the Advance Variation: 5.Be2 c5 6.Be3 Qb6, where Black grabs the b2…
notes.original: One of the most debated modern lines of the Advance Variation: 5.Be2 c5 6.Be3 Qb6, where Black grabs the b2 pawn and White gets active pieces in return. This is a different branch than our main recommendation (which meets 4.Nf3 e6 with the calmer 5.Bd3, trading light-squared bishops immediately) - it's included here purely as supplementary reference, so you understand the objective status of the sharper try too, in case you ever want it or face it from the other side of the board. White's most testing try is this calm developing move, meeting the pawn grab with active pieces instead of rushing.

notes.original: Nbd2 - routes the knight to a flexible square instead of the main lines with c4 or castling, keeping the option of Nb3 or Nb1-c3 open depending on how Black continues.

notes.original: White regains the pawn and opens lines against your king while the queen is out of play on b2. You castle long, and the knight lands on d5 to cover c3 and e3. The sequence is sharp but level.

notes.original: ...Nc6 (Solid & Optimal) - simple, natural development that keeps pressure on d4 without taking any risks; the safest route to a normal, comfortable middlegame.

notes.original: ...Qxb2 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - grabs the offered pawn at once, accepting a sharper position where White gets some initiative for the material but nothing immediately decisive.

notes.original: Prepare ...c5 and support e5. Plan: ...Ne7 and ...Nf5, then ...c5 to hit d4. Keep the center pawns on e6 and d5 safe, and do not hurry to castle before you see what White does with the dark-squared bishop. If White plays Bf4 you answer with ...Ne7 and ...Nf5 anyway.

notes.text: Also fine, and it keeps ...Nf5 in mind.

notes.original: This is a useful lever: you will play ...h4 or ...Be7 and aim for ...c5. Avoid playing ...g5 too early without a knight on f5. Equal and comfortable. This is a closed French-style position where your light-squared bishop has been traded for White's d3 bishop, so White has doubled pawns on d3 and d4, and you have good squares on f5 and g6. Your plan: complete development with ...Be7, then hit d4 with ...c5 and, with the knight on f5, use ...h4 to cramp the kingside. White wants Ng3 to challenge your knight, then Nxf5 and exf5, or Qd2 with Bg5. Meet Ng3 calmly and recapture with the e-pawn. The mistake is ...g5 early, because it weakens the light squares without support. If White plays Ng3, retreat only if needed.

It is a natural, solid move that is common in practice (played in about 872,000 games). So the tension on d4 is going to be resolved soon, so choose your piece placement with that in mind.

notes.original: The knight heads for the best square at once: from d7 it adds another attacker to d4, keeps e5 under watch and leaves c6 free for your other knight, which will come via e7. You plan ...cxd4 followed by ...Bb4+ to force White to use a knight on d2, then ...Ne7 and ...Ba5 to keep the bishop active on the a5-e1 diagonal. Aim for the knight to land on c6 or f5 and for the ...f6 break to challenge e5.

notes.original: The check is useful because it drags the b1 knight to d2, where it blocks the bishop on c1 and leaves the d4 pawn short of support.

notes.text: Develop, and ...Nb6 or ...Nc6 follow.
notes.original: Develop, and ...Nb6 or ...Nc6 follow. Avoid taking on d4 with the knight too early; the pawn is poisoned only when everything else is ready.

notes.text: White has more space, but you have a healthy position and targets on d4; ...Nc6 and ...f6 are your breaks.
notes.original: White has more space, but you have a healthy position and targets on d4; ...Nc6 and ...f6 are your breaks. This is a closed Advance structure with White's pawn chain on d4 and e5 and yours on c5, d5 and e6. White has more space, but d4 is your target. Your plan: finish development with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7, castle short, then keep hitting d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 and prepare the break ...f6 to open the position. White wants to hold d4 with c3 and Nbd2 and to keep the centre closed while his space tells. You meet that by trading pieces and attacking the base of his chain. The risk is playing ...cxd4 too early, which frees his game and gives him the c-file. If White plays Bb5 or Qe2, just castle and keep your knights coordinated.

notes.original: Ng3 prepares h4-h5 to chase your bishop on g6. Your answer is ...c5, hitting d4, and Bb5+ is met by ...Nc6. White cannot easily keep an edge.

notes.original: White builds a quiet centre: c3 protects d4 and gets ready for Bd3 or Bb5+. The knight on g3 also eyes h5 and f5.

notes.original: White parts with the bishop and your rook lands actively on c6. Your pieces are better placed and there is nothing to fear.

notes.original: Stop the pawn dead. Now h4 is fixed and the knight on g3 has no way to harass your bishop.

notes.original: The structure is symmetrical with an isolated d5 pawn, but all your pieces are active and the pin is harmless. Equality is easy to hold.

notes.original: The sharper try is h4-h5 to trap your bishop. Answer with ...h5, and you stand fine.

notes.original: White develops the bishop to challenge your light-squared bishop on f5. If you trade, the advanced pawn on e5 loses its protector, but your structure remains sound. It is a very common move (played in about 776,000 games).

notes.original: White offers a queen trade on b6 to open the a-file for you, which does you no harm. Instead of trading, you develop the knight and plan ...h5-h4, which cramps White's kingside so that g4 is never possible. Then ...Ne7-g6 attacks e5.

notes.text: Qb3 hits b7 and offers a queen swap that would leave you passive.
notes.original: Qb3 hits b7 and offers a queen swap that would leave you passive. Keep the queens on: the knight supports ...c5 and ...h5, and your queen stays active on b6.

notes.text: Quiet development.
notes.original: Quiet development. The bishop eyes g5 and prepares castling, since White's queen on b3 has no real targets.

notes.original: Fix the kingside before you develop. This stops White expanding and keeps ...Nd7 and ...h4 in reserve.

Now Ng3 is no longer possible either, so the bishop keeps its diagonal.

notes.original: The h4 pawn has fixed White's kingside and your knight reaches g6, pressuring e5. The position is level, and ...Rc8 with ...c5 is your way to challenge d4.

notes.text: The position stays level and is easy to play.
White shuffles back to prepare f4.
notes.original: White shuffles back to prepare f4. You have a sound structure and no weaknesses to worry about.

notes.text: Equally fine and keeps the queens on.

notes.text: You develop the knight to e7 so that, after the bishops are exchanged, the knight can reach f5 and pressure…
notes.original: You develop the knight to e7 so that, after the bishops are exchanged, the knight can reach f5 and pressure the d4 pawn. The plan is ...Bxd3, then ...h6 to deny the knight on g5, ...Nf5 and finally ...c5 to hit the d4 pawn. Keep the knight flexible and castle short when ready. Avoid retreating with ...Bg6 without a plan, since White can then play h4 with attacking ideas. The position is level.

notes.text: Trading at once is also fine.
notes.original: Trading at once is also fine. After Qxd3 you aim for ...c5 and ...Nc6 with a free game, then ...h6 and ...a6 as useful waiting moves.

notes.text: Stops any Ng5 or Bg5 tricks and prepares ...Nf5.
Your knight sits happily on f5, you hold the e4 and d5 squares and your structure is sound, so the…
notes.original: Your knight sits happily on f5, you hold the e4 and d5 squares and your structure is sound, so the game is equal with plenty of play for you. This is a closed French-style position where White has more space with pawns on e5 and d4, but your knight on f5 attacks d4 and you hold the e4 and d5 squares. Your plan: bring the other knight to d7 to hit e5, play ...Be7 and castle short, then challenge d4 with ...c5. White wants Nc3 and Ne4 to reach d6, or Qb3 to hit your pawn on b7. If Qb3 comes, defend with ...Qb6 and keep your pieces coordinated. The mistake is leaving b7 hanging while you develop. If White plays Bd2, continue ...Nd7.

notes.text: ...and the position stays balanced.
You add a defender for the ...f6 break: the pawn on e5 is the base of White's space, so attack…
notes.original: You add a defender for the ...f6 break: the pawn on e5 is the base of White's space, so attack it and the advantage becomes a liability.

notes.original: Your queen on b6 is awkward: c5 will gain a tempo on it, and the bishop on f5 is exposed to Nc3-b5. So you prepare ...f6 to chip away at e5 and let the queen go back to d8. After the exchange on f6, c5 is not dangerous.

notes.original: Be3 and Qc1 exist only to cover b2 against your queen, so White has already spent time before c4 hits d5. Developing the knight supports d5 and prepares the usual ...f6 lever against e5.

notes.original: White's c4 questions your d5 pawn while Qc1 keeps b2 safe. The knight supports d5 and keeps the queen free.

notes.original: The immediate lever. Be3 and Qc1 only protect b2, so you attack the head of the chain at once before White has a developed centre.

notes.original: c5 gains time on your queen, but it also gives up control of d4 and b4, so the retreat costs you very little.

notes.original: c5 gains a tempo on your queen, but it also gives up control of d4 and b4, so the retreat costs you little.

notes.original: You are fully developed with a safe king after castling, and the c5 pawn can later be undermined with ...b6. White has no lasting edge.

notes.original: After castling you have an easy position. The c5 pawn can later be undermined with ...b6.
