notes.original: Grabbing c4 also works and the knight lands on d5, but White gets time against your queenside pawns, so it is a shade less clean.

notes.text: Simple and solid - Black keeps developing normally rather than reacting to a threat that hasn't been played yet.
g4 strikes at the centre immediately and expands on the kingside.
notes.original: g4 strikes at the centre immediately and expands on the kingside. The extended pawns are useful later, since White will proceed with a powerful kingside attack. The question is what happens if the attention shifts and Black is the one attacking.

notes.text: Now White follows up with the pawn storm, gaining space on the kingside at the cost of real structural commitments…
notes.original: Now White follows up with the pawn storm, gaining space on the kingside at the cost of real structural commitments (the g- and h-files will be easier for Black to use later, and e5/f4 can become weak).

notes.text: White will usually harass the light-squared bishop further, and here is clearly planning to trap it with h5.
Black is clearly better.
7.Be3 develops before committing to h4, supporting d4 and preparing queenside castling.
Idea: White throws the kingside pawns forward with g4 and h4.
notes.original:
Idea: White throws the kingside pawns forward with g4 and h4. Drop the bishop back to g6, hit the centre at once with ...c5, and meet h4 with ...h5. Counterattack in the centre rather than wait.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 Bg6 6.Nge2 c5 7.h4 h5
Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Bxf2+? loses material on move 12.
Next: 🔵 13 continues the Advance Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 07. Model game: 🟡 Game 04.

notes.text: ...h5 is needed because White is going to expand on the queenside.
notes.original: ...h5 is needed because White is going to expand on the queenside. White would usually castle queenside and attack Black's king if ...h6!? is played instead of ...h5, and Black may have to sacrifice a pawn.

notes.text: h6!? Looks like a safer option but in case you missed Be3 followed by f4!
notes.original: h6!? Looks like a safer option but in case you missed Be3 followed by f4! Would give white a very feasible position indeed.

notes.text: Black cannot leave the bishop alone on g6, since the knight would take it and Black's kingside would deteriorate further.
Black gives up the h-pawn on purpose.
notes.original: Black gives up the h-pawn on purpose. It opens the h-file for Black's rook, and the pawn would have come under pressure anyway.

notes.text: The key tactical point: White grabs the h5-pawn, but the bishop is completely safe on h7 and Black has two…
notes.original: The key tactical point: White grabs the h5-pawn, but the bishop is completely safe on h7 and Black has two move orders here that both work well, as the game below shows (Aabling Thomsen vs Schandorff, Denmark 2010). The common idea in both: meet Nxh5 with an immediate strike on d4, either right away with ...cxd4 or after first developing the knight to c6.

notes.text: 9.g5 pushes through immediately rather than trading on g6 first, trying to lock the bishop out of the game entirely.
The position is equal.
Extra: only needed if White plays 4.Nc3 or 4.g4 against 3...Bf5.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays 4.Nc3 or 4.g4 against 3...Bf5.
Idea: The same 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 set-up as 🔵 12, but here you take on d4 with 9...cxd4. Develop with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7 and keep your king flexible. The 4.g4 lines are covered at move 4.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 Bg6 6.Nge2 c5 7.h4 h5 8.Nf4 Bh7 9.Nxh5 cxd4
Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 4 to 6.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White had to exchange on c5, for two reasons.
notes.original: White had to exchange on c5, for two reasons. The knight on c3 stops him from supporting d4 with c3, and if he leaves the pawn alone Black plays ...cxd4 and gets the better game.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
A necessary move to suppress black's attack on the center.
notes.original: A necessary move to suppress black's attack on the center. Loosening up the grip eh? Bg2 is more accurate.

notes.text: Trap: 12...Nxe5? 13.Nxg7+ Kf8 14.Nxe6+ fxe6 15.Bxd8 Rxd8 and Black is losing.
The position is equal.
The knight on g7 is nearly trapped, so White cashes it in for the e6 pawn with check.
notes.original: The knight on g7 is nearly trapped, so White cashes it in for the e6 pawn with check. The plan is to fix your structure with fxe6 and then use the queen on d2 to trade bishops. You have the knight on b4 to hit c2. The material is gone and the position is balanced.

notes.text: You keep the slightly better pawn structure.
A kingside pawn storm is tempting but it leaves White worse.
White does best to exchange bishop for queen to loosen up black's pressure on the center.
This wins a pawn for White but loses the knight in exchange.
notes.original: This wins a pawn for White but loses the knight in exchange. Black's tactic is ...Kf7, forcing Nh5, then ...d4 to evict the knight, and ...Qa5 wins the bishop, forking the king on e1 and the bishop on b5.

notes.text: The threat now is ...d5, and Black would be winning.
Qf3 is forced because of the ...d5 threat; it is the only good move that holds for White.
13...O-O-O is the most accurate move.
notes.original: 13...O-O-O is the most accurate move. The alternative 13...Be4 is also playable: it is about as good.

notes.text: Black is winning.
Playable, but Ne7 is more accurate.
The tactic Be4 does not work only because of the dark-squared bishop, which can come to help in an assault.
notes.original: The tactic Be4 does not work only because of the dark-squared bishop, which can come to help in an assault. With that bishop gone, White is lost.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's strongest try here, stronger than Bxe3.
Black's pressure is so strong that White can hardly hold: Black dominates the d-file, White's king is stuck and the…
notes.original: Black's pressure is so strong that White can hardly hold: Black dominates the d-file, White's king is stuck and the kingside is weak.

notes.text: White wants to open the h-file for the rook on h1 against your rook on h8, and the knight on…
notes.original: White wants to open the h-file for the rook on h1 against your rook on h8, and the knight on g7 supports that attack. But you take the bishop on e3 and bring the rook into the seventh rank with ...Rd2. White's pawns on e3 and c2 become targets.

notes.text: Your king is safe on b8 and all your pieces are working.
Taking the a7 pawn only wins a pawn for a moment, since the bishop falls.
Black is winning.
White wants to trade a pair of rooks to relieve the pressure on the second rank; your rook on d2…
notes.original: White wants to trade a pair of rooks to relieve the pressure on the second rank; your rook on d2 hits c2 and f2, so it is the most dangerous attacker. After the rooks go off, the queen trade on f1 leaves you with the better pieces and an ending White cannot save.

notes.text: You win the exchange of queens and keep a big plus.
Kicking the queen with the pawn opens the g1-a7 diagonal for the check and White loses material.
White is losing: the pawn on e2 and the queen on f3 are too much to handle.
White has to remove the advanced pawn that attacks f1 and prepares to queen.
notes.original: White has to remove the advanced pawn that attacks f1 and prepares to queen. Your queen on f3 and the rook on d8 are ready to attack the king on g1, and the g4 pawn is a free target. After ...Qxe2 the threats on the d-file and Be3 are decisive.

notes.text: You get an extra piece and keep the attack.
Giving up the queen for a pawn leads to a forced loss.
Black is clearly better.
The position is equal.
Your plan is to remove the knight on c3 so you can play ...d4 and open the long diagonal against…
notes.original: Your plan is to remove the knight on c3 so you can play ...d4 and open the long diagonal against White's king, since you are down material. The checks on h1 and e4 keep you in the game.

notes.text: The queen checks keep the position level.
Retreating the bishop passively makes White's extra material count, which gives White an edge.
Black's pressure is strong and White will struggle to hold.
White is a lot of material up but his knight on g7 is nearly trapped and the king is stuck…
notes.original: White is a lot of material up but his knight on g7 is nearly trapped and the king is stuck in the centre. The queen on e2 guards the king and the e4 pawn, while Nh5 later tries to rescue the knight. You keep the initiative with ...e3 and ...Rhg8.

notes.text: Your king is safer and the pieces are more active, so you stay a little better.
This natural queen move just loses to the check on b4.
Attacks the rook and the knight!
White castles to save the rook from the diagonal, but the d4 fork gets there first.
notes.original: White castles to save the rook from the diagonal, but the d4 fork gets there first. After ...dxc3 you add the pressure on f2, and ...Qf3 with ...Be4 would threaten mate on g2. White grabs the g7 pawn but his queen is too far from his own king.

notes.text: The extra pieces tell.
Nd5 tries to deflect the queen from the long diagonal, but you take it and everything stays defended, so White…
notes.original: Nd5 tries to deflect the queen from the long diagonal, but you take it and everything stays defended, so White just loses a piece.

notes.text: Black is winning.
White attacks the queen and wants to trade it so that the extra material (a piece for you, a few…
notes.original: White attacks the queen and wants to trade it so that the extra material (a piece for you, a few pawns for White) becomes less relevant. But you take b2 and keep the queen trade on your terms. Then the passed d-pawn runs and the bishops dominate.

notes.text: The d3 pawn cramps White and you have an extra bishop.
Defending with the bishop only delays the loss.
10.Be3 is another option, but it costs a tempo.
notes.original: 10.Be3 is another option, but it costs a tempo. After 10...cxd4 the b2 pawn is weak and ...Qa5 would breach White's position.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White is a pawn up and the knight on h5 eyes g7, but your queen on b4 attacks the b2…
notes.original: White is a pawn up and the knight on h5 eyes g7, but your queen on b4 attacks the b2 pawn and the d4 bishop. After the bishop retreats you castle long and aim at b2 and a2. White's extra pawn means little compared with your lead in development.

notes.text: The queen picks up pawns while your pieces are active.
The greedy pawn grab cannot save White, who lags in development.
Trap: 10.Nxh5? dxc3 11.Bb5+ Nc6 12.Bxc6+ bxc6 13.bxc3 and White is losing.
...and Black's central counterplay with ...cxd4 proves faster.
White is trying to use the rook on h3 to swing to b3 and hit b7, while the knights on…
notes.original: White is trying to use the rook on h3 to swing to b3 and hit b7, while the knights on d4 and f4 are well placed. You develop with ...Ne7 and ...Nbc6 so you can trade off the strong knights with ...Nf5. After the exchanges on f5 you keep a clear edge.

notes.text: The knight develops and supports ...Nbc6 and ...Nf5, so White's rook lift on h3 comes too late.
Rb3 hits b7, so cover it and keep the pressure on e5.
You have the more active pieces and a safe king.
Your pieces are better placed and White's rook lift on h3 has not led to anything.
notes.original: Your pieces are better placed and White's rook lift on h3 has not led to anything. You are clearly better.

notes.text: This allows White to win the h5 pawn back, so you are only a little better.
A greedy try that is less accurate, since White gets counterplay.
White is slightly better.
You regain the pawn immediately, because White's pawn on c5 is attacked by both the bishop and the knight, and…
notes.original: You regain the pawn immediately, because White's pawn on c5 is attacked by both the bishop and the knight, and trading the dark bishops removes White's best piece. Then ...Ne4 trades off the strong knight, and Bg2 faces the bishop on e4.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge with the bishop pair gone, but the position is safe for you.
Taking with the knight lets White open the position against you.
Black is winning.
White castles and prepares Nb5, which threatens Nc7+ forking king and rook.
notes.original: White castles and prepares Nb5, which threatens Nc7+ forking king and rook. You answer with ...Nge7 and ...O-O, then ...Nxb4 hits the loose queenside. Your queen on h4 and bishop on c5 keep everything pointed at f2 and the king.

notes.text: You are a pawn up with an attack.
A natural queen move walks into the knight jump to d4 and the trade on f2.
...and Black holds the balance.
Your idea is to regain c5 and keep the extra pawn on g4 under pressure.
notes.original: Your idea is to regain c5 and keep the extra pawn on g4 under pressure. The knight heads for f5 to hit the d4 knight and the e3 bishop. The bishop trade on d3 lets your queenside develop with ...Nc6 and ...Bxc5.

notes.text: The knight guards the g4 pawn and heads for f5 where it hits the knight on d4 and the bishop…
notes.original: The knight guards the g4 pawn and heads for f5 where it hits the knight on d4 and the bishop on e3.

notes.text: Challenge the knight on d4 and prepare ...Bxc5.
You regain the pawn and the opened files are fine for you.
You recover the c5 pawn and White's pawn structure on the kingside is wrecked.
notes.original: You recover the c5 pawn and White's pawn structure on the kingside is wrecked. Black is slightly better.

notes.text: This also holds, but gives White the extra counterplay on the g-file.
A tricky line where White returns material with Nxe6 tactics and you lose some of your advantage.
Keeping the central tension instead, with a later ...c5 break in mind, is equally playable - a matter of style…
notes.original: Keeping the central tension instead, with a later ...c5 break in mind, is equally playable - a matter of style rather than necessity.

notes.text: Simplest and most reliable response - just take the pawn.
notes.original: Simplest and most reliable response - just take the pawn. White has to spend real time winning it back, and Black gets a free, comfortable structure in return.

notes.text: A well-prepared opponent may play a3; Plan B is to take the pawn and then play ...c5.
White does not want to ruin the pawn structure.
White is slightly better.
White opens the position to use the bishop pair, and queens come off on d5.
notes.original: White opens the position to use the bishop pair, and queens come off on d5. Then h4 and Nh3 aim to shut your bishop out with g-pawn play. You neutralise this with ...h5 and ...f6.

notes.text: White has a small edge with the bishops, but your position is solid.
Offering the queen trade is another try.
Black is slightly better.
White wants to play g4 and trap the bishop on f5.
notes.original: White wants to play g4 and trap the bishop on f5. You answer with ...h6 so the bishop can retreat to h7. The a3 move then forces you to decide about the bishop on b4. After the trade on c3 the pawn break ...c5 gives you fine play.

notes.text: You keep a slight edge.
Quiet development lets you strike in the centre.
The position is equal.
White has grabbed b7 and now attacks the rook on a8 while pinning the knight on d7.
notes.original: White has grabbed b7 and now attacks the rook on a8 while pinning the knight on d7. Your reply is ...Rc8, moving the rook out of danger and unpinning the knight indirectly, and then ...Bc5 and ...Bd3 harass the white pieces that wandered out.

notes.text: Everything is balanced.
Taking a second pawn is risky for White and gives you play.
4...Be4 keeps the bishop active and centralized rather than retreating passively.
notes.original:
4...Be4 keeps the bishop active and centralized rather than retreating passively. The point is that after 5.f3, the bishop is kicked again, but Black has already provoked White into weakening the e3-square and slightly loosening the kingside.
Trap: 4...Qa5+? 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.gxf5 Qxd4 7.Nf3 Qe4+ and Black is losing.

notes.text: 4...Bg6 is the most natural retreat - the bishop stays on the same diagonal and steps back one square, without…
notes.original: 4...Bg6 is the most natural retreat - the bishop stays on the same diagonal and steps back one square, without inviting the further f3 tempo-gain that 4...Be4 allows.

notes.text: 4...Bd7 is the most modest retreat - the bishop gives up its active diagonal entirely and tucks in next to…
notes.original: 4...Bd7 is the most modest retreat - the bishop gives up its active diagonal entirely and tucks in next to the king, but in exchange Black avoids all the immediate tactics of the other two retreats and keeps the position simple.

notes.text: Trap: 5...Qa5+? 6.Bd2 Qb6 7.fxe4 Qxd4 8.Nc3 e6 and Black is losing.
Trap: 5...Qa5+? 6.Bd2 Bxc2 7.Qxc2 Qb6 8.e6 Qxd4 and Black is losing.
The thematic pawn sacrifice of this whole system: White offers the e5-pawn to rip open the center and the f-file…
notes.original: The thematic pawn sacrifice of this whole system: White offers the e5-pawn to rip open the center and the f-file while Black's king is still uncastled. Black has two ways to answer it, both fully playable.

notes.text: 7.e6 sacrifices a pawn to rip open Black's kingside before the bishop on g6 can retreat safely.
With the open h-file and the bishop pair, Black has enough compensation for the pawn.
notes.original: With the open h-file and the bishop pair, Black has enough compensation for the pawn. The pawn is a sacrifice for the initiative, so keep the light-squared bishop to maintain both the initiative and the bishop pair.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
You took h4 with check.
notes.original: You took h4 with check. The tempting Rxh4 fails to Qxh4+, so the king has to move. Kd2 is the best square because Ke2 lets you take on h5 with the rook. White then develops with Bd3 and Ne2 to harass your bishop on h4, while you play ...Nh6 and ...c5.

notes.text: Everything is balanced.
The king step to e2 allows ...Rxh5 and leaves you slightly better.
...and Black is already better after accepting the pawn accurately.
The e6 gambit is over and material is level, but you own the bishop pair and White's pawns on f3,…
notes.original: The e6 gambit is over and material is level, but you own the bishop pair and White's pawns on f3, g4 and h4 are loose. White develops the bishop to e3 and brings the queen to d2, while you answer with ...Nd7 and ...e5 to open the centre. After ...hxg4 the h-file is yours too.

notes.text: Now your central pawn mass is strong.
Offering the queen trade does not solve White's problems.
Black's plan in this whole system: the h4/h5 pawns are now fixed, which means the g4-square is permanently weak for…
notes.original: Black's plan in this whole system: the h4/h5 pawns are now fixed, which means the g4-square is permanently weak for White and the h4-pawn itself is a long-term target once rooks and knights get active. Black's recipe is almost always the same regardless of which fifth move White chooses: trade off the light-squared bishop or reroute it to a safe square (h7 or g6), meet the center with the freeing ...c5 break at the right moment, and look to land a knight on f5 or use the half-open h-file/g4 hole in the middlegame. None of this requires memorizing forcing lines - it is a structural plan, and the two main branches below (5.Bd3 and 5.c4) both show it in practice.

notes.text: A real try from established theory, not just a blunder.
notes.original: A real try from established theory, not just a blunder. The bishop develops actively and rules out ...Qb6 for a move, but the critical test below shows Black equalises comfortably with precise play.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The calmer, more positional approach - White offers the trade of light-squared bishops rather than letting Black keep the good…
notes.original: The calmer, more positional approach - White offers the trade of light-squared bishops rather than letting Black keep the good bishop. Very safe for White, but also gives up any hope of a quick attack.

notes.text: White finally develops and prepares c4 to hit your centre, while the pawn on h4 stays as support for an…
notes.original: White finally develops and prepares c4 to hit your centre, while the pawn on h4 stays as support for an attack on the kingside. It is a common move after this pawn push. So White wants to open the centre while you have not castled.

notes.text: The sharper, more aggressive try - open the center immediately while Black's king is still uncastled, rather than trading pieces…
notes.original: The sharper, more aggressive try - open the center immediately while Black's king is still uncastled, rather than trading pieces off.

notes.text: Striking at b2 and d4 at once, exactly as in the simpler 5.Bd3 and 5.c4 lines.
White's only real try.
notes.original: White's only real try. Defending b2 with 6.b3?! is well met by 6...e6 followed by ...c5, which is very bad for White.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qb6 8.Bxf5 e6 9.Bd3 Qxd4 and Black is clearly worse.
Simplest.
notes.original: Simplest. Grabbing the pawn with 6...Qxd4?! allows 7.Nf3 Qg4, and after the trades 8.Bxf5 Qxf5 White castles with 9.O-O, which produces the sort of tangle Black's opponents would gladly steer clear of; Black may well be fine there too, but there is no need to go looking for complications when the position is already comfortable.

notes.text: ...e6 reinforces the central pawn.
The point: the queen chases White's queen off d3 and offers a trade, a thoroughly Caro-Kannesque resource.
notes.original: The point: the queen chases White's queen off d3 and offers a trade, a thoroughly Caro-Kannesque resource. (7...Qxb2?! is dangerous here because of 8.e6!, hitting f7 with real force; stick with 7...Qa6.)

notes.text: This move order avoids heavy theory: c4 is the main line but runs into well-known theory after ...c5.
notes.original: This move order avoids heavy theory: c4 is the main line but runs into well-known theory after ...c5. Both are covered here, but this set-up is the one preferred. c5 was stronger.

notes.text: c5 was stronger.
The position is equal.
A queen trade would only allow Nxa6, which would favour both sides; still, an endgame is also acceptable for Caro-Kann…
notes.original: A queen trade would only allow Nxa6, which would favour both sides; still, an endgame is also acceptable for Caro-Kann players.

notes.text: Your queen on a6 faces the queen on d3, so c4 blocks that diagonal and hits d5.
notes.original: Your queen on a6 faces the queen on d3, so c4 blocks that diagonal and hits d5. After ...Bb4 pins the knight on d2, b3 supports the pawn, and you counter with ...c5 and ...Nc6.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White asks the bishop on b4 to decide.
notes.original: White asks the bishop on b4 to decide. After ...Bxd2 Nxd2 White has traded your active bishop and plans c5 to gain space. Your plan is ...Nd7 and ...Rac8, followed by ...Qb6 to hit the c5 pawn.

notes.text: White has more space but no clear attack.
The ...c5 break is your main resource.
The Tal Variation has been expanded with a new idea: after Nd2 the main recommendation is ...c5.
notes.original: The Tal Variation has been expanded with a new idea: after Nd2 the main recommendation is ...c5. White typically expects to play c3; the sharper c5 is highly theoretical, so extra variations have been added to cover it.

notes.text: This discourages White from playing b4.
The position is equal.
White stops ...a4 and fixes your a5 pawn.
notes.original: White stops ...a4 and fixes your a5 pawn. The idea is to trade knights and take the d4 square. You castle and take the c-file with ...Rfc8, so queen and rooks come into play.

notes.text: You hold comfortably.
Taking on c5 is also level.
10.Rb1 attacks the queen, but 10...Qxd4 is possible: the queens come off and Black is up two pawns.
Nb3 is another variation, a highly theoretical line in the Tal Variation.
notes.original: Nb3 is another variation, a highly theoretical line in the Tal Variation. The pressure on the centre from both sides makes it very complicated, so Black must take care to avoid errors in the opening.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White is two pawns down and calls on the queen to hold the position together.
notes.original: White is two pawns down and calls on the queen to hold the position together. You push ...d4 to take space from the knight on f3, then trade White's dangerous bishop with ...Bxg5 so your king can walk to e7.

notes.text: You hold the extra pawns.
The e6 break is White's only way to open lines, but you stay ahead.
...Nc6! Black's plan is ...Nb4, forking the king and the rook.
Black cannot play Nb4 because of Qb5+!
notes.original: Black cannot play Nb4 because of Qb5+! A horrible position for white in this particular position.

notes.text: 12...Qxa2 grabs a second pawn.
notes.original: 12...Qxa2 grabs a second pawn. White has more pieces developed, but cannot easily make that count.

notes.text: Bxc5 is made possible because Qa5+! with a fork on the king and knight would give his pieces back.
White needs to cover up the d4 pawn since the knight would later land in there.
The position is equal.
White hits the queen at once and wants to use the open c-file, since you are two pawns up but…
notes.original: White hits the queen at once and wants to use the open c-file, since you are two pawns up but your pieces are tangled in the centre. You give the check with ...Qb5+ and then bring the knight into play with ...Nh6, aiming to trade queens.

notes.text: It is an equal, double-edged position.
The e6 push does not work.
Black is clearly better.
White has traded a pawn for activity.
notes.original: White has traded a pawn for activity. The rook on c1 supports the central break d4, which would open the c-file against your queenside. You respond with ...a5 to stop b4, develop the knight on d7 and regroup the bishop to f8. You are a pawn up, so a calm position is enough.

notes.text: You keep an extra pawn and a safe position.
The quieter alternative to 6...Qa5+ - simply completing development.
notes.original: The quieter alternative to 6...Qa5+ - simply completing development. A very safe, thoroughly tested structure. Both choices are fine; 6...Qa5+ is included in more depth above because it leads to a clearer middlegame.

notes.text: Idea: Meet 4.h4 with 4...h5 so the pawn can't go any further.
notes.original:
Idea: Meet 4.h4 with 4...h5 so the pawn can't go any further. Trade bishops with ...Bxd3, then play ...Qa5+ and ...e6. The Bayonet Attack, 4.g4, has its own branch at move 4.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4 h5 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.Qxd3 Qa5+
Watch out: ...Qxd2+? loses material on moves 7 to 8. ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 10 to 12.
See also: 🟢 07 covers more of the Advance Variation. Plans: 🟠 Plan 04, 🟠 Plan 07. Model games: 🟡 Game 07, 🟡 Game 08.

notes.text: The critical, most-tested continuation - and the one both real games below actually chose over the quieter 6...e6.
notes.original: The critical, most-tested continuation - and the one both real games below actually chose over the quieter 6...e6. The check gains a tempo and keeps options open for where the queen and king want to be.

notes.text: A natural developing move that supports d4 and prepares c3 or Bg5.
notes.original: A natural developing move that supports d4 and prepares c3 or Bg5. White keeps a slight lead in development.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge.
If the queens come off you hit d4 and equalise.
You support the d5 pawn and open a retreat for your bishop on f5.
notes.original: You support the d5 pawn and open a retreat for your bishop on f5. Your plan is ...Bg4 or ...Be7, ...Nh6 and ...Nf5 to put a piece on f5, and ...c5 to attack d4. Avoid ...Qb6 too early, which loses time.

notes.text: After the queen comes to b3 you play ...Qc8 or ...Nc6 to cover b7 and keep your king in the…
notes.original: After the queen comes to b3 you play ...Qc8 or ...Nc6 to cover b7 and keep your king in the middle for one more move. White's other approach is 6.Bd3 instead of c4, and then you take the bishop with ...Bxd3 and settle into a solid structure. You are fine and roughly equal, but be careful about the b7 pawn. This is a semi-open position after the h-pawn push: your pawns on c6, e6 and h5 face White's centre, and your bishops are active. Your king may stay in the centre for a move or two. Your plan: protect b7 with ...Qc8, bring the knight with ...Nf5 or ...Nd7, trade bishops on g5 with ...Bxg5 when useful, and then castle short. White wants to attack b7 and e6 with Qb3 and Bc4 and use the h4 pawn as a hook. Meet that with ...Qc8 or ...Nc6. The risk is the b7 pawn and a sacrifice on e6. If White plays Bd3 instead of c4, take with ...Bxd3.

notes.text: This is also playable but slightly less accurate.

Perhaps the most testing try here.

Choice guide: 4...e6 or 4...Nc6?
notes.original: Choice guide: 4...e6 or 4...Nc6? Choose 4...e6 (this section) IF you want to win the c5-pawn back at once and reach a healthy position with a simple plan (the ...f6 break, ...Ne7-g6); it needs less memorisation. Choose 4...Nc6 (the main line of this chapter) IF you want to keep more tension and accept heavier theory. Risk level: low to medium. After 4...e6 Black intends ...Bxc5 next, so White has to pick a way to deal with that. The main tries are 5.a3, 5.Nf3, 5.Be3, 5.b4, 5.Bd3 and 5.Qh5; each is covered below with the practical answer.

notes.original: Choice guide: 4.c3 Nc6 (safe to balanced). Choose this if you want a French-style Advance structure with a good bishop on f5: ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bg6, then break with ...cxd4 at the right moment. The main line 5.Be2 and the sidelines 5.Bb5, 5.f4, 5.a3 and 5.Be3 are shown. 4.c3 Nc6 invites White to build a classical Advance centre. This is a closed Advance structure with White's pawns on d4 and e5, you with c6 and d5, and your light bishop already out on g4. White has more space but your pieces are active. Kings will probably stay in the centre for a while before you castle. Your plan: keep the pin with ...Bg4, develop the rook to c8 with tempo, then aim at d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qd7 and prepare ...f6 or ...Nf5 to undermine e5. White wants to hold d4 and break with c4 or push on the kingside. You meet it by trading pieces. The risk is castling too early or releasing the tension with ...cxd4 before your pieces are ready. If White deviates, stay calm and keep the c-file in mind.

notes.original: White supports the e5 pawn and prepares f5 to trap your bishop. It is very common in practice (played in about 204,000 games). So the bishop on g6 can be harassed by f5, so you must react precisely.

notes.original: You have given a pawn back but your structure is healthy and your pieces are active, so the position is balanced. Avoid the tempting 5...Qa5+, which allows 6.Nc3 and gives White a clear edge. This is an open, gambit-style position where material is level, White's king is still on e1 and his queen on h3 is exposed. Your pieces are active with Nd7, Nh6 and the bishop on f7. Your plan: play ...Nf5 to hit the queen and d4, then ...e6, ...Be7 and ...Qc7, and castle long when safe. White wants Bd3 and Ne5 to trade your active pieces, and to open the h-file with h5. The mistake is grabbing pawns with your queen and neglecting development. If White plays Bd3, meet it with ...e6 and keep trading the most dangerous attackers.

notes.text: This supports d5 and prepares ...Be4 or ...h5.
notes.original: This supports d5 and prepares ...Be4 or ...h5. Your plan is ...Be4 to avoid being kicked, then ...h5 to undermine g4. Keep your bishop active and castle long or short later. Avoid ...h5 immediately, because f5 would then trap the bishop on h7 and leave you short of squares. If White ever delays f5, you can play ...c5 and attack d4 at the right moment, trading White's centre for activity. Your knights go to d7 or c6 and f5 or h6 at the right time.

notes.original: This is an open, tense position after the bayonet g4 line: you have an open h-file with a rook on h8, and White's king is stretched. Your plan: develop with ...Ne7 and ...Nd7, then strike with ...c5 against d4, and put pressure on the h4 pawn with ...Rh8. Your king can go long or stay for now. White wants to play f5 to open the centre and bring his queen to g4 and g7. Meet f5 with ...exf5 and the queen. The risk is leaving g7 and the h-file loose and grabbing h4 hastily. If White plays f5 first, recapture and pile up on d4.

notes.original: This is too slow, since after f5 your bishop is stuck on h7 and White is the one with the initiative.

notes.original: White backs up the e5 pawn with a second pawn and plans Nf3, Be3 and a knight or bishop to a good square, keeping a big grip on space. The cost is that the king side is stretched: the f4 and g4 pawns can become targets and d4 is guarded only by pieces. So attack the base of the chain at once. The move is common in practice (played in about 106,000 games).

notes.original: White develops naturally rather than committing to an immediate pawn sacrifice - since the bishop is no longer on an exposed diagonal, there is less to gain from ripping the position open early.

notes.original: The other main try: strike in the center immediately rather than committing to ...h5 first. Both approaches are fully playable.

notes.original: Striking in the center immediately, while White's kingside pawns are stretched out and the rook on h5 needs a moment to get back into the game.

notes.original: A sharp, roughly balanced position where Black's activity (the h5-rook, the half-open c-file pressure) compensates fully for the slightly awkward-looking rook placement.

notes.original: White's pawn on e5 is the only thing holding the position together, so take it. The knight exchange keeps your rook active and the exchanges favour you.

notes.original: You win the c5 pawn back, and White's doubled e-pawns are weak. The position is balanced, with your king safer.

notes.original: Black regains the pawn next move with ...Qxc5 and stands at least equal, with a healthy structure and no weaknesses - a clean, low-theory way to meet the Bayonet Attack for players who would rather not memorize the sharper 4...Be4/4...Bg6 tactics.

notes.original: White's c3 prepares to protect the bishop on b5, but you win back the e5 pawn that cramps you and take the queen to the centre. The pawn on c5 is also under fire from ...Bxc5.

notes.original: Both kings are safe and the position is balanced. Your knight on e7 guards c6 and prepares ...Nd5.

notes.original: Asking the bishop a question at once is slower: White gets f4 in and the lines open while you are underdeveloped. You are slightly worse here.

notes.original: This is the thematic break: you hit d4 before White finishes development. After 6.dxc5 you answer ...e6, rebuilding a solid centre and preparing ...Bxc5 to win the pawn back with a good bishop. notes.original: White covers d4 but you do not mind, because ...h5 attacks g4. If White ignores it, ...hxg4 opens the h-file for your rook.

notes.original: Now your pawn kicks the bishop and the c5 pawn is doomed. After 9.Bf2 Bxc5 your bishop eyes f2, and you follow with ...Ne7 and ...Nc6. Avoid dropping back with ...e5 ideas; the point is to keep White's pawns overextended. White has more space but a loose pawn chain, and you are slightly better.

notes.text: This is an open, sharp position with a loose white pawn chain on e5, f4 and g5, against your active…
notes.original: This is an open, sharp position with a loose white pawn chain on e5, f4 and g5, against your active bishops on c5 and d7 and a pawn on d4. You are a little better. Your plan: defend d4 with ...Nc6, then play ...Nge7 and ...Qb6, and castle long once the queen has moved. White wants to win d4 with Nxd4 and Bxd4, and use his space on the kingside with h4. The risk is that d4 is attacked twice and defended once, so add a defender at once before anything else. If White plays Bxd4, recapture with the bishop and keep the c5 bishop active.

notes.text: This is playable but slower: White gets Nf3 and g5 in without being disturbed and you are the one who…
notes.original: This is playable but slower: White gets Nf3 and g5 in without being disturbed and you are the one who has to defend a cramped position instead of striking at d4.

notes.text: A sound alternative, though White is a touch more comfortable with the extra space in the centre.
c4 tries to open lines, but your queen takes d4 and the queen trade leaves you comfortable.

notes.original: White has to accept the weak pawn structure on the kingside. The position is level and your pieces have easy squares.

notes.original: The Two Knights Attack: White develops a second piece first and delays d4. In these chapters Black takes on e4, so White's knight has to recapture and White loses a tempo. Black then follows with ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6, as in the Karpov Variation.

notes.original: 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Ne5!? is sometimes called the Apocalypse Attack - a trappy try that looks scary (the knight eyes f7 and c6) but has no real venom once Black knows the refutation.

notes.original: 3.d3 - a quiet try that avoids committing the knight to c3 yet, keeping d3 flexible for either c4 or Nbd2 setups.

notes.text: This is the Classical System of the Caro Kann Defence against the standard "Two Knights Attack".
notes.original: This is the Classical System of the Caro Kann Defence against the standard "Two Knights Attack". Black's suppressive light square bishop is trying to loosen white's grasp on the center.

notes.text: The ...a6 system.
notes.original: The ...a6 system. This chapter covers a flexible ...a6 idea for sidestepping memorised theory against the Two Knights Attack. First and foremost, a6!? is a waiting move: rather than committing immediately, Black keeps an eye on the b5 square, denying White's pieces that outpost, and waits to see whether White occupies the centre with d4 or resolves the tension with an early exchange on d5. If White plays d4, the game usually transposes into normal Two Knights structures a tempo down for White's would-be b5 ideas; if White exchanges on d5 instead, Black recaptures freely and reaches a comfortable, no-theory position. The idea of the line is practical: it is easy to remember, hard for White to punish, and it steers the game away from whatever sharp theory White may have prepared. Playable, but Bg4 is more accurate.

notes.text: Choice guide: choose 4...Nf6 (as in 🔵 15 to 17 and 🟢 08) if you want a repertoire that works…
notes.original: Choice guide: choose 4...Nf6 (as in 🔵 15 to 17 and 🟢 08) if you want a repertoire that works in every Two Knights line. 4...Bf5 is shown mainly as a warning: with White's knight on f3 the standard Bf5-g6-h6 plan runs into Ne5 and Qh5 tactics, which is why this repertoire avoids it against 2.Nf3. The 5.Ng3 h5 gamble is shown as well. Risk level: high. After 4.Nxe4 Black normally develops with 4...Nf6; the alternatives below show why.

notes.text: A further option is ...Nf6, which usually ends up in a Classical Caro-Kann after the knight trade and the recapture,…
notes.original: A further option is ...Nf6, which usually ends up in a Classical Caro-Kann after the knight trade and the recapture, followed by d4. That central push is the natural continuation.

notes.original: 4...Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6 6.h4 h6 7.Ne5 Bh7 8.Qh5 g6 9.Bc4 leaves Black in trouble. Avoid this move order against 2.Nf3.

notes.original: 5.Qe2 - sidesteps the main 5.Nxf6+ trade entirely, pinning the e4-knight's retreat square and preparing to meet ...Nxe4 with a recapture that keeps the queen centralized.

Idea: Against the Two Knights, take on e4 at once and play ...Nf6.
notes.original:
Idea: Against the Two Knights, take on e4 at once and play ...Nf6. After 5.Nxf6+ exf6 you get the same easy set-up as 🔵 08: ...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Re8. Against 5.Qe2, remember that ...Nbd7?? allows Nd6 mate.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6
Watch out: ...Bxc4? loses material on moves 11 to 14. ...Bxh2+? loses material on moves 8 to 10.

notes.original:
Extra: an optional sharper reply, 5...gxf6, against the Two Knights. The core repertoire does not need it.
Idea: 5...gxf6 against the Two Knights. You get the open g-file and play with ...Bg4, ...e6 and ...Rg8. It is sharper than 🔵 15, and White keeps an edge with good play.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ gxf6
Watch out: ...Qxd2+? loses material on move 4. ...Qxd4? loses material on move 6.

notes.text: The Bronstein-Larsen Variation of the Two Knights Attack, also called the Dano-Russian Variation.
notes.original: The Bronstein-Larsen Variation of the Two Knights Attack, also called the Dano-Russian Variation. Black accepts doubled pawns and a weakened kingside in return for the open g-file and a flexible position, with play aimed at White's kingside. Playable, but exf6 is more accurate.

5...Na6!? is the cleanest reply: the knight heads for c7 or b4 rather than committing to d7, and sidesteps any…
notes.original: 5...Na6!? is the cleanest reply: the knight heads for c7 or b4 rather than committing to d7, and sidesteps any awkward pin along the e-file once White recaptures on e4. Choice guide: choose this if you want a surprise weapon against 5.Qe2: it sets a trap at once (the e7-pawn is pinned, so ...Nbd7?? loses to Nd6#) and often drags the game into quiet structures where Black is perfectly fine. Risk level: medium. If you prefer a completely safe structure, answer 5.Nxf6+ exf6 as in 🔵 15 and answer 5.Qe2 with 5...Nxe4 6.Qxe4 Qa5. After 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 White threatens Nd6 mate, because the e7-pawn is pinned against the king. 5...Na6 solves that problem and prepares ...Nc7 and ...Nxe4.

notes.original: White retreats the knight from e4 to c3 to keep the position solid and avoid exchanges; the knights on c3 and f3 help control d5 and e4. It is a very common choice, played in about 304,000 games, and the position is level.

notes.original: White opens the bishop on c1 and prepares g3 and Bg2, a quiet set-up in which he keeps his knight on e4 supported by the d-pawn. It is very common in practice (played in about 234,000 games). So White is not trying to refute you, so you can aim for ...e5 and a healthy centre.

notes.original: White develops and attacks your f5 bishop twice over, since the bishop and the e4 knight both look at it. He hopes to win the bishop pair or force concessions. It is very common in practice (played in about 214,000 games). So the bishop must stay protected.

notes.original: A natural developing move. Your plan is ...Nbd7 and ...e6 or ...e5, followed by ...Bc5 and kingside castling. If the knight from f3 jumps to h4, the bishop goes to g6. Avoid shutting the bishop in with ...e6 before it has a safe square.

notes.original: The bishop retreats to g6 where it stays active, and White may take it with Nxg6 if he wishes, after which you recapture with the h-pawn and gain an open h-file. Do not be afraid of the doubled pawns.

notes.original: Strike in the centre. The pawn on e5 gains space and opens the f8 bishop.

notes.original: Develop and aim at f2. You have a comfortable game with all your pieces out and a flexible centre; keep castling short and avoid pushing pawns carelessly.

notes.text: This is a semi-open position with doubled g-pawns, so you have an open h-file and a flexible centre with pawns…
notes.original: This is a semi-open position with doubled g-pawns, so you have an open h-file and a flexible centre with pawns on c6 and e5. White has a solid structure and a g3 fianchetto. Your plan: bring the queen to e7 and knight to b6, keep the bishop active on c5 aiming at f2, put a rook on h8 against the h3 pawn, and castle long, since the h-file belongs to you. White wants Bg2, then f4 or d4 to undermine e5. Meet d4 by ...exd4 and ...Bb6, and meet f4 with ...exf4. The risk is a hasty ...Rxh3 or a rushed kingside castle; the doubled pawns are fine, but do not leave f2 and h3 stuff loose.

notes.text: You develop the knight and prepare ...e5 and ...Ngf6 in a way that avoids doubled pawns.
notes.original: You develop the knight and prepare ...e5 and ...Ngf6 in a way that avoids doubled pawns. The e4 knight is White's only active piece, so your plan is to trade it off and play ...e5 and ...Bd6. Do not allow Nd6+ ideas by neglecting the e7 pawn.

notes.text: You take the centre and give your bishop f5 a retreat.
Your queen is active and supports e5 and f5.
Your bishop takes a good diagonal and your king will castle short.
You have a solid and active position with a space advantage in the centre and a plan of ...O-O and…
notes.original: You have a solid and active position with a space advantage in the centre and a plan of ...O-O and ...Rae8. This is an open, active position where White's knight on d2 has been moved and you have a space advantage in the centre with pawns on c6 and e5, and both kings castle short. Your plan: castle short, then play ...Rae8 and keep your bishop on f5 and queen on f6 coordinated. When ready, push ...e4 to gain space, or play ...Nf6 to bring the last knight in. White wants to play a4-a5, trade your bishop with Nh4 or Nd2-c4 and pressure e5. Meet Nh4 by ...Bg6 and Nxg6, hxg6. The risk is a loose e5 pawn, so keep it protected and never push ...e4 without checking that d3 is covered.

notes.original: This protects the bishop with a pawn and opens the f8 bishop. Your plan is ...Nf6, ...Nbd7 and ...Be7 or ...Bxd6. If White plays Nd6+ you can recapture with the bishop. Avoid ...Nd7 too early because White gets Nd6+ ideas that damage your structure. White keeps only a small edge here.

This is a semi-open position in which White has two bishops against your one after the exchanges, but your pawn structure is healthy and you are solid. Both kings will castle short. Your plan: recapture sensibly and play ...e5 or ...c5 to challenge the d4 pawn, then ...Qe7, ...Rfe8, and bring the knight to f8 and g6. White wants to open the game for the bishop pair and use the weak light squares such as e6 and f5. The risk is those light squares and the bishop on h3 attacking e6: do not let a bishop pin your knight on d7, and avoid weakening g6. If White deviates with Ng3 earlier, play ...Bg6.

notes.original: Black should play ...Nd5 to cover against the Nxf7 idea. ...Nb6 is an alternative, but the knight does little on the queenside; ...Nd5 followed by ...Bf7 is the better order.

notes.text: Black has fallen for the Nxf7 trap and is effectively lost.
White threatens mate in one.
notes.original: White threatens mate in one. The only good defence is ...N7f6; ...N5f6? would be a serious mistake since Black's position would be cramped.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's queen eyes e6 and h6, and with Rae1 and g4-g5 to follow it is a direct kingside attack.
Trade the attacking knight.
White keeps the initiative, so you must defend carefully; the king goes to h7 and the rook to d8.
A slower move lets you trade the dangerous pieces.
White trades pawns at once to open the game.
notes.original: White trades pawns at once to open the game. The idea is to use the knight already on c3 for quick development, then play d4 and Nf3 and hope you misplace a piece. It is very common in practice, so be ready for it. Your only question is which recapture keeps your structure healthy.

notes.text: White pushes the pawn to gain space and cramp your pieces, planning d3 and f4 and a quick Nf3 and…
notes.original: White pushes the pawn to gain space and cramp your pieces, planning d3 and f4 and a quick Nf3 and d4. It is very common in practice and White is hoping for a closed game where you have no space. For you the fight is for the center.

notes.text: 3.Qf3 - an early queen sortie, adding a second attacker to d5 and eyeing a future Qxf7-style idea if Black…
notes.original: 3.Qf3 - an early queen sortie, adding a second attacker to d5 and eyeing a future Qxf7-style idea if Black is careless. Trading in the center neutralizes the idea completely.

notes.text: 3.Qf3, full treatment in 🔵 19.
Qe2 is an unorthodox reply but a logical one, as White wants to launch an aggressive kingside attack.
3.Qe2 - a similar idea to 3.Qf3, adding pressure to e4/d5 and keeping options open for a later e5 push…
notes.original: 3.Qe2 - a similar idea to 3.Qf3, adding pressure to e4/d5 and keeping options open for a later e5 push without blocking the f-pawn.

notes.text: 3.Qe2!?, an unorthodox but logical try aiming to meet ...dxe4 while keeping the queen centralized.
notes.original: 3.Qe2!?, an unorthodox but logical try aiming to meet ...dxe4 while keeping the queen centralized. Full treatment in 🔵 19.

notes.text: 3.f4 - a more committal, gambit-flavored try that grabs extra central space at the cost of some structural weaknesses (the…
notes.original: 3.f4 - a more committal, gambit-flavored try that grabs extra central space at the cost of some structural weaknesses (the e4-square and the long diagonal toward White's own king).

notes.text: Plan: ...Bxf3, then play ...e6, ...dxe4 and ...Nf6
Another interesting sideline: White does not want Black to restrict White's piece activity, and Black will find it hard to…
notes.original: Another interesting sideline: White does not want Black to restrict White's piece activity, and Black will find it hard to counter White's centre.

notes.text: 4.d4 (instead of the quieter 4.Be2 or 4.h3) - grabs the center immediately while the pin on f3 keeps White…
notes.original: 4.d4 (instead of the quieter 4.Be2 or 4.h3) - grabs the center immediately while the pin on f3 keeps White from castling right away.

notes.text: White opens the position and takes on d5, hoping your bishop on g4 is loose.
notes.original: White opens the position and takes on d5, hoping your bishop on g4 is loose. White often follows with h3 to challenge it. For you the plan is to recapture with the pawn and keep trading on f3.

notes.text: Trap: 5.exd5? Bxd1 6.dxc6 Nxc6 7.Nxd1 e6 8.Bb5 and White is losing.
Idea: 3...Bg4 pins the knight.
notes.original:
Idea: 3...Bg4 pins the knight. After 4.h3 give up the bishop with ...Bxf3, then play ...e6, ...dxe4 and ...Nf6. Fianchetto the other bishop and castle.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bxf3 5.Qxf3 e6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 7 to 11. ...Qxa5? loses material on move 12.
See also: 🟢 08 covers more of the Two Knights Attack. Plan: 🟠 Plan 01. Model games: 🟡 Game 03, 🟡 Game 09.

notes.text: A very solid position, black's solid position would have been a very difficult task to crack.
notes.original: A very solid position, black's solid position would have been a very difficult task to crack. White sure do have the advantage due to his piece development but black do have some attacking chances on the queenside.

notes.text: Also possible: d4.
The same position as in 🔵 17.
notes.original: The same position as in 🔵 17. Our choice, d4, is as good as anything here. Another direct validation: your existing repertoire choice here is correct, not merely reasonable.

notes.text: Also possible: g3.

Your solid structure holds and ...e5 is the break.
The position is equal.

Forced: the knight on e4 is hanging and White must take it back, otherwise he has lost a piece.
White has the bishop pair for a small edge, but ...c5 gives you counterplay.
Not taking back leaves White a knight down.
White is slightly better.
White accepts the structural damage in exchange for the bishop pair and open b-file.
The bishop on a3 prevents castling because it covers f8.
White gets an edge, but you can still play ...Bb7.
Ignoring the recapture loses material.
8.Bg2 - fianchettoes immediately instead of the main 8.Qe3, aiming the bishop at the long diagonal before Black can block…
notes.original: 8.Bg2 - fianchettoes immediately instead of the main 8.Qe3, aiming the bishop at the long diagonal before Black can block it with ...c5 or ...Bc5.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White castles and keeps the bishop pair.
notes.original: White castles and keeps the bishop pair. His motive is to open the long diagonal with d4 and c3 and to use the extra space, while the Qe4 hits the b7 pawn.

notes.text: The knight hits the queen with tempo.
You aim at b2 and d4, and the queen is well placed for ...c5.
White has the bishop pair for a small edge, but your pieces are active and ...c5 is a natural break;…
notes.original: White has the bishop pair for a small edge, but your pieces are active and ...c5 is a natural break; do not rush it, first complete development with ...Rfe8.

notes.text: A slower alternative that reaches the same structure.
8...Bc5 (Solid & Optimal) - develops to an active, flexible square and prepares to castle without any immediate commitments; straightforward…
notes.original: 8...Bc5 (Solid & Optimal) - develops to an active, flexible square and prepares to castle without any immediate commitments; straightforward and easy to play.

notes.text: 8...d4 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - grabs space in the center right away, closing the long diagonal and steering for a…
notes.original: 8...d4 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - grabs space in the center right away, closing the long diagonal and steering for a sharper, more committal structure rather than quiet development.

notes.text: White finishes development before you can strike with ...d4, which is less attractive now that the Bg2 looks down the…
notes.original: White finishes development before you can strike with ...d4, which is less attractive now that the Bg2 looks down the long diagonal.

notes.text: You castle at once and the king is safe.
You take the centre and block the Bg2 diagonal.
White wanted Qe2 and d3 to support e4 and now has to reroute the knight from b1.
notes.original: White wanted Qe2 and d3 to support e4 and now has to reroute the knight from b1. The position is balanced with a small White edge, so complete development with ...Rad8 and ...Rfe8 and watch the c5 bishop.

notes.text: Na4 chases the bishop but you retreat with tempo and nothing has changed.
White attacks d4 at once.
notes.original: White attacks d4 at once. His motive is to remove the pawn that cramps him before you can support it, and the Qf3 also eyes the b7 pawn.

notes.text: Defends d4 and hits b2 in one move.
The knight hits the queen and takes a central square for good.
Bd6 supports e5 so you are not forced to give up the knight.
The knight on f4 is kicked away and you keep the d4 pawn that gives you space.
notes.original: The knight on f4 is kicked away and you keep the d4 pawn that gives you space. White is about level and you have the easier game, the only worry being the weaknesses ...g5 leaves behind.

notes.text: Castling leaves the c3 knight en prise to the d4 pawn, and the rook on b1 does not repay a…
notes.original: Castling leaves the c3 knight en prise to the d4 pawn, and the rook on b1 does not repay a whole piece.

notes.text: d3, white wants to keep the pressure on the center.
A French-type structure has arisen.

A horrible decision which fall short after Nc6
