White's idea is to undermine d5 and use the bishop pair.
Gaining space with tempo on the queen.
White can grab the b7 pawn, but the open lines give you compensation.
Another try.
Trap: 12.Qxd4? Nc6 13.Qxd5 exd5 14.exd6 Nce5 15.c3 and White is losing.
Black is clearly better.
White tries to open lines to compensate for the pawn; the d6 pawn is his spearhead.
Kick the Bg5 out; ...Rf7 follows and the d6 pawn will fall.
Black is clearly better.
The c3 pawn drops.
The position is equal.
White builds a Queen's Gambit structure and targets your doubled f-pawns.
The knight attacks your bishop.
...g6 stops Nf5 and your position is solid.
The position is equal.
4...e6 is simplest: finish development and meet White's center with a solid structure; the pin means White still needs an…
notes.original: 4...e6 is simplest: finish development and meet White's center with a solid structure; the pin means White still needs an extra move (Be2 or h3) before castling.

notes.text: White unpins and prepares to castle; the pin means he needs this extra move first.
White has a little extra space, but you have no weaknesses.
notes.original: White has a little extra space, but you have no weaknesses. Play ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c5 and the position is fine.

notes.text: Grabbing the d4 pawn is safe here, White's only compensation is development.
Recapture with the pawn.
notes.original: Recapture with the pawn. Plan: ...Bxf3 when White plays h3, then ...Nf6 and ...Nc6, ...e6, and castle short. Your break is ...e5 later. Avoid ...Nf6 now, because White gets the center with d4 and a free game.

notes.text: Tempting but loses a pawn structure battle: White takes on c6 and gets a big lead.
Your knights hit d4 and pressure the position.
Now your knight pressures d4 and heads for b4, and White's queen on f3 has few good squares.
You have a solid setup, with all pieces developed and castling short next.
notes.original: You have a solid setup, with all pieces developed and castling short next. If White tries to avoid trades with Bg5 or Qe2 you still play ...Be7 and ...O-O, and keep ...Rc8 for the open c-file. The long-term plan is to pressure the pawn on d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Rc8, while White tries to hold the isolated-looking center with Rd1. Equal. This is a Caro-Kann Exchange position with symmetrical pawns on d4 and d5 and a half-open c-file for you. White has a slight space advantage, but you can challenge it. Your plan: play ...Nb4 to hit the bishop on d3 and the pawn on c2, then ...Be7 or ...Bd6, castle short, and ...Qd7 and ...Rc8. White wants a3 to kick the knight and then Bb5 or a minority attack with b4. If a3 comes, take ...Nxd3+ and recapture. The mistake is playing ...Nb4 without a follow-up, so know your next move. If White plays Bb5+, block with ...Nc6.

notes.text: Recapture with the c-pawn.
notes.original: Recapture with the c-pawn. You keep a solid pawn on d5 and a half-open c-file for a rook later. Because the knight stands on c3, White cannot support d4 with c3, so the center is a little less stable. Plan: ...Nc6, then ...a6 to stop Nb5 jumps, then ...e6 and ...Bd6 or ...Be7, and castle short. Your breaks are ...e5 and ...f6 against a pawn on e5.

notes.text: The natural developing move is the tempting reply, but White takes on c6 and gets a lead in the center…
notes.original: The natural developing move is the tempting reply, but White takes on c6 and gets a lead in the center and in development.

notes.text: Another move order is ...Nc6, which is preferable to ...Nf6.
When White puts a knight on e5, trade it.
notes.original: When White puts a knight on e5, trade it. It is White's most active piece and you do not want it jumping on to other squares.

notes.text: Now the e5 pawn is cramped and becomes a target.
notes.original: Now the e5 pawn is cramped and becomes a target. Hit it with ...Nd7, ...Qc7 and the lever ...f6, and bring your bishop out to d7 or pin the knight with ...Bb4. Your structure is healthy and the plan against e5 is easy. This is a Caro-Kann Exchange structure with White's pawn on e5 locked against your pawns on d5 and e6, and the bishops of both sides still on the board. White has a small space edge, but the pawn on e5 can become a target. Your plan: develop the knight with ...Nd7, bring the queen to c7 to hit e5, and play ...f6 to undermine it, with ...Bb4 or ...Bd7 for your bishop. White wants Bg5, Qg4 or Qh5 for a kingside attack, and h7 is the target. The mistake is playing ...f6 before you are developed, since Qh5+ becomes annoying. If White plays Qh5, answer calmly and keep your king flexible.

notes.text: Kick the knight and gain space at once.
notes.original: Kick the knight and gain space at once. Plan: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Bd7 and ...e6, then castle short. Your pawn chain on c5-d4 gives you a space advantage, and your pieces can use e5 and f5. Aim for the break ...f6 or ...Qb6 to hit b2. Avoid leaving the pawn on d4 without support, and avoid trading all your pieces, because the space you gain is your main trump. If White plays d3 early you can strike with ...c5 and ...Nc6 at once, and if White castles you can safely do the same. White's usual alternative is to play f4 and Nf3, and then you hold d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6.

notes.text: Also playable and keeps the d5 pawn.
Your center is solid and your pieces go to e7, f5 and g6 as needed.
notes.original: Your center is solid and your pieces go to e7, f5 and g6 as needed. Balanced with a clear plan. This is a closed centre where your pawn chain c5-d4 gives you space on the queenside, and White has the pawn chain e5-f4. Both kings are likely to castle short. Your plan: play ...Nge7, then ...Qb6 to hit b2, and ...Nf5 or ...Ng6 to hold your centre. White wants c3 to undermine d4, Bb5 and h4 to attack your king, so you hit back with ...Qb6 and ...f6. The mistake is leaving d4 unprotected; after c3 take with ...dxc3. If White deviates with Bb5, keep the knight on c6 protected with ...Be7.

notes.text: e6, this variation has a Semi Slav taste against the Fantasy Variation.
notes.original: e6, this variation has a Semi Slav taste against the Fantasy Variation. First of all you create a very solid and fortified center. This is another alternative choice against the Fantasy Variation if you like positional and solid gameplay. You are going to try and set up a Solid Semi Slav like structure. This can even transpose into a French Defence like position if white were to advance his central pawn forward.

notes.text: 3...Qb6!? (Aggressive Alternative) - instead of meeting 3.f3 with the structural ...e6 or ...dxe4, Black immediately presses on b2 and…
notes.original: 3...Qb6!? (Aggressive Alternative) - instead of meeting 3.f3 with the structural ...e6 or ...dxe4, Black immediately presses on b2 and d4, forcing White to react right away rather than Black settling into a slow structure. Choice guide: choose 3...Qb6 if you are happy to play a more active, slightly unusual line that puts the queen on the b6-g1 diagonal and meets f3 with immediate counter-pressure on d4 and b2 (medium risk). For a calmer game stick with 3...dxe4 (🔵 18) or 3...e6 (the main line of this chapter). 3...Qb6 puts pressure on d4 and b2. White's main tries are 4.Nc3, 4.a3, 4.a4 and 4.c3.

notes.text: 4.Nc3!? - a Milner-Barry-style gambit idea, developing immediately rather than recapturing the pawn on e4 right away.
White shores up d4 and prepares to meet ...exd4 with cxd4, hoping to open the centre while the king is…
notes.original: White shores up d4 and prepares to meet ...exd4 with cxd4, hoping to open the centre while the king is still on e1. The trouble is that it ignores the weakened e1-h4 diagonal, since the f2 pawn is gone.

notes.text: Idea: Take on e4 and strike back with 4...e5.
notes.original:
Idea: Take on e4 and strike back with 4...e5. White's king is a little loose after f3, so develop fast: ...Bg4, ...Nf6, ...Bd6 and castle.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 e5 5.Nf3 Bg4
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on move 4.
See also: 🟢 11 covers more of the Fantasy Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 05.

notes.text: Trap: 6.Nxe5? Bxd1 7.Kxd1 Qxd4+ 8.Nd3 Na6 9.Nc3 and White is losing.
6.Bc4 prepares O-O and Ng5 once the queen is out of the pin.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 prepares O-O and Ng5 once the queen is out of the pin. White is happy to give a pawn for quick development, and it also threatens Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ Ke8 Qxg4, winning the bishop on g4 and leaving the black king stuck in the centre.

notes.text: Theory note: Black should develop as actively as possible here.
A knight, a bishop and, once White has castled, a rook can all bear down on f7.
notes.original:
A knight, a bishop and, once White has castled, a rook can all bear down on f7. Watch what White is planning, as hidden dangers lurk in the opening.
Trap: 7.Nxe5? Bxd1 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 9.Bc4+ Ke8 10.Kxd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: White keeps the bishop on e2 instead of putting it on c4.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop on e2 instead of putting it on c4. The idea is quiet development: castle, then play h3 to deal with your bishop on g4. If you take on f3, White recaptures with the bishop and keeps a healthy structure with the bishop pair. This is a calmer way to play than 7.Bc4, and the pin on the knight is less annoying here.

notes.text: White puts the bishop on d3, eyeing your kingside and the h7 pawn.
notes.original: White puts the bishop on d3, eyeing your kingside and the h7 pawn. The drawback is that the bishop blocks the queen's protection of the d4 pawn. Many club players play this because it looks natural.

notes.text: 7...Bh5 adds a defender to f7.
notes.original: 7...Bh5 adds a defender to f7. Other moves, such as ...Nbd7, run into 8.Qb3, which hits b7 and f7 together. Black can only defend one of them, and White gets a lot of play on the seventh rank.

notes.text: Qb3 doesn't work because of b5 thus eliminating white's threat of Qxb7 and at the same time lose one tempo.
The e-file is open and Black, still uncastled, is on the verge of losing.
notes.original: The e-file is open and Black, still uncastled, is on the verge of losing. Poisoned pawns should not be taken: with so little development, Black lacks the pieces to hold against White's strong winning combination starting with Qe1.

notes.text: 9...h6 kicks the bishop and also gives Black's light-squared bishop some breathing room in case White plays g4.
Black is slightly better.
The Fantasy Variation.
White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White opens the a-file with axb5 and drops the bishop back to c2 to support e4.
notes.original: White opens the a-file with axb5 and drops the bishop back to c2 to support e4. Your counter is ...Ng4, aiming at h2 and e3, followed by ...exd4 and ...Be5 to put your bishop on a strong central square. Rf5 harasses the bishop on h5, but ...Ngf6 holds everything together. White keeps a small, annoying edge.

notes.text: The quieter plan, with the bishop retreating to f2 and the knight to h4, leaves you fully equal.
Bxd5 is also possible for White here.
White has too many hanging pieces - the bishop, the d5-pawn and h2 - and is on the verge of…
notes.original: White has too many hanging pieces - the bishop, the d5-pawn and h2 - and is on the verge of collapse.

notes.text: Nd2 attacks the pawn on e4 and opens the f-file against your knight, but it comes too late: the bishop…
notes.original: Nd2 attacks the pawn on e4 and opens the f-file against your knight, but it comes too late: the bishop takes with check, and the queen on c7 covers h2, so the king cannot take it.

notes.text: White's last tactical try: a knight sacrifice to get a pawn to e6 hitting your knight on d7.
The sacrifice runs out of steam: you keep an extra pawn and the white king is still exposed.
Trading the bishop does not stop the bleeding: the h2 pawn is gone and the e-pawn rolls on.
Black is clearly better.
Here is the point: White's last bishop is nearly trapped, and every retreat costs a tempo.
notes.original: Here is the point: White's last bishop is nearly trapped, and every retreat costs a tempo. Your pawn push attacks the knight on f3 and opens the diagonal for the bishop on h5.

notes.text: You are clearly better: the pawn on e4 cramps White, your knights are centralised and the bishop on a5 is…
notes.original: You are clearly better: the pawn on e4 cramps White, your knights are centralised and the bishop on a5 is far from the action.

notes.text: Rd1 looks natural, but after ...Nf5 and ...e4 everything goes your way: White's rook has to take on d7 and…
notes.original: Rd1 looks natural, but after ...Nf5 and ...e4 everything goes your way: White's rook has to take on d7 and ends up a piece down.

notes.text: Black has an isolated pawn.
Instead of Qg4 in the main line, the more testing try is Qf5, keeping the queen more centrally placed and…
notes.original: Instead of Qg4 in the main line, the more testing try is Qf5, keeping the queen more centrally placed and creating immediate threats against Black's slightly exposed king.

notes.text: This is just a horrendous position for Black.
The bishop supports the e5 pawn that White's queen and bishop are eyeing, and prepares ...h5 later.
notes.original: The bishop supports the e5 pawn that White's queen and bishop are eyeing, and prepares ...h5 later. The numbers say White is only modestly better, so the plan is to get your pieces out and look for a queen trade.

notes.text: A useful resource: ...h5-h4 would kick the queen off g3, and it takes the g4 square away from White's pieces.
You offer a queen trade on g4 and reach a solid defensive set-up.
Pushing the pawn only creates a target: rooks and knights pile onto e4, and White's pieces are better placed.
Trap: 13...exd4? 14.Qxf8# and Black gets mated.
Trap: 14...exd4? 15.cxd5 h5 16.Qf7+ Kh7 17.Qxh5+ Kg8 18.Qf7+ Kh7 19.Rh3# and Black gets mated.
White keeps a lasting initiative here that the main line's Qg4 understates.
notes.original: White keeps a lasting initiative here that the main line's Qg4 understates. This is the critical test of this whole sharp line.

notes.text: This is the point of White's initiative: when your queen went to c4 it stopped guarding the knight on d7,…
notes.original: This is the point of White's initiative: when your queen went to c4 it stopped guarding the knight on d7, so that knight falls. The rest of the line is damage control.

notes.text: White has an extra knight for two pawns, but the knight on b1 and bishop on c1 are still undeveloped,…
notes.original: White has an extra knight for two pawns, but the knight on b1 and bishop on c1 are still undeveloped, so you get a few tempi to push the d-pawn and bring the king and bishop into play. White must untangle first with Nd2 and Bf4.

notes.text: The alternative d5 lets you win time with ...e4 and is less testing.
White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
You must hold b5: a4 attacks it directly, and ...a6 supports it so that axb5 axb5 does not open the…
notes.original: You must hold b5: a4 attacks it directly, and ...a6 supports it so that axb5 axb5 does not open the a-file with tempo on your rook.

notes.text: White tries Nxe5 Nxe5 dxe5 to open the d-file and the diagonals towards your king, but your bishop on d6…
notes.original: White tries Nxe5 Nxe5 dxe5 to open the d-file and the diagonals towards your king, but your bishop on d6 is waiting to take back on e5.

notes.text: The check gains the tempo you need to save the bishop, and material is level; you will castle and the…
notes.original: The check gains the tempo you need to save the bishop, and material is level; you will castle and the position is balanced.

notes.text: Here you answer the pin by trading bishops, then take on e4 while White takes on c6, and the game…
notes.original: Here you answer the pin by trading bishops, then take on e4 while White takes on c6, and the game is level.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
This forced liquidation is White's best try: your queen is facing White's on the e-file with only your knight in…
notes.original: This forced liquidation is White's best try: your queen is facing White's on the e-file with only your knight in between, and the bishop on d2 is attacked by both bishop and knight, so White trades everything. You keep the extra pawn, but White's rooks reach the open files before your knight and king are developed, so the position is balanced. Bring the king to safety and the knight into play.

notes.text: Castling is too slow: you remain a clean pawn up with the e-file in your hands.
Bring the last knight out and keep the centre solid.
notes.original: Bring the last knight out and keep the centre solid. You do not need to hurry. Your pieces head for d6 and c7, and your king goes short.

notes.text: The bishop eyes the kingside and supports the e5 pawn, so White's d4 break loses force.
This is a balanced centre where both sides have a pawn on e4 or e5 and the e5 pawn is…
notes.original: This is a balanced centre where both sides have a pawn on e4 or e5 and the e5 pawn is yours to guard. Your plan: castle short, put a rook on e8 or d8, and play ...h6 to ask the bishop on g5 what it wants. Aim for ...Bxf3 only when it wins the bishop pair or wrecks White's pawn on f3 (it forces Nxf3). White wants d4 or Nc4, hitting the e5 pawn, and a later Qd3 or Qe3 with pressure on your king. Meet d4 with ...exd4 and ...Bxf3 so that the white queen is dragged out. The risk is greed: taking on e4 with ...Nxe4 looks free but after O-O and Nxe5 your knights lose their grip on the centre. If White plays Bc4 or Bd3 instead, keep the same set-up.

notes.text: This trade opens the centre while White is a move ahead in development.
notes.original: This trade opens the centre while White is a move ahead in development. You can survive, but you will have to defend the e-file, so prefer ...Nbd7.

notes.text: Take on d4 straight away.
notes.original: Take on d4 straight away. White cannot simply recapture because the pawn on d4 has lost the queen's support.

notes.text: White pushes to gain a tempo and open the long diagonal for the bishop.
notes.original: White pushes to gain a tempo and open the long diagonal for the bishop. Your knight retreats to d7 and is ready for ...Nxe5 if the pawn is loose.

notes.text: This is an open position where White has the bishop pair and the open f-file, but your position is solid…
notes.original: This is an open position where White has the bishop pair and the open f-file, but your position is solid and the e5 pawn is a target. Your plan: play ...e6 to guard d5 and f5, then ...Nb6 or ...Qb6 to hit the pawns on d4 and b2. Castle short and put a rook on c8 or d8. White wants Bxh7, e6 or Qf3-f4, so keep your king safe and watch the h7 pawn and the f7 square. Meet e6 with ...fxe6 or ...Nb6 depending on what is hanging. The risk is castling too early into the attack on h7. If White avoids e5, play ...Be7 and ...O-O and sit comfortably.

notes.text: This quiet route also works, but taking on d4 is more ambitious.
7.Bxf7+ does not work.
notes.original: 7.Bxf7+ does not work. Black takes the bishop and consolidates with ...Ngf6, and White cannot follow with Ng5 because the black queen covers g5.

notes.text: With plans of opening up the f file s
Black is clearly better.
The position is equal.
The e4-e5 push gains space and kicks the knight, but your pieces find good squares: the knight lands on e6…
notes.original: The e4-e5 push gains space and kicks the knight, but your pieces find good squares: the knight lands on e6 heading for d4 or g5, the bishop is safe on h5, and the rooks take the open files. The position stays level.

notes.text: Shows the tactical point: once Bxf3 deflects the knight from d2, the pawn on e4 hangs.
Black is clearly better.
White's Qe2 allowed you to win a pawn on e4.
notes.original: White's Qe2 allowed you to win a pawn on e4. Nbd2 attacks the knight, so you retreat it to f6 and keep the extra pawn. Then ...b5 gains a tempo on the bishop, and ...exd4 and ...Re8 pile pressure on the e-file. You are a clean pawn up and only need to finish development.

notes.text: Even the direct Qc2 hitting e4 is met by the same retreat, and you stay clearly better.
Rather than the immediate Qf2, repositioning the bishop to b3 first is a cleaner try, keeping it safely out of…
notes.original: Rather than the immediate Qf2, repositioning the bishop to b3 first is a cleaner try, keeping it safely out of tactics on the long diagonal before continuing the attack.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White retreats the bishop to avoid ...Bxg5 and keep the bishop pair, advances the a-pawn for queenside space and wants…
notes.original: White retreats the bishop to avoid ...Bxg5 and keep the bishop pair, advances the a-pawn for queenside space and wants the f4 break (f3-f4) to open the f-file. You aim your knight at f4 and tuck the king onto h8, away from the b3-g8 diagonal. If White plays f4 anyway, ...Nxf4 Bxf4 exf4 wins a pawn but White regains it with Qxf4. A modest White edge.

notes.text: The knight tour fails to a tactic: ...Nxe4 takes a pawn and the pin on g5 is broken by taking…
notes.original: The knight tour fails to a tactic: ...Nxe4 takes a pawn and the pin on g5 is broken by taking the bishop.

notes.text: A real, moderate improvement for White - not as sharp as the Main Line #1 note above, but still meaningfully…
notes.original: A real, moderate improvement for White - not as sharp as the Main Line #1 note above, but still meaningfully stronger than the main line's original try in this sub-line.

notes.text: White is a pawn down, but has the g-file, the bishop on b3 aimed at f7 and the queen on…
notes.original: White is a pawn down, but has the g-file, the bishop on b3 aimed at f7 and the queen on the kingside: Rg1 and Bg5 threaten to remove your knight on f6 and then play against g7. Kh8 steps off the b3-g8 diagonal, and ...c5 and ...Bd4 gain space and activity. The queen trade on e6 takes the sting out of White's play, leaving a modest White edge.

notes.text: The same set-up with another move order lets you equalise.
Black is winning.
White's Bxf7+ was a sacrifice that dragged your king out, but White has no follow-up: no more checks, and the…
notes.original: White's Bxf7+ was a sacrifice that dragged your king out, but White has no follow-up: no more checks, and the open f-file is not enough. Taking on f3 first wrecks White's kingside pawns, and ...Qb6 hits b2 and d4 at once. You are clearly ahead in material and only have to keep the king covered.

notes.text: The intermezzo e6+ does not help: your pieces swarm the white king.
This move looks aggressive and gambit-like, but it is not: the e5 pawn will soon fall because Black's pieces are…
notes.original: This move looks aggressive and gambit-like, but it is not: the e5 pawn will soon fall because Black's pieces are active and White is cramped, so White must eventually give it up to develop. Lines where White tries to hold e5 need more detailed study.

notes.text: You are a pawn down on paper, but White's king is stuck in the middle and the pawn on e4…
notes.original: You are a pawn down on paper, but White's king is stuck in the middle and the pawn on e4 is weak. You pile on it with ...Rhe8 and ...Bg6, and when b4 tries to kick your knight, ...Ncxe4 only gives up a piece for a moment: after Nxe4 your bishop jumps to e5, the knight on e4 is attacked twice and d4 is hit as well, so the material comes straight back. You end with the more active rook and a clear edge.

notes.text: Pushing the a-pawn loses a tempo and you pick up pawns while the king is exposed.
The bishop on h2 won a pawn but is in danger of being trapped by g3, so White hits it…
notes.original: The bishop on h2 won a pawn but is in danger of being trapped by g3, so White hits it with the knight at once and it has to run.

notes.text: White's knights hunt for f5 and h6 to harass the g7 pawn and your rook; you answer with ...g6 and…
notes.original: White's knights hunt for f5 and h6 to harass the g7 pawn and your rook; you answer with ...g6 and ...Rd7, then take the pawn on e4. You stay a pawn up with a small edge, because White's pieces are active and you must keep your king safe.

notes.text: The attempt to trap the bishop fails, because it takes another pawn and escapes.
White's compensation for the pawn is the bishop pair: Be5 hits the knight on f6 and the rooks come off.
notes.original: White's compensation for the pawn is the bishop pair: Be5 hits the knight on f6 and the rooks come off. You march the king to the centre, which is safe now that the queens are gone, and after the trade on f6 the bishops are of opposite colours. That is why the extra pawn is hard to convert and the position is only slightly better for you.

notes.text: This is the idea: the check forces the king to move.
notes.original: This is the idea: the check forces the king to move. White cannot block with g3 because ...Qxe4+ wins material, so he plays Kd2 and the king is stuck in the middle. Your plan is to bring pieces with tempo, ...Nf6, ...Qf2+ or ...Nxe4+, and open the position with ...exd4. Keep checking only while it gains time; avoid pushing the queen alone far into the enemy camp. This is clearly better for you.

notes.text: Developing the knight is natural but misses the check; after Nf3 exd4 Bc4 White gets a comfortable game and the…
notes.original: Developing the knight is natural but misses the check; after Nf3 exd4 Bc4 White gets a comfortable game and the position is about equal. Do not play it.

notes.text: Open the e-file and the centre while the king is exposed.
notes.original: Open the e-file and the centre while the king is exposed. Your knights and bishops are all better coordinated than White's.

notes.text: White's king on c2 is the target, and you keep the initiative.
notes.original: White's king on c2 is the target, and you keep the initiative. This is an open position where White's king stands on c2 and your pieces are more active, so you keep the initiative. Your queen on f2 and knight on e4 are annoying, and it is your move. Your plan is, first, to bring the dark bishop out with ...Bc5 or ...Bb4, hitting the knight on d4. Second, develop ...Nc6 to chase it away. Third, keep checking and opening files toward the king rather than grabbing pawns. White wants to trade queens or to consolidate with Rd1 and Be3. The typical mistake is to play the queen alone to g2 and get trapped. If White trades pieces, keep the bishop pair active.

notes.text: 4...Nf6 is simplest: hold onto the extra pawn and develop normally.
notes.original: 4...Nf6 is simplest: hold onto the extra pawn and develop normally. White's pawn on e4 is extra material, not enough compensation for the lost tempo.

notes.text: A safe way to avoid every gambit trick: Black returns the pawn at once.
Extra: only needed if White plays a rare second or third move.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays a rare second or third move.
Idea: Everything else: rare second and third moves, each with a pointer to where it is covered. The answer is nearly always the same: ...d5, take on e4 when it's safe, and develop.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.f3 exf3

notes.text: Simplest and best: take the second pawn too, planning to give one back later for a clean structural edge rather…
notes.original: Simplest and best: take the second pawn too, planning to give one back later for a clean structural edge rather than trying to hold onto both.

notes.text: Strictly, your extra pawn lasts only until White recaptures on e4, and the knight is well placed there eyeing d6…
notes.original: Strictly, your extra pawn lasts only until White recaptures on e4, and the knight is well placed there eyeing d6 and f6. What you keep is a healthy structure and an easy game.

notes.text: White pins the knight on f6 to the queen and wants to rid you of your best defender, intending to…
notes.original: White pins the knight on f6 to the queen and wants to rid you of your best defender, intending to recapture on e4 with a good structure, or to follow with Qd2 and queenside castling. It is very common in practice (played in about 51,000 games). So the pin on f6 must be handled calmly, and you should not drop the pawn back without gaining something.

notes.text: This is the slow move: White develops the bishop but leaves the centre unprotected.
notes.original: This is the slow move: White develops the bishop but leaves the centre unprotected. The Fantasy position after the knight trades is tricky because White's e-pawn is gone and your pieces are free.

notes.text: A quiet position with only a tiny Black edge.
notes.original: A quiet position with only a tiny Black edge. It works, but you give up the extra pawn for nothing, and 4...exf3 scores clearly better.

notes.text: White's g4 lunge wants g5 and h4-h5 to harass the bishop, but the bishop is safe on g6; if h4-h5…
notes.original: White's g4 lunge wants g5 and h4-h5 to harass the bishop, but the bishop is safe on g6; if h4-h5 arrives you drop back to h7, where it still eyes the long diagonal. You are a little more comfortable.

notes.text: You strike at the centre at once, taking advantage of the missing white pawn on e4.
This is an open position where you have a lead in the centre and good piece play.
notes.original: This is an open position where you have a lead in the centre and good piece play. Your plan: bring the bishop to d6 or e7, castle short, and add ...Bg4 or ...Be6 to speed up development. White wants f4 or Nf3 to kick your queen and win time. Watch for tricks on the e-file when your king is in the centre. If White plays c3 and Bd3 or f4 early, trade queens only if it helps your structure, and keep the extra central pawn. The risk is grabbing too many pawns and leaving the king in the centre; castle first. If White deviates with Be3 or Bd3, take the d4 pawn only after checking that the queen still has an escape square.

notes.text: White develops the kingside knight and adds a second attacker against d4, so that dxe5 or d5 both stay available…
notes.original: White develops the kingside knight and adds a second attacker against d4, so that dxe5 or d5 both stay available next move. There is no trap here; it is the most natural move and it is very common in practice (played in about 71,000 games). So White is happy to wait, and you must decide how to settle the tension between your e5 pawn and the d4 pawn.

notes.text: The other recapture lets you strike with ...e5, trade queens and win the e4 pawn, and the bishop gets hit…
notes.original: The other recapture lets you strike with ...e5, trade queens and win the e4 pawn, and the bishop gets hit by ...Nb6.

notes.text: You take on d4 and accept the queen trade that follows.
notes.original: You take on d4 and accept the queen trade that follows. After Qxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 you have no weaknesses, and your dark-squared bishop gets to hit the knight on d4 with tempo.

notes.text: Pinning the knight looks natural and many players choose it, but White just plays dxe5, trades queens with Kxd1 and…
notes.original: Pinning the knight looks natural and many players choose it, but White just plays dxe5, trades queens with Kxd1 and has the easier game: the pin is not a real problem for White, and your bishop is misplaced. This leaves White a slight edge, so avoid it.

notes.text: Hit the knight at once.
Your plan is simple: keep pressure on the knight on c3 with the bishop, castle short, and bring the b8…
notes.original: Your plan is simple: keep pressure on the knight on c3 with the bishop, castle short, and bring the b8 knight to d7 or a6. You can aim for ...c5 or ...Nxe4 later when the c3 knight is overloaded. Do not rush the knight forward before your king is safe.

notes.text: After the early queen trade you have a healthy structure and easy development, and you keep a small edge.
notes.original: After the early queen trade you have a healthy structure and easy development, and you keep a small edge. You have reached a queenless middlegame with a healthy structure and an easy game, and you are a little more comfortable. The bishop on f4 attacks your knight on b8, so your first step is ...Nbd7 or ...Na6. Then put a rook on e8 to pressure the e4 pawn, and keep the bishop on b4 pinning the c3 knight. Your third step is to look for ...Bxc3 followed by ...Nxe4 when the pawn becomes loose. White wants to castle long, double on the d-file and push e5. The risk is rushing ...Nxe4 before the pin is built; if White plays e5, hit it with ...Nd7 and ...Nxe5.

notes.text: Capture the f3 pawn before White can recapture on e4.
notes.original: Capture the f3 pawn before White can recapture on e4. After Nxf3 you play ...Bg4, pinning the knight in return, and ...Nbd7 to bring the second knight out. Your plans are ...e6 or ...e5 once the bishop on g5 is traded or when it leaves, castling short, and ...Qb6 pressure. This leaves you slightly better.

notes.text: Ask the bishop a question at once.
notes.original: Ask the bishop a question at once. Avoid ...Nxe4 here, because the pin on f6 and the queen on d2 leave you tactically exposed.

notes.text: After the bishop trade you keep a solid structure, the bishop pair is not a worry, and you aim for…
notes.original: After the bishop trade you keep a solid structure, the bishop pair is not a worry, and you aim for ...Bf5 or ...e6 and ...Be7 next. This is an open position after the bishop trade, with White's pawn on d5 attacking your c6 pawn and your bishop on g4 attacked by the knight on e5, and you are slightly better. Your plan is, first, to move the bishop with ...Bf5, keeping it protected. Second, challenge d5 with ...cxd5 or ...e6. Third, complete development with ...Qc7, ...e6 and ...Be7, castling on the side that is safe. White wants to use the knight on e5 and the d-pawn to cramp you, and checks Nxf7 tricks. The risk is dropping the bishop or leaving f7 loose. If White plays Nxg4, recapture with the knight.

notes.text: White is eventually aiming for a King's Indian-type structure with Ngf3, g3, Be2 and 0-0.
The main King's Indian Attack move order - White prepares Ngf3 and a kingside fianchetto without touching the center pawns…
notes.original: The main King's Indian Attack move order - White prepares Ngf3 and a kingside fianchetto without touching the center pawns yet.

notes.text: 3.f4!? - a more ambitious try than the main 3.Nd2, grabbing extra central space at the cost of some kingside…
notes.original: 3.f4!? - a more ambitious try than the main 3.Nd2, grabbing extra central space at the cost of some kingside structure. Nothing to fear: just develop.

notes.text: 3.Qe2!? - an unusual developing move, preparing to meet ...dxe4 with a recapture that keeps the queen centralized.
3.Nc3 - transposes toward a Two Knights-style setup a tempo behind the usual move order, since White already spent a…
notes.original: 3.Nc3 - transposes toward a Two Knights-style setup a tempo behind the usual move order, since White already spent a move on d3.

notes.text: 3.Be2 - a quiet developing move, keeping options flexible rather than committing to the main 3.Nd2 King's Indian Attack plan.
The alternative move order, sometimes called the 'Leela' set-up, after the engine that made the early Nf3 (instead of Nd2)…
notes.original: The alternative move order, sometimes called the 'Leela' set-up, after the engine that made the early Nf3 (instead of Nd2) popular.

notes.text: White is voluntarily giving Black the chance to take over the centre, and Black should seize it.
Grab the center immediately - this is the single most important practical lesson against a King's Indian Attack setup as…
notes.original: Grab the center immediately - this is the single most important practical lesson against a King's Indian Attack setup as White: if Black is slow, White gets to choose the structure; if Black grabs the center first, White's whole setup loses most of its point.

notes.text: Transposing to the 2.d3 lines.
notes.original: Transposing to the 2.d3 lines. Full coverage in 🔵 19 and 20; a short version is given here.

notes.text: The simplifying alternative: just take the pawn at once rather than building the same King's Indian Attack structure Black gets…
notes.original: The simplifying alternative: just take the pawn at once rather than building the same King's Indian Attack structure Black gets anyway after 3...e5.

notes.text: White's most natural follow-up, developing before committing the dark-squared bishop.
Also natural, fianchettoing immediately; transposes to the same structures after a normal developing sequence.
Idea: Against 2.d3, take the centre with ...d5 and ...e5.
notes.original:
Idea: Against 2.d3, take the centre with ...d5 and ...e5. Put the bishop on d6 or c7, the knight on f6, and castle. You get an easy, roomy position.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 e5 4.Ngf3 Bd6
Next: 🔵 20 continues the 2.d3 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.text: Choice guide: choose this if you want a classical, symmetrical set-up against the King's Indian Attack: ...e5, ...Bd6, ...Nf6 and…
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want a classical, symmetrical set-up against the King's Indian Attack: ...e5, ...Bd6, ...Nf6 and ...O-O, with ...Re8 and ...a5-a4 for queenside space (low risk, easy to learn). Against 5.d4 you can also play the open structures shown below. White's main set-ups are 5.g3 (King's Indian Attack) and 5.d4 (transposing to an open game).

notes.text: The standard developing scheme: the bishop takes its most natural diagonal before Black castles.
Playable, but Bd6 is more accurate.
White is settling for some sort of an "Inverted Hanham Structure".
notes.original: White is settling for some sort of an "Inverted Hanham Structure". This involves Be2 0-0 c3 Qc2 and b4! Trying to find some play on the queenside.

notes.text: 5.d4 is an energetic break and fine for White.
notes.original: 5.d4 is an energetic break and fine for White. Black can take on d4, but ...f6 is the easier and more natural reply.

notes.text: Other options include d4, but g3 is much safer for White; Bg2 followed by short castling is fine for White.
Preparing the long fianchetto, the point of this whole King's Indian Attack set-up.
Black maintains his spacious advantage.
White finds play on the queenside.
Black must not allow a White counter-attack on the queenside.
Black's centre is manageable.
With ideas of Ng6 to support the e5 pawn without having to block the light square bishop.
This prevents any hasty pin.
Black is clearly better.
Black has everything going: the knights head for f4, the rooks double on the a-file and ...c5 prepares ...d4 and…
notes.original: Black has everything going: the knights head for f4, the rooks double on the a-file and ...c5 prepares ...d4 and ...Bd7. White's pieces are passive and the queenside pawn storm with b4 has run out of steam. Your plan is to keep improving (...Bd7, ...Rea8) and only open the position when it favours you.

notes.text: Another way to meet it
A safer option, black exchange central pawn aiming for a less theoretical simplification in the opening.
Rather dubious, but maintain black's central advantage.
notes.original: Rather dubious, but maintain black's central advantage. exd4 was stronger.

notes.text: 11.exd5 resolves the center immediately instead of recapturing with the knight first, trading into a simple structure a move early.
Prevents any piece from jumping on the g4 square.
The position is equal.
White's idea is to prepare exd5 so that the e-file opens with a tempo on your rook.
notes.original: White's idea is to prepare exd5 so that the e-file opens with a tempo on your rook. The knight on e7 blocks your own rook, so ...Ng6 unmasks it and lets you answer exd5 with ...Rxe1+.

notes.text: The queen steps off the d8-g5 diagonal where Bg5 was hitting it.
notes.original: The queen steps off the d8-g5 diagonal where Bg5 was hitting it. The knight on d5 is a fine central piece and the position stays level.

notes.text: White can open the centre at once, but ...c5 and ...h6 give you an easy game
5.d4 exd4 6.exd5 cxd5 leads to an open position with a symmetrical pawn structure.
notes.original: 5.d4 exd4 6.exd5 cxd5 leads to an open position with a symmetrical pawn structure. Black has no problems.

notes.text: ...reaching a calm, balanced position with roughly symmetrical chances.
Black castles and puts the rook on the e-file, where Be2 and the white king are lined up.
notes.original: Black castles and puts the rook on the e-file, where Be2 and the white king are lined up. The bishop steps back to c7 before Nb5 can hit it, and it keeps an eye on h2.

notes.text: Bc7 and Qd6 now form a battery aimed at h2, so White has to spend time covering it.
White regains the d4 pawn but the position is level.
notes.original: White regains the d4 pawn but the position is level. Your plan is to finish development with ...Bg4 or ...Bf5 and play for the e-file; there is nothing to fear.

notes.text: An equally good setup: you trade the bishop for the knight that guards d4 and plant a knight on e4
White is slightly better.
Pawn takes pawn would not be so necessary for white since this would give black two powerful central pawns.
White is slightly better.
Your isolated pawn on d5 is the whole story.
notes.original: Your isolated pawn on d5 is the whole story. White piles up on it with Qb3, Be3 and the rook, hoping to force a concession, and the e-file gives White an easy plan. You answer with active piece play: Na5 kicks the queen, Bc7 eyes the h2 diagonal and Rfe8 contests the open file. White keeps a small edge but you have no real weaknesses besides d5.

notes.text: Black's two central pawns on d5 and e5 are isolated and hard to keep, so Black will probably have to…
notes.original: Black's two central pawns on d5 and e5 are isolated and hard to keep, so Black will probably have to give one up later.

notes.text: A surprising, unorthodox move that is nevertheless playable.
notes.original: A surprising, unorthodox move that is nevertheless playable. Black's kingside is not under threat and an attack would be easily refuted, so the idea is to place the king on the safest available square.

notes.text: Protects the e4 pawn, black intends to castle short now 0-0.
Also possible but the over extended e pawn could be risky.
You must play this thrust.
notes.original: You must play this thrust. It cuts the f3 knight off from d4 and gives your rook on f8 the f-file.

notes.text: White's motive is the loose c4 pawn and the dark squares: Qxc4+ ideas are always in the air and Nb5…
notes.original: White's motive is the loose c4 pawn and the dark squares: Qxc4+ ideas are always in the air and Nb5 hits your queen and the a7 pawn at the same time. Taking on a7 is greedy, though, because the knight is now short of squares. Keep c4 defended and use ...Nd5 or ...Nb6 to hit the b-pawns.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is a pawn up for a moment, so you hit the knight at once.
notes.original: White is a pawn up for a moment, so you hit the knight at once. If it moves, ...Qxb4 regains the pawn and your queen lands on the weak doubled b-pawns.

notes.text: White's plan is to use the open lines and the bishop against your king, while the doubled b-pawns remain a…
notes.original: White's plan is to use the open lines and the bishop against your king, while the doubled b-pawns remain a target for you. Your pieces are active: the knight on e5 heads for d3 or c6 and the rook sits on the d-file. White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Pushing the b-pawn gives your knights great squares
Rather than retreating the knight to b3 as the main line does, castling first is White's more accurate try, getting…
notes.original: Rather than retreating the knight to b3 as the main line does, castling first is White's more accurate try, getting the king to safety before deciding how to meet Black's central expansion.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
White's motive is to blow the position open while your king is stuck on f8.
notes.original: White's motive is to blow the position open while your king is stuck on f8. a4 pries at b5, c4 opens the c-file towards your queen and Rc1, and the piece sacrifice on d4 lets the c-pawn run with tempo on Bd6 and then c6. This is why 13...b5 loosens too much: it hands White the lever. After the exchanges you are in trouble.

notes.text: The calmer try is less dangerous for you
This keeps a clear, lasting edge for White thanks to the extra central pawn and safer king - a meaningful…
notes.original: This keeps a clear, lasting edge for White thanks to the extra central pawn and safer king - a meaningful improvement over the main line's Nb3, worth having as the critical line in this sideline chapter.

notes.text: White's point is simple: win the e4 pawn (Nxe4 and cxd5) and then play against a king that cannot castle.
notes.original: White's point is simple: win the e4 pawn (Nxe4 and cxd5) and then play against a king that cannot castle. The extra pawn and the c-file are the trumps, so after ...Qxd5 White develops with tempo by Be3 and Rc1, while your bishop on g4 and the knight on a6 try to cause trouble. White keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: 12.Ne2 is nearly as strong; even the shot ...Bxh2+ does not rescue Black
The position is equal.
Keeping f6 free for the other knight and preparing a timely ...f5 or ...Nf5 reroute later.
The position is equal.
White has the bishop pair, so the plan is to open the e-file with exd5 and then bring the knight…
notes.original: White has the bishop pair, so the plan is to open the e-file with exd5 and then bring the knight round Nh2-g4 to hit your f6 knight and the e5 pawn. ...h5 takes g4 away from the knight, ...Qb6 hits b2 and the a-pawn moves fix the queenside. You are fine with the d5 and e5 pawns controlling the centre; the position is level.

notes.text: White can also hold the knight back
A normal, balanced King's Indian Attack structure.
notes.original: A normal, balanced King's Indian Attack structure. Black's simplest plan from here is ...Bg4 or ...Re8 and ...Nd7-f6 regrouping; there is nothing sharp or dangerous for Black to worry about.

notes.text: Black wants to provoke h3, which weakens White's kingside, and then build a bishop-and-queen battery against the h3-pawn.
White sacrifices a pawn but has prepared a tactical sequence that breaks through in the centre and wins the material…
notes.original: White sacrifices a pawn but has prepared a tactical sequence that breaks through in the centre and wins the material back.

notes.text: Trap: 9.Nxd4? Bxd1 10.Rxd1 Nd7 11.N2f3 Bc5 12.exd5 and White is losing.
Black has the bishop pair and White's kingside pawns are overextended, so White will have a hard time defending.
The position is equal.
White is a pawn up after the bishop sacrifice on h2, but the king on h2 is the target.
notes.original: White is a pawn up after the bishop sacrifice on h2, but the king on h2 is the target. You keep the initiative with checks: ...Rfe8 takes the open file and eyes the bishop's squares, ...Qd6+ and ...Qd5+ drive the king back and forth and ...Ne5-d3 plants a knight with tempo on the bishop. White's only way to cash the extra pawn is to run the king to safety with Kg2 and c3, so you should keep making threats rather than slow moves. The result is level.

notes.text: Simple development is enough; if White pushes 4.e5 the knight just retreats to g8 and comes back via f6 or…
notes.original: Simple development is enough; if White pushes 4.e5 the knight just retreats to g8 and comes back via f6 or h6 later, while Black's structure stays sound and White's kingside is slightly loosened.

notes.text: White's motive after e5 is space: f4 backs up the e5 pawn and g4-g5 will cramp your pieces and kick…
notes.original: White's motive after e5 is space: f4 backs up the e5 pawn and g4-g5 will cramp your pieces and kick your bishop. You answer with ...Bd7 and the counter-thrust ...h5, which undermines g4 and fixes the g5 pawn, and then ...Bg4 hits the queen and keeps the light squares under your control. You can follow up with ...e6, ...c5 and ...Ne7 to undermine e5. White keeps a small edge but his kingside is very loosened.

notes.text: After e5 White wants space: f4 backs up the e5 pawn and g4-g5 will cramp your pieces and kick your…
notes.original: After e5 White wants space: f4 backs up the e5 pawn and g4-g5 will cramp your pieces and kick your bishop. You answer with ...Bd7 and the counter-thrust ...h5, which undermines g4 and fixes the g5 pawn, and then ...Bg4 hits the queen and keeps the light squares under your control. notes.original: Your advanced pawn on d4 cramps White, but it also needs defending, so you shore it up with ...Rfd8 and develop around it. White's plan is pressure on the b-file with Qb5 and Rfb1, so you answer with ...b6 and keep the c-file. You keep a small edge.

notes.original: White plays g4-g5 and h4 for a kingside pawn storm, with the bishop pair as a bonus. You meet it with ...Bd6 and ...h6, break open g6 on your terms and develop the knight to f6.

3.exd5 is the main line.

notes.original: Another interesting idea is the Hillbilly Gambit, in which White sacrifices a pawn and aims for a quick attack or mate.

notes.text: 3.Bb3!?, the "Hillbilly Gambit": White sacrifices a pawn hoping for a quick kingside kill.
notes.original: 3.Bb3!?, the "Hillbilly Gambit": White sacrifices a pawn hoping for a quick kingside kill. Full treatment in 🔵 19, deepened here with the critical trap and the 4.Nc3 alternative.

notes.text: Your d5 pawn attacked the bishop on c4, so White saves it with check and a tempo.
notes.original: Your d5 pawn attacked the bishop on c4, so White saves it with check and a tempo. White hopes to follow with a4, d4 and Nf3 and reach a comfortable game with no weaknesses. It is very common in practice, so you should have a clear answer.

notes.text: White develops the knight and keeps the bishop on b3 pointing at your d5 pawn and at f7.
notes.original: White develops the knight and keeps the bishop on b3 pointing at your d5 pawn and at f7. The idea is to follow with d4 and reach a comfortable isolated-pawn type of position. This is a very common choice (played in about 861,000 games), so expect it. For you, d5 is the target, so keep it defended while you develop with tempo.

notes.text: White avoids sharp theory and plans a slow build-up with Nf3, c3 or Nbd2 while the bishop on b3 keeps…
notes.original: White avoids sharp theory and plans a slow build-up with Nf3, c3 or Nbd2 while the bishop on b3 keeps eyeing your d5 pawn. It is very common, played in about 497,000 games, but d3 is a modest move that spends a tempo, so you get a free hand in the centre. You are slightly better here.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White offers a bishop trade to remove your good bishop and aims the queen along the c-file.
notes.original: White offers a bishop trade to remove your good bishop and aims the queen along the c-file. You accept, then gain queenside space with ...b5 and ask the dark-squared bishop what it wants with ...h6. After the bishops swap, your bishop on f6 puts pressure on d4 together with Nc6. Your plan is ...Rc8 and ...Qd6 with a slightly better, safe game.

notes.text: The immediate Nbd2 lets you hit the bishop with ...g5
Nc6 adds a second defender to d5 and prepares ...e5, the central break this whole line is built on.
notes.original: Nc6 adds a second defender to d5 and prepares ...e5, the central break this whole line is built on. Your plan is to play ...e5 at once, answer d4 with ...e4 to gain space and chase the knight, then bring the bishop to d6 and the other bishop to e6 and castle short. Avoid slow set-ups with ...e6, which lock in your c8 bishop and leave d5 weak and static. The numbers give you a small edge.

notes.text: A solid alternative.
notes.original: A solid alternative. Put the bishop outside your pawn chain first, then play ...e6, ...Nc6 and ...Be7. It is a quieter game: you give up the quick ...e5 break but keep a healthy structure against 6.d4.

notes.text: This stops ...Bg4, so you cannot pin the knight.
notes.original: This stops ...Bg4, so you cannot pin the knight. It is slow, and that is why you can strike in the centre immediately.

notes.text: The pawn on e4 attacks the knight and is protected by d5.
notes.original: The pawn on e4 attacks the knight and is protected by d5. White must decide where the knight goes.

notes.text: You challenge the knight at once; if White supports it with f4 you keep a firm grip on the light…
notes.original: You challenge the knight at once; if White supports it with f4 you keep a firm grip on the light squares. Develop Be6, castle, and look for ...Qe7 or ...Nxe5 to remove the strong piece when it suits you.

notes.text: You hold more space in the centre and have easy development, while White has to prove the knight on e5…
notes.original: You hold more space in the centre and have easy development, while White has to prove the knight on e5 is not just overextended. This is a space-gaining position where you have e4 and d5 supported by pieces, and White's knight on e5 is strong but not unassailable. You have more space in the centre and easy development. Your plan: castle short, then ...Qd7 or ...Qe7, and challenge the knight with ...Nxe5 when it suits you, using ...Ng4 or ...Nd7 to bring pieces over. White wants Nxc6, then Bxd6, to ruin your structure, or f3 to break up the e4 pawn. The mistake is allowing Nxc6 bxc6 with a damaged structure; if White plays f3, answer with ...exf3 and keep control of d5.

notes.text: Develop with a purpose.
notes.original: Develop with a purpose. The knight hits d4 and prepares ...e5, the break you want: with pawns on d5 and e5 you own the centre and White's pieces have little room. Your plan is ...e5, then the light-squared bishop to e6 or g4, ...Bd6 or ...Be7, and castle kingside. Avoid the passive ...e6 set-up that locks in your c8 bishop; you do not need it.

notes.text: White stops ...Bg4, so you spend a move on ...h6 to take the sting out of Bg5 pins.
notes.original: White stops ...Bg4, so you spend a move on ...h6 to take the sting out of Bg5 pins. Do not drift with ...Bf5 and ...e6; keep the e5 break in mind.

notes.text: White challenges the centre, and you gain space with ...e4, which shuts out his knight from e4 and cramps his…
notes.original: White challenges the centre, and you gain space with ...e4, which shuts out his knight from e4 and cramps his position.

notes.text: The knight on e5 looks strong, but you can challenge it with ...Nxe5 or ...Nd7 and ...Bd6, and ...Be6 develops…
notes.original: The knight on e5 looks strong, but you can challenge it with ...Nxe5 or ...Nd7 and ...Bd6, and ...Be6 develops while keeping d5 protected. Avoid ...exd4, which opens lines for White. You hold a big centre and develop easily while White's pieces tie themselves to d4 and e5.

notes.text: This is an open centre where you hold the e4 and d5 pawns and have space, so you are slightly…
notes.original: This is an open centre where you hold the e4 and d5 pawns and have space, so you are slightly better. Your knight on e5 is attacking, but White's own knight hits your c6 knight. Your plan is, first, to trade the strong knight with ...Nxe5. Second, play ...Bd6 to trade the dark bishops and castle short. Third, support the centre with ...Qd7 and ...Rd8. White wants c4 to undermine d5 and a quick attack on f7. The risk is playing ...Bd6 first, which lets White play Nxc6 with tricks. If White plays c4, answer with ...dxc4 and keep your centre solid.

notes.text: If White develops first, you play ...e5 anyway and answer Bg5 with ...Be7.
Block with the bishop and offer a trade.
notes.original: Block with the bishop and offer a trade. If White retreats with Be2 you have gained time, and if White takes on d7 you recapture with the knight or queen and are comfortable. Plan: ...e6, then ...a6 to challenge the bishop, ...Bd6 and ...Ne7, and castle short. Your d5 pawn is well supported and the structure is sound. Avoid trading your light-squared bishop for no reason, because that leaves d5 weaker.

notes.text: A playable alternative, aiming for an early ...e5, but the knight blocks your own bishop on c8 and is a…
notes.original: A playable alternative, aiming for an early ...e5, but the knight blocks your own bishop on c8 and is a little less good.

notes.text: White has spent several moves on the bishop and you have a compact setup.
notes.original: White has spent several moves on the bishop and you have a compact setup. Castle, bring a knight to c6 and push ...f5 or ...b6 only when needed. Your later breaks are ...Nbc6 followed by ...e5 or ...f6. You are slightly better thanks to the lost time. This is a closed, compact position where White has spent several moves on the bishop and you hold a solid centre with pawns on d5 and e6. Your plan: castle short, bring the other knight out with ...Nbc6, then free your game with ...e5 or ...f6 once your pieces are placed. White wants Ba3 to trade your dark-squared bishop, or c4 to challenge d5. You are happy to trade bishops on a3, and you meet c4 with ...dxc4 bxc4. The typical mistake is drifting passively because the position looks quiet, so keep making useful moves. If White delays castling, you have time for ...Nbc6.

notes.original: White's motive for f3 is to drive away your strong bishop on f5 and win the e4 square back. notes.original: 3...Qc7!? - an 'Endgame Offer' trick: the queen eyes h2 along the long diagonal and discourages White from ever playing e5, since after an eventual ...dxe4 the position can simplify toward an endgame where Black's structure is at least as pleasant. White still keeps a small, normal edge with careful play, but has to find it rather than being handed one automatically.

notes.text: Choice guide: choose this if you want to answer a quiet, non-committal 3.d3 with ...Qc7 and simple development (low risk,…
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want to answer a quiet, non-committal 3.d3 with ...Qc7 and simple development (low risk, little theory): the plan is ...dxe4 and ...Nd7, then ...e5 or ...e6 and ...Ngf6. Against 3.d3 the alternative is 3...dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ which leads to a drawish endgame. Risk level: low. After 3.d3 Qc7 Black keeps the queen active and avoids the symmetrical endgame. White's main moves are 4.Nc3, 4.Nbd2, 4.Qe2, 4.e5 and 4.exd5.

notes.text: This is an unorthodox gambit in which White trades a pawn for fast development.
notes.original: This is an unorthodox gambit in which White trades a pawn for fast development. It is not a cause for concern: Black should develop normally and try to disrupt White's set-up.

notes.text: Believe it or not, this simplification is completely fine for Black.
notes.original: Believe it or not, this simplification is completely fine for Black. Yes, White has to recapture with the king, but the position is so simple and symmetrical that this costs nothing concrete - no real attack is possible on an open board with almost no pieces left to attack with.

notes.text: Pin the knight right away.
notes.original: Pin the knight right away. Black already has a very comfortable, easy position with no theory to memorize.

notes.original: A sample line all the way into a simple, balanced middlegame: Black trades the light-squared bishop for a knight, then the dark-squared bishop as well, reaching a position with no weaknesses and no real winning try for White - the kind of safe, low-maintenance equality this line is meant to offer against an opponent trying to avoid main-line theory.

notes.text: White's plan is to gain space on the queenside with a4, c4 and b5 and to fix your pawns there,…
notes.original: White's plan is to gain space on the queenside with a4, c4 and b5 and to fix your pawns there, hoping that the knights end up passive. You hold the queenside shut with ...c5 and ...b6, give the king room with ...f6 and ...Kf7 and then counter on the kingside with ...h5. Your knights have good squares on e6 and d7 and White has no breakthrough, so the position stays a small, safe plus for White.

notes.text: This prevents Bf4.
notes.original: This prevents Bf4. Black should keep disrupting White's ideal development, otherwise Black ends up cramped and difficult to play.

notes.text: White is forced to move his queen to e1.
notes.original: White is forced to move his queen to e1. If f3 then his knight cannot go back to f3 anymore.

notes.text: Comfortable position for Black.
notes.original: Comfortable position for Black. Black should consolidate his central control and develop comfortably.

notes.text: Bd4 aims at your f6 knight and the g7 pawn.
notes.original: Bd4 aims at your f6 knight and the g7 pawn. ...Qa5 hits the c3 knight and keeps the queen active, and after Be5 you castle and challenge the bishop with ...Nd7 and ...Bf6. White's f4 only weakens his own king. You keep a small, comfortable edge.

notes.text: White's f4-f5 lever opens the f-file, but your king on c8 is far from the action and you have the…
notes.original: White's f4-f5 lever opens the f-file, but your king on c8 is far from the action and you have the extra space in the centre

notes.text: White retreats the knight to a safe square instead of exchanging it, so he keeps an extra piece for the…
notes.original: White retreats the knight to a safe square instead of exchanging it, so he keeps an extra piece for the middlegame and eyes f5 and h5 for later. The move is simple development with no direct threat and it is very common (played in about 101,000 games). So the centre is yours to fight for: you have a free hand to play the usual pawn breaks.

notes.text: Another way to trade queens that costs White castling
Your plan is to take space in the centre and the queen side with ...c5, then ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...Be7,…
notes.original: Your plan is to take space in the centre and the queen side with ...c5, then ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...Be7, castling short. The pawn on c5 stops White from ever playing d4 comfortably and gives your pieces natural squares. Avoid rushing ...e5 and ...Bd6 without preparation, because White's knight on g3 then looks at f5 and e4 and can become annoying.

notes.text: Develop with tempo-free simplicity: the knight on c6 pressures d4 and supports ...e5 or ...d5 ideas later.
Now the pawn on e6 opens the bishop's diagonal and defends d5 and f5.
notes.original: Now the pawn on e6 opens the bishop's diagonal and defends d5 and f5. If White tries 8.Ng5 hitting f7 and h7, you answer ...h6 or ...Be7 and the knight has nowhere good to go.

notes.text: White wants to pin and annoy your knight on c6.
notes.original: White wants to pin and annoy your knight on c6. You can answer with ...Qc7 and ...b5 ideas when needed. You have a comfortable, flexible game and are slightly better here. This is a flexible semi-open position: your pawns stand on c5 and e6, White has d3 and c3, both kings have castled short and neither side has a space edge. Your plan: first meet the queen on a4 with ...Qc7 or ...Bd7 so the knight on c6 is comfortable; then bring a rook to d8 and c8; then consider ...e5 or ...Nd4 to claim the centre. White wants to regroup with Nbd2-c2 or Re1 and play d4 at the right moment, so keep the c5 pawn solid. The risk is ...e5 played too early, when Nf5 and Ng3 pieces become annoying. If White deviates with d4, recapture calmly.

notes.text: White finally brings out the last knight to eye e5 and d4.
notes.original: White finally brings out the last knight to eye e5 and d4. The motive is plain development: Bd3, castling and perhaps Ne5 follow. The key point for you is that your c8 bishop is still free to jump to g4 before you play ...e6, so use it.

notes.text: White pins the knight on f6 to the queen's side and wants to trade it, doubling or weakening your pawns.
notes.original: White pins the knight on f6 to the queen's side and wants to trade it, doubling or weakening your pawns. This is very common (played in about 791,000 games). So every capture on f6 has to be recaptured sensibly, so decide early how you want to meet it.

notes.text: White may play this to prevent a ...Ng4 pin.
Extra: only needed if White plays a 4th move other than 4.Bd3 or 4.c4.
notes.original:

notes.original: You trade the bishop for the knight, which removes a defender of the d4 pawn and of the e5 pawn. notes.original: Your queen attacks the d4 and b2 pawns at once. White has to decide how to defend.

notes.original: You have won a pawn but White has activity on the queenside, so be ready to return it or bring the queen back. Your plan is ...Nxd4 and castling, with your king safe. This line is slightly better for you. This is a position where you have grabbed the b2 pawn and White has more active pieces, so your queen on b2 is a target. Your plan: retreat the queen at once with ...Qb6 so it cannot be trapped by Rb1, then develop with ...Nge7 and ...Nf5, and castle short. White wants Rb1 or Nb3, hoping to win your queen or take compensation for the pawn. If White plays Rb1, drop the queen back to b6 or b4 and be ready to give the pawn back. The risk is greed: do not play ...Nxd4 when d4 is protected by the bishop on e3, because the tactics favour White.

notes.original: You add pressure to d4 and e5, develop a piece and keep the option of ...e6. Your plan is to trade on d4, take on e2 when it helps, and use the light squares left by the exchanged bishops. Be careful with the d5 pawn: if White takes on d5 you want to recapture with the queen or the pawn without losing time. Avoid ...c4 here, which gives away your pressure on d4.

notes.original: The position is balanced, your king will castle long or short, and White's king on e2 gives you targets. This is a semi-open position where your pawns are on c5, d5 and e6 against White's pawns on d4 and e5, with White's king on e2 and no castling for him. You have the more comfortable game because his king is awkward. Plan: recapture on d5 with ...exd5, trade on d4 with ...Nxd4 only when it works, then develop with ...Nf6, ...Bc5 and castle short, aiming at his king along the e-file. White wants to hide the king and play Nc3 or Rd1 with pressure on d5. The risk is the pin on c6: if the knight moves carelessly, Qxd7 wins material. If White plays Nc3 first, recapture ...exd5 anyway.

notes.text: Trading is the right answer.
notes.original: Trading is the right answer. After Qxf3 White's queen is out early and you can take on d4. Your plan is ...cxd4, ...Qd7 to stop Qb3 from hitting b7, then ...Nc6 and ...e6, followed by short castling. Avoid retreating with the bishop, which loses time and a good minor piece.

The pawn on d4 will often fall because White has no easy way to defend it. You hold a slight edge, with no weaknesses. This is a semi-open position in which you hold a small but real edge, with pawns on d5, e6 and the tension in the centre; you will probably castle short once g7 is safe. Your plan: protect the d4 pawn with ...Nc6, develop ...Nge7 and ...Nf5 to hit the queen, then ...Bc5 and ...Qd7. White wants to take on d4, play Bd3 and use his queen on g3 against g7 and h7. The risk is leaving g7 loose: do not let Qxg7 come with tempo, and do not let a knight take on d4 for free. If White uses Nd2 instead, still play ...e6 and ...Nc6.

notes.original: 6...f6 hits e5 immediately and is the more aggressive option. It does weaken the e6-square and the king's diagonal, so it suits players who like open fights.

notes.original: The point of the maneuver - the knight eyes c5 and d4 and makes Black's usual ...c5 break slightly harder to execute for free, since ...c5 can sometimes be met by Nxc5 tricks depending on the position.

notes.text: Hit straight back at the undefended b2 pawn and develop with tempo - the most natural and testing response.
A realistic continuation showing what Black's setup is for: even though White's knight maneuver (Nb3-c5-d3) looks annoying, Black castles into…
notes.original: A realistic continuation showing what Black's setup is for: even though White's knight maneuver (Nb3-c5-d3) looks annoying, Black castles into safety and keeps the position balanced with no real weaknesses - which is what the 4.Nd2 sideline is trying, and failing, to avoid.

notes.text: White develops with tempo on your queen.
notes.original: White develops with tempo on your queen. The bishop prepares f4 to hold e5, then Ng3 to chase your bishop off f5.

notes.text: Step out of the bishop's attack and keep an eye on e5.
Your thematic break: hit the e5 chain before White consolidates with Ng3 and castling.
Your knight finally reaches d6 with a threat against the b5 bishop.
notes.original: Your knight finally reaches d6 with a threat against the b5 bishop. Your king is safe and your pieces cover each other, so White has found no target.

notes.text: Hitting the bishop at once is tempting, but ...d4 opens the centre and you win the e5 pawn back.
A perfectly normal, comfortable structure.
notes.original: A perfectly normal, comfortable structure. White's small lead in development is balanced out by Black's extra pawn and completely sound position - the knight lands on the excellent d5 outpost right on schedule.

notes.text: The bishop steps back because ...a4 was about to harass it on b3.
notes.original: The bishop steps back because ...a4 was about to harass it on b3. From a2 it still eyes e6 and f7. White's small edge comes from the h5 pawn, the knight on g3 and the d4 centre, so play accurately.

notes.text: Clamp down on the h5 pawn and take f4 away from the knight on g3.
White offers the trade of your best bishop, and you accept.
White opens the position with f4 while your king is still in the centre, and the resulting tactics keep White…
notes.original: White opens the position with f4 while your king is still in the centre, and the resulting tactics keep White somewhat ahead. Avoid extra pawn grabs and finish your development.

notes.text: Re1 and Qg4 hunt the king that has not castled yet.
notes.original: Re1 and Qg4 hunt the king that has not castled yet. You survive, but it is a more uncomfortable version.

notes.text: Trap: 8...Qa5+? 9.Nc3 c5 10.Nf3 cxd4 11.Nxd4 O-O-O and Black is losing.

notes.original: Simple, solid development pays off here: Black trades down comfortably and even grabs a loose pawn on b2 once the position opens up - a good demonstration that this sideline carries no real venom once Black knows the basic setup.

notes.text: The bishop hits your queen on b2, and the point is to win the g7 pawn back in return, with…
notes.original: The bishop hits your queen on b2, and the point is to win the g7 pawn back in return, with your queen running around.

notes.text: Your queen steps aside and keeps pressure on c3.
The rook on h8 was attacked, and f8 is a safe square.
Offer a queen trade to ease the pressure from the open position.
The queen is centralised and the material is back to balance, so you can play on freely.

notes.original: Hitting the queen looks natural, but after the queen trade White has nothing for the missing pawn and you are clearly better.

notes.original: This transposes back into the exact same structure and tactical point covered above (Nxh5 met by ...cxd4) - whichever move order White chooses to reach this pawn storm, Black's response is identical.

Black already has an initiative on the kingside (the rook eyes g4/g2 down the g-file) for nothing more than the…
notes.original:
Black already has an initiative on the kingside (the rook eyes g4/g2 down the g-file) for nothing more than the pawn White grabbed a few moves ago - a completely fair, often better, trade of assets.
Trap: 12...gxh6? 13.Nf6# and Black gets mated.

notes.original: The alternative move order - developing the knight first and only then resolving the center - reaches an equally comfortable position; a matter of taste rather than necessity.

notes.text: Your a-pawn threatens the b5 bishop, so White trades it off with check.
notes.original: Your a-pawn threatens the b5 bishop, so White trades it off with check. This gives you a slight edge.

notes.original: The queen trade leaves your pieces active and White's knight on h5 offside. You are a bit better.

notes.original: The queens come off and White's knight on h5 is offside. You keep a small, pleasant edge.

notes.original: White gains space on the queenside, but your pieces are active and the b4 pawn is a target. You are fine.

notes.original: 6.Bc4 is an alternative to 6.d4. White can castle quickly and follow up with Nc3, d5 or Be3. 6.d4 is more accurate.

notes.original: Your king is stuck in the centre since ...Rg8 gave up castling, so White removes your best defender and opens the position.

notes.original: White is clearly better: the rooks come to the c-file while your king is stuck in the centre. If you can, avoid this setup and castle before ...Rg8.

notes.text: This gives you time to castle long and White's edge shrinks.

notes.original: A sign of domination: Black finds a temporary outpost on h3 that stops White castling. White must bring the bishop back to f1, losing a tempo to get rid of the intruder.

notes.text: A pleasant feature of the Dano-Russian Variation: White has to defend against a quick kingside assault, and Black's play is…
notes.original: A pleasant feature of the Dano-Russian Variation: White has to defend against a quick kingside assault, and Black's play is comfortable and flexible, with queenside castling available.

notes.original: White gains queenside space with a4-a5 to kick the Nb6, and with a6 to follow he hopes to attack the long-castled king.

notes.original: The position is balanced and the kings are on the same wing, so everything depends on who is faster; your h-pawn plus the g-file is a fast attack.

notes.original: Pawn takes pawn only leads to total equality for both opposing sides. White lets go of his pressure on the center pawn which would lead to a simple game.

notes.original: There's frankly not much to be addressed. Bg4 e6 Bd6 0-0 as usual if h3 isn't played.

notes.original: The position is equal and quite symmetrical. Play ...b5 and ...Rfc8 or ...Rac8, keep the d5 pawn protected, and try for a queenside play.

notes.original: Rather than retreating with Ned2, White keeps more pieces on and more central control by playing Bd3 directly, meeting a future ...Nxe4 with a simple recapture.

notes.original: Equal. White has traded one pair of knights, you have the c-file and an easy plan with ...O-O, ...Rc8.

notes.text: A small, normal opening pull for White - fully within the range of what's expected from this system, and worth…
notes.original: A small, normal opening pull for White - fully within the range of what's expected from this system, and worth having on record as the more testing option.

notes.text: White removes your active bishop at once.
notes.original: White removes your active bishop at once. His motive is to follow with Qb3 and hit b7, since your queen cannot recapture on f5 yet.

notes.original:

notes.original: A completely level, slightly better for Black endgame - the doubled f-pawns are of no consequence since Black has the bishop pair and a sound structure everywhere else.

notes.original: After the queen is kicked back with tempo by the natural developing move, Black is already comfortably ahead in development for nothing.

notes.original:

notes.original: Black continues to generate easy, natural piece play (...c5, ...Bg4, ...Nd4) against a White setup that has spent multiple tempi with the queen instead of developing - a small but real and lasting initiative.

notes.original: Trading in the center immediately is again the simplest answer. Black is already very slightly better here, and the position is easy to play with normal developing moves - no memorization needed beyond recognizing that ...dxe4 is always fine.
