notes.original: Just meet it exactly like the main Advance Variation chapters - develop the bishop to f5 and follow the same structural plans covered in 🔵 11 to 13 and 🟢 05 and our other Advance Variation material.

notes.text: A quiet move: g3 takes f4 and h4 away from your pieces and prepares Bf1, which frees e2 for the…
notes.original: A quiet move: g3 takes f4 and h4 away from your pieces and prepares Bf1, which frees e2 for the queen. Your thematic answer is the lever ...f6, hitting the e5 pawn that cramps you; do not wait for White to reinforce it with f4.

notes.text: Once e5 is gone, your fianchettoed bishop becomes a strong Bf6 on the long diagonal, and the doubled h-pawns matter…
notes.original: Once e5 is gone, your fianchettoed bishop becomes a strong Bf6 on the long diagonal, and the doubled h-pawns matter little in this semi-closed position. White keeps a little more space on the queenside with b4 and c3, you have the bishop pair, so it is a small White edge at most.

notes.text: White speeds up queenside play, but after b5 your knight retreats and the queen hits the c3 pawn that holds…
notes.original: White speeds up queenside play, but after b5 your knight retreats and the queen hits the c3 pawn that holds the chain together, so it is balanced.

notes.text: Choice guide: choose this if you want a safe, structural answer to an unusual knight sortie: the plan is ...Nc6,…
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want a safe, structural answer to an unusual knight sortie: the plan is ...Nc6, ...a6 and ...e6, accepting a Carlsbad-type pawn structure. It is a low-risk line but demands care in the early moves. 4.Ne5 is an early knight raid aimed at provoking weaknesses. Black answers with the natural 4...Nc6 and keeps solid.

notes.text: White adds a second attacker against d5, planning d4 and then Ne5, Bf4 or Bb5.
notes.original: White adds a second attacker against d5, planning d4 and then Ne5, Bf4 or Bb5. It is a natural developing move and very common in practice. White is not trying to dodge theory, just to build a comfortable setup. For you the task is to guard d5 sensibly and finish development with a clear plan.

notes.text: White checks to force you to decide a minor piece at once.
notes.original: White checks to force you to decide a minor piece at once. The idea is to continue with d4 and O-O, perhaps trading the bishop for your knight to wreck your structure. Because White has not yet played Nc3, you have a flexible answer.

notes.text: This queen sortie looks threatening (it eyes both f7 and the knight's follow-up ideas), but it's met by returning the…
notes.original: This queen sortie looks threatening (it eyes both f7 and the knight's follow-up ideas), but it's met by returning the piece for a pawn and consolidating - the resulting position is completely safe and, if anything, favors Black's better structure.

notes.text: Trap: 6.Bb5+? Nc6 7.d4 Bd7 8.Nc3 Nf6 9.Qd1 and White is losing.
White has nothing better than to recapture the hanging knight - any other move just loses material outright.
notes.original: White has nothing better than to recapture the hanging knight - any other move just loses material outright. From here Black finishes development (...f6, ...Bd7, ...Nc6) and reaches a fully comfortable position with an extra central pawn majority to work with in the long run.

notes.text: The knight on b5 hits the bishop on d6 and eyes a7 and c7.
notes.original: The knight on b5 hits the bishop on d6 and eyes a7 and c7. Retreating to b8 keeps your bishop pair (Nxd6+ Qxd6 would give it up), guards a7 and stays on the b8-h2 diagonal. White's only active idea is the break c4: after dxc4 Bxc4 your knight hops to a5 with a tempo on the bishop, and you castle without worries.

notes.text: Bh6 only chases the rook sideways.
notes.original: Bh6 only chases the rook sideways. You are fully developed and the position is level.

notes.text: Also holds: you give up a bishop for the knight and the king is safe enough on f7.
White trades the knight and Black gets a half-open b-file and a solid centre.
notes.original: White trades the knight and Black gets a half-open b-file and a solid centre. 8.Nd2 Nf6 9.Be2 Bd6 is fine for Black.

notes.original: A useful move. It stops Bb5+ and Nb5 ideas and prepares ...Nc6 and ...Bf5 without worry. Plan: ...Nc6, ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, ...e6, ...Nf6 or ...Bd6, then castle short. Your break is ...e5 once the pieces are out. Do not let White pin your knight with a quick Bb5 while d5 is loose.

notes.text: Equally good, and it develops a piece at once.
Recapturing with the b-pawn gives you the half-open b-file and a flexible pawn center.
notes.original: Recapturing with the b-pawn gives you the half-open b-file and a flexible pawn center. The pawn on c6 supports d5 and your bishop is already outside the pawn chain.

notes.text: White heads for c5 or b6 with the knight, so keep your queen ready for ...Qa5 or ...Qd7 and play…
notes.original: White heads for c5 or b6 with the knight, so keep your queen ready for ...Qa5 or ...Qd7 and play ...Nf6 and ...Be7 to finish development. Equal and your structure is healthy. This is a balanced Caro-Kann position with a pawn structure close to a French, where White has a knight on a4 that is a little offside. Your bishop on f5 is already outside the pawn chain. Your plan: develop with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, then castle short, using ...Qa5+ or ...Qc7 when it helps. White wants to bring the knight to c5 and use the bishop on f4 to build pressure on c7. Meet Nc5 by guarding b7 with ...Qc7. Remember that ...Qa5+ is answered by Nc3, so it is a resource, not a win. The mistake is ignoring the knight and leaving your king in the centre.

notes.text: Block with the bishop and offer a trade.
notes.original: Block with the bishop and offer a trade. If White retreats with Be2 you gain time, and if White takes on d7 you recapture with the knight or queen. Plan: ...Nc6, ...Bg4 to pin the knight on f3, ...Nf6 and ...e6, then castle short. Your break is ...e5 or ...f6 once the pieces are in place.

notes.text: Tempting because the knight guards c5 and b6, but it blocks your bishop and White gets the easier game.
White gains space with c5, but the pawn cannot easily be supported.
notes.original: White gains space with c5, but the pawn cannot easily be supported. Aim at it with ...b6 and ...Be7, and keep your knights on c6 and f6 ready to jump to e4. Avoid letting your pawn on d5 become isolated. Equal with a clear plan. This is a fairly closed position where White has gained space with c5 and d4, and your pawns stand on d5 and e6. Your bishop on g4 and knights on c6 and f6 are well placed. Your plan: play ...Be7, then undermine the pawn on c5 with ...b6, and castle short. White wants b4-b5 to hit the knight on c6, or Ne5 to trade your active pieces. Trade on f3 with ...Bxf3 when it helps, and keep a knight ready for e4. The mistake is letting your pawn on d5 become isolated. If White plays b4, answer ...b6 at once and open the queenside.

notes.original: 4.exd5 - resolves the central tension at once rather than developing past it, testing whether Black's queen placement on c7 was worth the tempo.

notes.original: 4.Nc3 - declines to resolve the center and just develops, daring Black to take on e4 and hand White a lead in development.

notes.original: 4...cxd5 recaptures naturally; the queen on c7 is already well-placed for the resulting structure, eyeing h2 along the b8-h2 diagonal once the position opens.

notes.original: 4.e5 grabs space immediately rather than developing with Nc3 or Be3 first, trying to punish Black's slower 3...e6 setup before it's consolidated.

notes.text: White grabs space on the queenside and attacks d5 at once, hoping you will push or exchange and that his…
notes.original: White grabs space on the queenside and attacks d5 at once, hoping you will push or exchange and that his lead in the centre will grow before the f3 pawn becomes a liability. It is very common in practice (played in about 70,000 games). Note that the knight on b1 has not moved, so White is a little loose and you can use that.

notes.text: White supports d4 so that he can meet ...dxe4 with fxe4, and prepares Nd2 or Bd3 with a flexible set-up.
notes.original: White supports d4 so that he can meet ...dxe4 with fxe4, and prepares Nd2 or Bd3 with a flexible set-up. It is a quiet, solid choice that is common in practice (played in about 48,000 games), and it avoids the sharp lines with Nc3. So a fight for a small positional edge, not a tactical melee.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
5.Nge2 - develops the second knight flexibly instead of committing the bishop yet, keeping Nf4 or g3 available later.
Extra: only needed if White plays 3.f3 and you answer 3...e6 or 3...Qb6.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays 3.f3 and you answer 3...e6 or 3...Qb6.
Idea: 3...e6 is a calmer, French-style answer. Develop with ...Nd7, ...a6 and ...Be7, then take on e4 and play ...e5 once White has committed. The sharp 3...Qb6 is covered here too.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 e6 4.Nc3 Nd7 5.Be3 a6
Watch out: ...Qxc3? loses material on move 13. ...Qxh2? loses material on move 14.
Next: Plan: 🟠 Plan 05.

notes.text: The ...a6 idea again.
notes.original: The ...a6 idea again. The same ...a6 idea from the Two Knights Attack chapters shows up here too: a6 keeps an eye on the b5 square, ruling out any White piece landing there and preparing a future ...b5 expansion of Black's own queenside space. In this particular structure it also gains a tempo for development, since White's pieces are not yet ready to punish the small loss of time.

notes.text: Black strikes at the centre with ...e5 and does not let White take over the game.
Another option for White.
e5 needs to be played in order to develop the knight with ease on Ngf6.
The quieter Be2 (rather than Bc4 in the main line) is actually the more accurate try, keeping the bishop safely…
notes.original: The quieter Be2 (rather than Bc4 in the main line) is actually the more accurate try, keeping the bishop safely out of any future ...Nb6 or ...b5 ideas while still eyeing the kingside.

notes.text: Be2 is more accurate.
A small, normal edge for White after the further simplification shown - manageable for Black with careful play, and a…
notes.original: A small, normal edge for White after the further simplification shown - manageable for Black with careful play, and a minor but real improvement on the main line.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The knight jumps to f5 to hit your queen and the g7 pawn; you take it, accept White's f5 pawn…
notes.original: The knight jumps to f5 to hit your queen and the g7 pawn; you take it, accept White's f5 pawn and castle. When White pushes g4 you check, trade queens and take the e-file with the rook, so White's pawns end up bent but the pieces stay active.

notes.text: An easy line for you: queens come off and you take the open e-file.
White has an isolated pawn.
White has an isolated pawn.
Black is slightly better.
With the queens off you keep the bishop pair and a powerful bishop on d4.
notes.original: With the queens off you keep the bishop pair and a powerful bishop on d4. The h3 move kicks your bishop on g4, so you trade it for White's good bishop, which opens the f-file for you. Both sides castle long and your bishops give you the better of it.

notes.text: The knight jump hits your queen, but you trade queens with check and keep a lead in development.
Black is slightly better.
The queen on d3 attacks your strong bishop on d4, so you develop with tempo: ...Be6 brings the last minor…
notes.original: The queen on d3 attacks your strong bishop on d4, so you develop with tempo: ...Be6 brings the last minor piece out, ...Qg5+ gains time with a check, and castling long adds a rook to the defence of d4 and takes the d-file. You keep the bishop pair and the better development.

notes.text: The knight move allows a queen trade, but you keep your bishops and the better structure.
White is slightly better.
The bishop on c2 and queen on d3 aim at h7, and the g5 pin on your knight adds to…
notes.original: The bishop on c2 and queen on d3 aim at h7, and the g5 pin on your knight adds to it; h4 followed by h5 is White's kingside plan. You block the h7 diagonal with ...g6 and hit the centre with ...e5, and the knight lands on d5 with an attack on e3, so White's extra pawn on e5 will not be easy to keep.

notes.text: The pawn storm gives up the g5 pawn, though White still has some play for it.
5...Ngf6 meets this with simple, solid development; nothing here needs memorizing beyond normal piece placement.
This is an Advance French structure with f4 included: White gains space with e5 and f4, you kick back and…
notes.original: This is an Advance French structure with f4 included: White gains space with e5 and f4, you kick back and reroute your knight to f5. Your queen hits d4 and b2, which forces Rb1, and the knight on f5 adds to the pressure on d4. The key plan is ...c5: keep hitting d4 until White has to resolve the tension. You are only a little worse.

notes.text: With the bishop out you answer in the same way.
Trap: 6...Qxd4? 7.c3 Qd8 8.cxb4 Ne7 9.Bc4 O-O and Black is losing.
The critical position of the 3...e6 4.Nc3 Bb4 line.
notes.original: The critical position of the 3...e6 4.Nc3 Bb4 line. This particular branch (4...Bb4, pinning the knight before deciding on a central break) is not the line this course actually recommends - our main choice against 4.Nc3 is the simpler 4...Nd7, covered in 🟢 11. This is included purely as supplementary reference for a related, well-known try, along with a real practical warning worth knowing: if you ever reach this position and follow up carelessly with an immediate ...Nd7 before resolving the pin on b4, White wins material outright with Bxb4! - there is no way to recapture. The correct, sound continuation trades the bishop off first with ...Bxd2+, exactly as shown here, before continuing development.

notes.text: The best move here.
notes.original: The best move here. White has a small, normal edge, nothing alarming.

notes.text: Also fine: Nf6.
Also fine: Ne7.
A small, stable White edge from the extra space and bishop pair, consistent with the overall known assessment of the…
notes.original: A small, stable White edge from the extra space and bishop pair, consistent with the overall known assessment of the Fantasy Variation - fully playable and well-trodden for Black.

notes.text: The queen develops and eyes e4, and it stays flexible for ...Nbd7.
notes.original: The queen develops and eyes e4, and it stays flexible for ...Nbd7. White's plan is a kingside pawn storm with g4 and g5; your counter is ...Nbd7, then ...Nxe4 and ...e5 so that your central play arrives first.

notes.text: The structure is now dynamic: White has a passed d-pawn but also doubled pawns, and you must watch the long…
notes.original: The structure is now dynamic: White has a passed d-pawn but also doubled pawns, and you must watch the long diagonal. You are slightly worse.

notes.text: Grabbing pawns with the queen costs time and the queen soon runs short of squares.
White is clearly better.
The queens come off first, because on the open d-file White's queen would otherwise take yours.
notes.original: The queens come off first, because on the open d-file White's queen would otherwise take yours. White's doubled e-pawns are not weak yet, since e6 gains time; you meet it with the king on e7. White's initiative with b4 keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: Avoiding the trade lets White keep the pawn on d6 as a thorn.
White is clearly better.
Kb1 prepares c4 and a grip on the d-file; your knight comes to d7 to cover f6 and e5, but…
notes.original: Kb1 prepares c4 and a grip on the d-file; your knight comes to d7 to cover f6 and e5, but the c4-c5 break opens lines and lets the knight jump to d6, an outpost you cannot easily remove. The g4 pawn storm comes with it. You are under pressure but your pieces are solid.

notes.text: Another setup, but White's pieces are active here too.
6...dxe4 (Solid & Optimal) - simply takes the pawn and meets the recapture with normal development; the simplest route to…
notes.original: 6...dxe4 (Solid & Optimal) - simply takes the pawn and meets the recapture with normal development; the simplest route to a comfortable, slightly favorable structure for Black.

notes.text: 6...Qb6 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - keeps the central tension and immediately eyes b2, provoking White into an early decision rather…
notes.original: 6...Qb6 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - keeps the central tension and immediately eyes b2, provoking White into an early decision rather than resolving the pawn structure yet.

notes.text: White recaptures on e4, but your check with the queen lets you take that pawn as well.
notes.original: White recaptures on e4, but your check with the queen lets you take that pawn as well. White's compensation is development: Qe2 defends the bishop on e3 and challenges your queen, and Bg2 hits it again. You answer by keeping the queen safe on f5 and checking on a5, ending with an extra pawn and a level game.

notes.text: You keep the pawn and hit the centre with ...c5.
The queen on b6 attacks d4 and b2; b3 simply protects the pawn and Qd2 shores up d4.
notes.original: The queen on b6 attacks d4 and b2; b3 simply protects the pawn and Qd2 shores up d4. You take e4, hit the bishop with ...Ng4 and undermine the e5 pawn with ...f6, so your pieces come to life. The position is level.

notes.text: The pawn grab works because the queen returns to b6, though White gets some development.
6...dxe4 (Solid & Optimal) - takes the pawn at once; after 7.Bxe4 Black develops normally and reaches a comfortable, well-tested…
notes.original: 6...dxe4 (Solid & Optimal) - takes the pawn at once; after 7.Bxe4 Black develops normally and reaches a comfortable, well-tested structure with no memorization required.

notes.text: 6...c5 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - strikes at the center immediately instead of resolving the e4-tension, aiming for a sharper, more…
notes.original: 6...c5 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - strikes at the center immediately instead of resolving the e4-tension, aiming for a sharper, more unbalanced middlegame with chances for both sides.

notes.text: Taking on d4 is safe because the bishop on d3 blocks White's queen from defending it.
notes.original: Taking on d4 is safe because the bishop on d3 blocks White's queen from defending it. The knight hit costs White time, so you retreat the queen and set up the e5 and Bg4 centre. White has a lead in development for the pawn and you must finish developing quickly.

notes.text: The bishop is hit and you stay a pawn up.
c3 supports d4 against your c5 lever.
notes.original: c3 supports d4 against your c5 lever. You pile on with ...Nc6, take on e4 and play ...cxd4, and ...Bh4+ comes with check, forcing a concession in front of the king (g3 weakens the light squares, Kd2 is worse). You get comfortable play.

notes.text: The white king is in the middle and your queen takes a pawn with tempo.
...and Black is already comfortably better once the center is challenged.
Bb5 pins the knight and White hopes for Bxc6+ and dxc5.
notes.original: Bb5 pins the knight and White hopes for Bxc6+ and dxc5. You hit the loose bishop with the queen; once it is supported by Qa4 you tuck the queen back, unpin with ...Bd7 and win time on d4. You are clearly better and the strike at d4 is the key to the position.

notes.text: Another good route.
Take the pawn.
notes.original: Take the pawn. White cannot simply recapture and keep an easy game, because his pieces are not ready. After Nc3 you play ...Bb4, pinning the knight, then ...c5 to undermine d4. Do not feel you must hold the pawn on e4; giving it back in exchange for a clean structure and active pieces is fine.

notes.text: This check looks active, but White answers Bd2 and after ...Be7 the bishop has lost time and White finishes his…
notes.original: This check looks active, but White answers Bd2 and after ...Be7 the bishop has lost time and White finishes his development with tempo. The game becomes near equal, so you throw away your best chance.

notes.text: The queen eyes b4 and b7, but ...c5 defends the bishop and hits d4 at once, so you answer the…
notes.original: The queen eyes b4 and b7, but ...c5 defends the bishop and hits d4 at once, so you answer the threat with a counter-threat. Then recapture on c5 and develop the knight to c6.

notes.text: You are fully developed, the bishop pair is active on c5, and you have a slight edge.
notes.original: You are fully developed, the bishop pair is active on c5, and you have a slight edge. Aim for ...Nf6 and short castling next. This is an open game with the centre cleared and both sides developed, and you are a little more comfortable. Your c5 bishop is attacked by the knight on e4, so your first step is to move it with ...Be7 or ...Bb6. Second, trade White's best piece with ...Nf6, recapturing on f6 with the queen or pawn as needed. Third, castle short and bring the rooks to the centre. White wants to use the queen on b3 against b7 and e6, so keep both pawns covered. The risk is leaving b7 or the bishop hanging in one move. If White plays Bg5 or Nf3, continue your development.

notes.text: Take on e4 and then ...exf3, stripping White of his centre pawn.
notes.original: Take on e4 and then ...exf3, stripping White of his centre pawn. After Nd2 exf3 Ngxf3 you have the better structure, since e4 and f3 have gone. Your plan is ...Nf6, ...c5 to undermine d4, bishop to e7 or d6 and castle short. Avoid leaving the pawn on e4 under attack from too many pieces. The edge is small.

notes.text: A fine alternative, but White gets an easy position with Bd3 and Ne2, and the advantage drops to about equal.
Strike at the centre now, before White castles.
Your pieces come out smoothly, you have a good structure, and you can aim for ...Bd6 and ...O-O with a…
notes.original: Your pieces come out smoothly, you have a good structure, and you can aim for ...Bd6 and ...O-O with a comfortable game. This is an open, healthy position with the f- and e-pawns exchanged, so you have the better structure and a smooth, comfortable game. Your plan is, first, to complete development with ...Nc6 hitting the knight on d4. Second, play ...Bd6 and castle short, aiming at the h2 pawn. Third, use the half-open c-file and the knight on f6 to pressure White's centre. White wants Nf5 or Nxe6 with Bxh7 ideas against your king. The risk is leaving e6 loose or letting Bxh7 work when your f6 knight leaves. If White plays Nb3, answer calmly with ...Bd6 or ...Be7, but do not lose time.

notes.text: 4.a4 is White's most testing try, gaining a tempo on a future ...a5/...Qb4 ideas while defending b2 indirectly; after 4...e5…
notes.original: 4.a4 is White's most testing try, gaining a tempo on a future ...a5/...Qb4 ideas while defending b2 indirectly; after 4...e5 the position opens into a sharper fight than the main 3...e6 lines.

notes.text: 4.c3 - the quieter alternative to 4.a4, supporting the center and ignoring the pressure on b2 for now.
4.Nc3 - simply develops instead of committing to a3/c3 right away, daring Black to take on b2 for real.
4.a3 stops ...Bb4 but wastes time.
notes.original: 4.a3 stops ...Bb4 but wastes time. 4...e5! gives Black a strong initiative.

notes.text: The lever hits d4 at once: the pawn has lost support because f3 blocks the g1 knight, so White has…
notes.original: The lever hits d4 at once: the pawn has lost support because f3 blocks the g1 knight, so White has to resolve the centre right away. After exd5 you take on d4 with the queen, offer a queen trade, and the pawn count is soon level again.

notes.text: Your pawn on d4 cramps the white pieces and the knight on a3 is trying to find a good square,…
notes.original: Your pawn on d4 cramps the white pieces and the knight on a3 is trying to find a good square, so you are fine.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White is clearly better.
The calmer route costs you a tempo with the queen and leaves White a little more comfortable.
4...e5! strikes back in the center immediately, exploiting the tempo White spent on move 2 (f3) rather than development; Black…
notes.original: 4...e5! strikes back in the center immediately, exploiting the tempo White spent on move 2 (f3) rather than development; Black already stands slightly better here.

notes.text: The a4-a5 jab chases your queen back, but White has spent time on it while you take the centre pawns.
notes.original: The a4-a5 jab chases your queen back, but White has spent time on it while you take the centre pawns. You win a pawn on e4, which White recaptures quickly, and the position is level.

notes.text: a safe route into a queenless position where you stay comfortable.
The position is equal.
Black is winning.
Black is slightly better.
4...e6 is the calmest and best-scoring reply: finish development and let White prove the pawn grab on b2 is worth…
notes.original: 4...e6 is the calmest and best-scoring reply: finish development and let White prove the pawn grab on b2 is worth anything (it generally isn't, since Qxb2 walks into Nb5 or Rb1 tricks).

notes.text: White's a3 takes b4 from your bishop and queen and prepares Na4 to harass the queen.
notes.original: White's a3 takes b4 from your bishop and queen and prepares Na4 to harass the queen. Your answer is to blast open the centre with ...e5 before White is ready: the pawn on d5 is given back for play, because f3 weakened the e1-h4 diagonal (...Bh4+ ideas) and your knight heads to f5 to hit d4. After Na4 the queen steps out of the attack. You have comfortable play for the pawn.

notes.text: The quieter Qd2 and b3 plan lets you develop with ...Bg4 and equalise.
White recaptures with the pawn and keeps a big centre on d4 and e4 with an open f-file.
notes.original: White recaptures with the pawn and keeps a big centre on d4 and e4 with an open f-file. The idea is to build with Nf3, Bd3 and Qe2, and to attack with e5 and Bc4 later. It is common in practice (played in about 49,000 games in the online database). It means White has a big centre, so you must hit it before it becomes a wall.

notes.text: The bishop pair is safe and Black's king can castle comfortably.
The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Strike the centre at once.
notes.original: Strike the centre at once. After dxe5 your queen is not hit, and after Nf3 exd4 you reach an easy ending. Your plan is simple: exchange queens, play ...Bd6 and ...Ne7 with your king on its home square, and enjoy the healthy pawn structure. Avoid delaying, since a pawn on e4 backed by d4 gives White a free hand.

notes.text: The natural developing move is a mistake here.
notes.original: The natural developing move is a mistake here. White plays 6.e5 and the knight is kicked, so you lose the centre and fall behind in development.

notes.text: Your bishop comes to d6 and then e5 to hit the knight on c3 and the pawn on b2.
The bishop is strong in the centre.
notes.original: The bishop is strong in the centre. Next you play ...Ne7, ...Nd7 and ...Nf6 or ...Bg4 and you can castle long, with a level ending.

notes.text: After the queens go off you are equal, with ...Ne7 and ...Be5 to come and no weaknesses to worry about.
notes.original: After the queens go off you are equal, with ...Ne7 and ...Be5 to come and no weaknesses to worry about. This is an open, queenless position with no centre pawns for you and a lone e4 pawn for White, so activity matters more than structure. Your bishop on e5 is attacked by the knight on f3, so settle it first: trade with ...Bxc3+ bxc3 to wreck White's queenside pawns, or retreat to c7 or f6. Then play ...Ne7, ...Nd7 and ...Nf6 or ...Bg4, and castle long or short. White wants Bc4, Be3 and Rd1 to use the open d-file; put a rook on d8 to answer. The mistake is leaving the bishop to be hit with tempo. If White plays Bf4, trade bishops.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White retakes with the queen to develop quickly and hit the f-file, but this loses the d4 pawn.
notes.original: White retakes with the queen to develop quickly and hit the f-file, but this loses the d4 pawn. Nxf3 was the correct move, so you should be ready to punish this common mistake.

notes.text: By far the most common try here, well ahead of 6.Bd3 above.
notes.original: By far the most common try here, well ahead of 6.Bd3 above. The same position comes from the Von Hennig Gambit via 4.Bc4 Nf6 5.f3 exf3 6.Nxf3 (see Part Three's Von Hennig branch below, which transposes straight back here).

notes.text: A developing move that aims at c7 and prepares Qd2 and long castling.
Black is just a clean pawn up, with a safe and comfortable position and no weaknesses to show for it.
Black keeps the extra pawn and has traded off White's best attacking piece.
notes.original: Black keeps the extra pawn and has traded off White's best attacking piece. The plan from here is simple: ...Nbd7, ...Qc7 and castle.

notes.text: Black's best and most natural try, developing actively before White can castle.
The same improving move as in the Rasa-Studier line.
notes.original: The same improving move as in the Rasa-Studier line. Black develops the bishop and prepares ...e6, keeping the extra pawn. White's sharpest try is 7.Ne5 e6 8.g4, to which Black must reply 8...Nfd7!, while 7.Nh4 Bg4 is harmless.

notes.text: Solid but noticeably less ambitious than 6...Bf5 - safe, but gives back a good chunk of Black's edge for no…
notes.original: Solid but noticeably less ambitious than 6...Bf5 - safe, but gives back a good chunk of Black's edge for no real reason.

notes.text: Watch out: this looks like the same natural developing move as in the 6.Bd3 line above, but here it runs…
notes.original: Watch out: this looks like the same natural developing move as in the 6.Bd3 line above, but here it runs into a real tactic - a very common practical mistake.

notes.text: The most dangerous try: the knight hits f7 and the bishop on f5 loses its retreat square.
A less dangerous alternative that also hits the bishop immediately.
White now attacks the bishop with the g-pawn.
The only good reply: Black challenges the knight and keeps the bishop.
Hitting the bishop is natural, but it walks into trouble.
White has won a bishop for the pawn but the white king is stuck in the middle and Black keeps…
notes.original: White has won a bishop for the pawn but the white king is stuck in the middle and Black keeps the initiative.

notes.text: Black has won a bishop back but the king is exposed on the open f-file and White's pieces flood forward.
The bishop is safe on h5 and the extra pawn is intact; White has not found a good way to…
notes.original: The bishop is safe on h5 and the extra pawn is intact; White has not found a good way to use the lead in development.

notes.text: The point: this sacrifices the bishop back, but opens the king up for a second strike.
Forced - there's nothing better.
The only move that actually cashes in the sacrifice - White's other tries here (8.h3 or 8.Bd2, say) just hand…
notes.original: The only move that actually cashes in the sacrifice - White's other tries here (8.h3 or 8.Bd2, say) just hand the advantage straight back and leave White clearly worse instead.

notes.text: Black can take a second pawn, but White's lead in development means it must be done accurately.
notes.original: Black can take a second pawn, but White's lead in development means it must be done accurately. The safe approach is to keep the structure intact with ...Nbd7 and ...Be7.

notes.text: You take the pawn and your queen lands in the centre, attacking the knight and the b2 area.
notes.original: You take the pawn and your queen lands in the centre, attacking the knight and the b2 area. Your plan is ...Nf6 and ...Bg4 to develop with tempo, and ...e6 to castle. Avoid taking pawns further and leaving your queen offside.

notes.text: White may instead try 6.Nb5, hoping to catch the queen out of position, but your queen retreats with ...Qb6 or…
notes.original: White may instead try 6.Nb5, hoping to catch the queen out of position, but your queen retreats with ...Qb6 or ...Qe5 while still being a pawn up. Do not rush and keep your king safe by castling soon. After the queen trade you only need to keep developing. You are a clean pawn up and White has little compensation. This is an open game where you are a clean pawn up and White has only some activity, with your queen in the centre and both kings short of safety. Your plan: develop with ...e6, ...Be7 and ...Nbd7, challenge the queen on h4 with ...Be7 at a good moment, and castle short. White wants to bring the pieces out and attack with Ng5, Bxh7 and Nb5 against your queen. Meet Nb5 by retreating ...Qa5 or ...Qd8 quickly. The risk is being greedy: do not grab b2 or d4 with the queen, because White gets tempi against it. If White plays Nb5 first, retreat and keep your extra pawn.

notes.text: This is a calmer path, but you are still clearly better.
Simplest and best: just finish development and meet whatever comes next.
Watch out: this natural-looking developing move walks straight into a forced mate.
Kicking the bishop at once is a good alternative to 4...Nf6.
Natural-looking, but it runs into 5.g4!
White's most natural try, developing the last minor piece before deciding what to do about the missing pawn.
By far White's most common try here (over ten times as popular as 5.Nge2 below) - and this is the…
notes.original: By far White's most common try here (over ten times as popular as 5.Nge2 below) - and this is the real main line of the whole gambit complex, not 5.Nge2.

notes.text: Black continues developing, a clean pawn up with no real weaknesses.
Kicking the bishop gains space, and it leaves the knight on e2 awkwardly placed.
The knight on a4 is offside and Black keeps the pawn comfortably.
Simplest and best - take the second pawn too.
Back into the main position of the Rasa-Studier Gambit (reached there via 4.f3 exf3 5.Nxf3 Nf6 6.Bc4) - see that…
notes.original: Back into the main position of the Rasa-Studier Gambit (reached there via 4.f3 exf3 5.Nxf3 Nf6 6.Bc4) - see that branch above (under 3.Nc3) for the full tree, including the 6...Bf5! recommendation and the 6...Bg4? trap. There is no need to learn this twice; it is the identical position either way.

notes.text: The point: nothing currently covers f7, so this threatens mate in one.
Forced, and just about sufficient - the queen gets chased off and Black keeps the extra pawn.
The losing mistake: this natural-looking developing move still does not cover f7.
Checkmate.
Black keeps the extra pawn and the queenside pawns have gained space.
White gets real play for the pawn, and the position is level.
notes.original: White gets real play for the pawn, and the position is level. Playable, but worse than 4...Nf6.

notes.text: The most popular try in practice: simple development, no immediate tactics.
The point missed above: e6 stops the bishop check but not this one.
notes.original: The point missed above: e6 stops the bishop check but not this one. Very popular in practice, and for good reason - the only safe square is narrow and two natural-looking tries fail badly.

notes.text: No longer check (the e6 pawn blocks the diagonal), just another developing try.
A developing move that heads for long castling and keeps the Ne5+ trick up White's sleeve.
Black is clearly better.
White tries the knight jump anyway, now that the bishop on d3 supports it.
White's pieces look active, but Black's bishop on c5 aims at f2 and ...Qa5+ will come with tempo, so Black…
notes.original: White's pieces look active, but Black's bishop on c5 aims at f2 and ...Qa5+ will come with tempo, so Black remains clearly better.

notes.text: The only move that keeps the full advantage.
notes.original: The only move that keeps the full advantage. Simple and safe - the king has no further checks to worry about from here.

notes.text: Watch out: this natural-looking retreat gives back almost all of the advantage and then some.
Watch out: this one loses material outright, not just the advantage - the king walks into a fork.
Develop first and keep the knight jump Ng6 in reserve.
Hitting the e6 pawn and trying to pile pressure on the king's diagonal.
The best way to meet unsound gambits is to play actively: ...c5 invites a queen exchange and challenges White's structure…
notes.original: The best way to meet unsound gambits is to play actively: ...c5 invites a queen exchange and challenges White's structure immediately.

notes.text: Also fine: the queen attacks the knight on g6 and protects the rook on h8 from behind the king.
White trades queens to relieve the pressure.
Piling on the e6 pawn.
Black forces White to capture and gets ahead in development.
The white king has lost castling and Black has the bishop pair and the more active pieces.
After the dust settles Black has an extra piece for a pawn and a safe king.
White has won the exchange back and material is roughly level, but the black knights are well placed and White's…
notes.original: White has won the exchange back and material is roughly level, but the black knights are well placed and White's king is stuck in the centre.

notes.text: Material is now roughly level on paper (a rook and pawn for two knights), but Black's pieces are far more…
notes.original: Material is now roughly level on paper (a rook and pawn for two knights), but Black's pieces are far more active and White's king is still in the centre, so Black keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: Black's king is safe on g8 and White has nothing left to attack with.

notes.original: White has castled and traded a pair of knights, but Black is still a piece for a pawn up and the c6 and e6 pawns hold everything together.

notes.original: Black has finished development and the king can tuck into g8 whenever needed. White has pieces out but nothing to hit. The extra piece decides.

notes.text: White has traded off the attacking knights and the queens come off.
notes.original: White has traded off the attacking knights and the queens come off. Black is a piece for a pawn up in a very simple ending and just needs to bring the king and bishop pair into play.

notes.text: White is winning.

notes.original: Black keeps the extra piece and can castle by hand with ...Kg8, but there is less to show for it than in the main lines.

notes.original: The knight escapes the pin with check, and the bishop that was pinning it is left hanging. The pattern to remember: with the king on f7 any pin on the f3-knight can be answered by Ne5+.

notes.text: Black has developed everything with tempo and the king is safe behind the pawns.
notes.original: Black has developed everything with tempo and the king is safe behind the pawns. It is still a clear edge, just slightly less than the main lines, so it is a reasonable choice if you prefer a calm game.

notes.text: Simplest: block the check by developing the other bishop, offering a trade on White's terms.
Also sound: the pawn blocks the diagonal and keeps the king on f7.
White trades down rather than retreat, since the bishop has no better square anyway.
Correct and only real choice: recapture with the king.
notes.original: Correct and only real choice: recapture with the king. It looks bold marching the king to e6, but there are no immediate checks available and Black's king is perfectly safe there with queens still on.

notes.text: Watch out: retreating instead of recapturing gives back almost the entire advantage for nothing.
Watch out: this one doesn't just give back the advantage, it walks straight into a forced mate.
The king goes back to f7 as soon as the checks have run out, and Black trades queens into an…
notes.original: The king goes back to f7 as soon as the checks have run out, and Black trades queens into an ending where the extra piece is decisive.

notes.text: Checkmate.
Black has an extra piece for a pawn and White has not developed much real pressure.
notes.original: Black has an extra piece for a pawn and White has not developed much real pressure. 7...Be6 is simpler, but this is perfectly good.

notes.text: The key reply.
notes.original: The key reply. Black offers to trade off White's only attacking piece. Without the light-squared bishop White has almost nothing left against the king.

notes.text: White has spent its whole attack and Black has all the extra material.
White keeps the sacrificed piece and wins a whole rook.
notes.original: White keeps the sacrificed piece and wins a whole rook. The lesson for Black: when the sacrifice is unsound, take the knight. All the traps below come only after 6...Kxf7.

notes.text: Black has the more comfortable endgame, with the bishop pair and no weaknesses.
Black is a whole knight up for a pawn.
notes.original: Black is a whole knight up for a pawn. The knight on g5 had no retreat once Black spent a tempo on ...h6, which is exactly why 6.Nxf7 or 6.N5f3 are the only real choices.

notes.text: You kick the knight at once, and it has only h3 as a decent retreat.
notes.original: You kick the knight at once, and it has only h3 as a decent retreat. After Nh3 you play ...c5 and ...e6, hitting the centre while the White knights sit on poor squares on h3 and f4. Your plan is ...Nbd7, ...Be7, castle short and ...a6. Avoid blocking your own light bishop and avoid ...e5 early, because the d4 pawn is not yet weak. The small edge is yours.

notes.text: Do not be afraid of Bb5+: you answer with ...Nbd7 and then ...a6 pushes the bishop back, since your king…
notes.original: Do not be afraid of Bb5+: you answer with ...Nbd7 and then ...a6 pushes the bishop back, since your king is safe in the centre until you castle. You have more active pieces, a healthy centre and an easy plan of ...Be7 and castling. This is an open-ish position where you hold a healthy centre and White's knights on f3 and f4 stand a little awkwardly, though your king is still in the middle. Your plan: complete development with ...Be7, castle short, and then play ...Qc7 and ...Rac8 so that ...cxd4 can come at the right moment. White wants to trade light-squared bishops with Bxf5 and open the centre with dxc5; recapture ...exf5 and keep the structure solid, or take back on c5 with a knight. The risk is the Nxe6 shot if your bishop leaves f5 carelessly. If White plays dxc5 at once, take back with ...Nxc5 and trade bishops.

notes.text: This is the tempting reply many players choose, but White trades your bishop and gets a stable centre, so you…
notes.original: This is the tempting reply many players choose, but White trades your bishop and gets a stable centre, so you only equalise.

notes.text: The sharp 6.Bc4 b5! gains space and keeps the bishop under pressure.
notes.original: The sharp 6.Bc4 b5! gains space and keeps the bishop under pressure. After 7.Bb3 e6 8.O-O Ngf6 Black has no problems.

notes.original: The critical test: White finally plays a real central move, though a full tempo behind a normal Exchange Variation because of the wasted g4. 4.c3 and 4.h3 score almost identically.

notes.text: Simplest, just developing.
notes.original: Simplest, just developing. 4...h5 first, hitting the overextended pawn immediately, is about as good.

notes.text: Black attacks the overextended g-pawn at once with ...h5.
notes.original: Black attacks the overextended g-pawn at once with ...h5. After g5 the pawn is cut off from support, the f5 square is firm for Black, and the break ...e5 opens the centre while White is still undeveloped.

notes.original: ...and the position is close to equal; the g4-h4 pawns give White some practical kingside space but Black's development is completely normal.

notes.original: The calmest reply, keeping the bishop safe rather than inviting g4-g5 or h4-h5 ideas against it on f5. 4...Be6 and 4...Bc8 give White a small but real plus instead.

notes.original: ...and White gets a small, real edge, the one try on this list worth remembering by name rather than just dismissing.

notes.original: The most direct try, grabbing extra space at once while the h5 pawn has already committed White's kingside. Simple development (4...Nd7, 4...e6) is just as sound.

notes.original: A natural-looking try, but it's a real blunder: capturing on d5 clears Black's own d-pawn off the c8-g4 diagonal, leaving the queen on g4 completely undefended on that same diagonal.
